# Volume I. Treatise I. Section I. Part I. Book I.

...all things were created and preserved both in the Archetypal world <note>The "Archetypal World" is the original blueprint or divine model of the universe existing in the mind of God.</note> and in this Typical one <note>The "Typical World" refers to the physical universe which serves as a reflection or "type" of the divine original.</note>.
Indeed, we see that the Holy, Holy, Holy Unity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which was first contracted within itself in the secret and mystical Archetypal World, has now (I say) expanded itself into a Trinity. It has sketched the image of a purely formal world within itself, so that according to that model, the material world might later be brought forth into the light from shapeless matter and potential (as if from unformed clay), and might be ordered in a triple proportion according to the image of the Trinity. For just as the **World is distinguished into three regions differing by nature** according to the dimensions of quantity—namely, the **Empyrean, the Ethereal, and the Elementary** <note>The Empyrean is the highest heaven of pure fire/spirit; the Ethereal is the middle heaven of the stars and planets; the Elementary is the lowest realm of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>—so too that Harmony, by which the structures of the World are joined together in harmonious peace, consists of three consonances: namely, the **Octave** <note>original: *Diapason*</note>, which in its perfection corresponds to the Empyrean Spirit; the **Fifth** <note>original: *Diapente*</note>, which is assigned to the Ethereal Spirit in its lesser perfection; and the **Fourth** <note>original: *Diateffaron*</note>, which, as it is the most imperfect of all consonances, seems most appropriately compared in its tone to the Elementary Spirit.

<margin>Pimander, 10</margin>
But *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic.</note> (that divine high priest) seems to commemorate this whole matter in a few words in this manner: *All things (he says) depend on one principle; the Principle is from the One alone. And: the Principle moves so that it may again exist as a Principle; yet it remains the One itself, nor does it depart from Unity.* These are his words. He then recounts that the world and man were afterwards made and formed in the image of these things. I shall now show how that material and sensible world was formed according to the Model of the aforementioned properties of the formal or archetypal world. <margin>Asclepius, 4</margin> The Will of the divine Monad, while still contracting its rays within itself, is that supreme perfection which Necessity itself follows. Moreover, effect accompanies Necessity. Just as the nature of the *Monad*—the radical and most ancient Principle—is said to be its counsel, and the nature of its will is supreme goodness, so it is certain that this Most Holy will is born of counsel, and that the act of "willing" comes from the will itself. He who is the fullest of all things does not desire anything excessively, and the things He wills, He possesses, insofar as all things are within Him.

It was therefore in His mind to fashion the sensible World according to the model of that Archetypal or intelligible world, and the effect immediately followed the will; for He said, "**Let it be made**" <note>original: *Fiat*</note>, and straightaway the vocal emanation occurred (accompanied by an immense and most pleasant light). By its presence, Light was divided from the Darkness, and the unformed waters once hidden in the abyss of darkness were revealed. By reflecting itself into the shapeless matter, the union of divine form with unformed matter was achieved through the third property, from which the created Light is said to have taken its origin. By this means, the threefold disposition and property was turned toward the creation of the sensible world into the unity of the World, in the same way that this sensible World was made the son of the eternal Monad or Archetypal World, seeing as God Himself is its father. For this reason, then, this *world* is called a "second *God*" by Hermes—not in an absolute sense, but through its participation in the Divine goodness, which is God Himself. For it exists in Eternity, or the Word, in no other way than Eternity exists in the most ancient Monad itself, or as the Son in the Father.

### CHAPTER III.

->*In which the arrangement of the second Unity or the manifest God is discussed, as far as the author’s ability allows: where it is also proved that this second Unity differs no less from the primary Monad (though both are one and the same in Essence) than a ray differs from the Sun. ---

Since this most holy Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate "One"—the singular, absolute principle of God before creation.</note> is in and through itself its own Root, Square, and Cube <note>These geometrical terms represent the dimensions of divinity: the 'Root' is the point/line, the 'Square' is the plane, and the 'Cube' is the solid, symbolizing the fullness of God's being.</note>, and yet remains one and the same indivisible and purely formal Being, not at all exceeding the breadth of its own Unity (from which the intelligible, archetypal, and purely formal World takes its beginning, and is nothing other than God himself, arising from, in, and through himself); nevertheless, when it was in His mind to create the sensible world according to His own image, the end and effect immediately followed His will. For God proceeded to produce the sensible fabric of the world, not by contracting His radical unity within Himself, but by expanding it into a Second Unity. Yet, both of these unities are but one single and individual Essence, and the same root of all things; so that the Son, leaping forth from the Father, remains in the Father, and again governs those things which belong to the Father from without. For the paternal Root is the fountain of the filial Square, and the radical form of the Father is the Square of the son; and although both of these are contained by no physical quantity, yet by reason of the divine property of final proportion and number, we can refer these Unities to those Geometrical terms, and not without reason.

<margin>John 1.</margin>
The Father, therefore, or the radical Unity, is the power of the Son, or the first-born Unity; while the Son is the beauty of the Father. Therefore, the second Unity, together with its **Wisdom** (which that primary Unity poured forth from its hidden and ineffable bosom), remains in its root, although derived from it, so that it may govern all created things by His all-knowing spirit. For the union of the offspring is inseparable in the parent, and the parent is in the offspring. Thus, the ineffable offspring, shining with the most pleasant light, is brought forth into the light through a wonderful birth by the counsel of the ineffable Father, who hides in secret, to make manifest the hidden things of the World. Indeed, this offspring is itself the mature counsel dwelling with the Father; it is, as it were, the very will of the Father leaping from the Father’s bosom. Neither time nor age ever knew or understood its beginning, because it is that very Eternity, consisting in the Father and appearing together with the Father, eternally born as that which was destined to be born. In this way, the power of the paternal Monad was infused into the most splendid Son; the divine Counsel itself was born—an ineffable middle nature which exists before all other natures, a sacred birth, an ineffable fetus, the bright Word <note>original: *verbum*</note>, the holy Speech <note>original: *sermo*</note>, infinite eternity, the living nature of the father, existing in the beginning, in God and with God, and God himself; remaining eternally.

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
And so that renowned **Wisdom** arose—the root of all things, the seed of fertility and generation, the maker of the entire world, the pure emanation (I say) of the clarity of the one God, the brightness and splendor of eternal light, and the mirror without blemish of the Majesty of the primary Monad now expanded, and the manifest image of that hidden goodness and beauty. In its clarity and perfection of light, it is to be placed many infinite degrees above the stars and the Sun.

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
Therefore, this is the true light of the world, illuminating all things in the world both intellectually and sensibly. It is single and simple in its arrangement, yet manifold in its properties and operations, possessing all power within itself. It is more mobile than all mobile things, and yet it adheres firmly and without end to its root and the immobile fountain from which it arose. It penetrates and passes through all Beings, reaching everywhere because of its purity and sharpness. It is the sole actor in the world, the mover of creatures, the shaper and illuminator of all things, and the driver away of darkness by its own clarity.

Yet, he is no more divided from the unity of the Father than a ray of the Sun is divided from the unity of the Sun. We conclude, therefore, that this first-born Emanation—this property and secondary monad, which is not at all distinct or divided from its first origin—is the *Intellectual Fire*. It does not possess a form within itself, *since it is, in itself, from itself, and through itself, the simplest form; yet it transforms all things into itself, desiring to assimilate itself to all things and all things to itself*. From this, it is clear to see that *it is all things in that respect; all things are from it, and all things exist by its will*. And (to speak with the Apostle) *from it, through it, and in it are all things*; namely, multifaceted qualities and quantities, however great, and all magnitudes exceeding measure and every form of species. Finally, the entire sensible world and the things within it were covered and everywhere imbued by the superior and purely formal world as if by a most brilliant garment. For this same reason, Hermes called it the *Place in which the world is contained*, concluding therefrom that the place containing the world was not born at all, since he makes it eternal with God. And just as he acknowledges the world to be in some respect "begotten" or created, when considering the material nature of the workmanship, so too he makes the workmanship itself not born, but eternal, when looking at its inner truth—by the mediation and presence of which the world was such as it is now. For Hyla <note>original: "Hyla," from the Greek "hylē," meaning the fundamental, unformed matter of the universe.</note> and the world-spirit and this divine power, moving and diffused through all things, were not present in the physical construction of the world [at first], but were already present in that place from which they had to be born—that is, in the holy radical Monad. In the power of this Monad, although it is one, there resides both the matter of the world and its form: the matter (I say) is moist or watery, reserved in the power of God (the holy, hidden Monad contracted within itself), or the *dark Aleph* <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the "Number One" or God. Although this [Wisdom] is one and the same with its root, it nevertheless spreads itself into a multitude in a wondrous way. In truth, the watery mass of the world is no less divided from its whole than the form is from its luminous source: for although they seem to differ in density and rarity, and appear to be divided into infinite particles (just as a genus is divided into its species, and species into the individuals subject to them), yet in the truth of the matter, the parts of the world-spirit are continuous with their whole. It is no different than drops of water within the entire mass of the sea, or a portion of Air within the immense spirit of the world. For whatever is found in this world, whether rare or dense, cannot be divided or separated from the world-spirit; because if this were ever to happen, it would then follow that a Vacuum would be admitted into the nature of things, which is impossible.

Therefore, having accurately considered these things, we shall see that all things are one, and one is all things; namely, one matter according to the pattern of God (the one monad lurking within itself), and one form according to the image of the manifest monad; wherefore both matter and form...

form seem to be this very same thing, made in the image of that hidden and radical unity or <term>monad</term> <note>From the Greek 'monas,' meaning 'unit' or 'one.' In this philosophy, it represents the indivisible Source of everything.</note> considered only in and by itself—namely, as having no regard for anything else. And by this reasoning, it is right to see how all things are one and one is all things; and although all things seem to be distinguished by number, yet if we look into the matter with a sharper mental gaze, we will perceive that number itself is nothing except the dilation of that same luminous Unity into the depth of Matter. Consequently, it is said, not without consideration, that one contains all things. For example: that Unity penetrates every number by its own simplicity, and contains every number joined within itself; similarly, it is the fountain and origin of all multitude, remaining always the same and immutable, as will be clearly enough declared from these points. 

First, it must be noted that Unity, when multiplied by itself, produces nothing but itself <note>original: "in ſe multiplicata nihil producat niſi ſeipſam"</note>: for it is indivisible, insofar as it lacks all parts. If unity is added to unity, you find nothing but Unity; similarly, a third Unity joined to a second will give birth to nothing but Unity. And so you will find that unity is nothing besides a single thing, which, by dilating itself, seems to chain and unite all numbers. For this reason, some have called Unity "concord," others "piety," and others "friendship." Both Martianus <note>Likely Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author who wrote on the liberal arts.</note> and Aristotle called it the true <term>Desire</term> <note>original: "Cupidinem." In this context, it refers to the cosmic force of attraction or Eros that holds the universe together.</note> of the world; inasmuch as its nature is to be one and alone, to be sought and desired, always willing and finding nothing beyond itself, it turns the proper rays of its own heat back upon itself. 

Hence, therefore, this is the beginning and end of all things: the <term>Alpha and Omega</term> <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the totality of God.</note>, having neither beginning nor end, insofar as nothing is before the one, and nothing is after the one. By this it is argued that it is the principle of all things, and that all things exist up to the one, and beyond it, there is nothing. And all things that exist desire this "one," because all things proceeded from the one, participate in the one, and consist and are sustained in the one; they remain in their being, both material and formal, and finally they strive most greatly to return into the nature of unity, insofar as they first emanated from it. For according to that ancient <term>Axiom</term> <note>A self-evident truth or established principle.</note>: *As the beginning of a thing was, so shall its end be;* <note>original: "Quale erat rei initium, talis erit ipſius finis"</note> which indeed will be best perfected by gradually laying aside multitude and number, and by slowly contracting all unities into their Center. For just as all things were derived from the divine Monad by multiplying, so conversely, all things tend toward God by subtracting—namely, by their resolution into their radical unity. 

Thus the world and all things that have arisen in the world and were produced by creation, so it will be necessary for all things existing in the world and the nature of things to finally be reduced and resolved into the cycle of the primary monad by dissolving and diminishing; and this is done by the operation of the luminous unity, divinely emanating and sent forth from the fountain of all Entity and Existence, and finally by the contraction of that sent-forth light into its own center.

Behold here two properties, in every way opposite to the human imagination, which arise and are derived from the single essence of the one Monad and the inscrutable fountain of eternity: namely, **darkness**, the primary covering of unformed matter and <term>hyle</term> <note>A Greek term for "prime matter," the raw, formless substance of the universe before God gave it shape.</note> existing only in potentiality; and **light**, whose role it is likewise to imbue the unformed and gloomy matter of the world with a luminous form and to cover and encompass all created things—that is, things brought into actuality by its presence—with light as if with a garment. It remains now for us to descend from the Monad to the condition of the <term>Dyad</term> <note>The number two, representing duality, division, or the first step away from the absolute unity of God.</note>, which, just as it is composed of two unities, so indeed each of them is of a nature quite opposite to the other.

# Of the Super-celestial Origin of Life and Health.

...in form, <note>original: "forma"; this completes the thought from the previous page regarding the "Intellectual Fire."</note> these things seem to be this same thing according to the image of the hidden and radical unity or <term>monad</term> <note>From the Greek 'monas,' meaning 'unit' or 'oneness.' Consequently, it is said, not without consideration, that the One contains all things.

This shall be declared clearly enough from these points: First, it must be noted that Unity, multiplied by itself, produces nothing but itself; for it is indivisible, insofar as it is devoid of all parts. If unity be added to unity, you will find nothing but Unity; similarly, a third Unity added to a second will give birth to nothing but Unity. And so you will find that unity is nothing except a single thing, which by dilating itself seems to chain and unite all numbers. 

For this reason, some have called Unity *concord*, others *piety*, others *friendship*; and <term>Martianus</term> <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century Latin author who wrote on the mathematical and mystical properties of numbers.</note> and Aristotle have called it the *true Desire of the world*; as it is the nature of the One to be alone, to be followed and desired; always willing and finding nothing beyond itself, it twists the proper rays of its own heat back into itself. Hence, therefore, this is the principle and end of all things: the **Alpha** and **Omega** <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end.</note>, having neither beginning nor end, insofar as nothing is prior to the One, and nothing is posterior to the One. By this argument, it is proved that the One is the principle of all things, and that all things exist up to the One, and beyond it, there is nothing. 

And all things that are desire the One itself, because all things proceeded from the One, participate in the One, consist and are sustained in the One; they remain in their being, both material and formal, within it; and finally, they strive greatly to return into the nature of unity, insofar as they first emanated from it. For according to that old <term>Axiom</term>: *As was the beginning of a thing, such shall be its end*; which indeed will be best perfected by gradually laying aside multitude and number, and by slowly contracting all unities into their Center. For just as all things were derived from the divine Monad by multiplying, so indeed, conversely, all things tend toward God by subtracting—that is, by their resolution into their radical unity. 

Thus the world and all things that have arisen in the world and were produced by creation—so it will be necessary for all things existing in the world and the nature of things to be finally reduced and resolved into the period of the primary monad by dissolving and diminishing. This is done by the operation of the radiant unity, divinely emanating and sent forth from the fountain of all Entity and Existence, and finally by the contraction of that light (emitted from God) back into its own center.

Behold here two properties, in every way opposite to the human imagination, arising and derived from the unique essence of the one Monad and the inscrutable fountain of eternity: namely, **darkness**—the primary covering of unformed matter and <term>hyle</term> <note>A Greek term for "primordial matter" or the raw "stuff" of the universe before it is given form.</note> existing only in potential—and **light**, whose role it is likewise to imbue the unformed and gloomy matter of the world with a radiant form and to cover and encompass all created things (that is, things brought into act by its presence) with light as if with a garment. It remains now for us to descend from the Monad to the condition of the **Dyad**, which, as it is composed of two unities, so indeed each of them is by nature quite opposite to the other.

### C H A P T E R IV.

->*In which the nature of the **Dyad** <note>original: "Dyadis"; the principle of duality or the number two.</note> is discussed: and it is clearly declared that it arises from a single Root.*<-

Indeed, the nature and condition of that abstruse and inscrutable primary **Monad** <note>The divine "Unity" or "One" discussed in the previous chapter.</note> surpasses all wonder and transcends the sense of Mortals; though it is one and the same, yet being impregnated with a seed, operation, and quality so varied, it was able to bring forth a living offspring so vastly different in essence and property: namely, **Darkness** and **Light**. But if we consider the matter with a somewhat more mature reflection, we—the children of light and life—will perceive that it is not so impossible to the mind, calling seriously to our memory that as it is the monad and the one, so indeed it can do all things and is "all in all"; and consequently, since both darkness and Light exist and have arisen, it is necessary that they be derived immediately from it, as from the sole principle of all things. And in respect to the root, which is one, the same, and eternal, those two are one and the same, even though to us mortals they seem to vary vastly in quality and nature.

<margin>Psalm 139:12</margin>
From this, therefore, it follows that God, or the primary Monad, is in every way and alone good, and is Goodness itself: so indeed this double offspring of His, in His presence, cannot wander from the goal and perfection of Goodness, though their goodness is regarded differently by Him. And this the Royal Psalmist <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> seems to acknowledge where he says, *that Darkness is to him even as Light itself*: as if he had said, All things are one in respect to God, who is the same and the one from whom all things come.

<margin>Wisdom 1:14</margin>
But truly, as for us who are penalized by the sensible distinction of multitude—as for us (I say) who, by the fall of Adam, eat continuously from the tree of Good and Evil, and think to distinguish good from evil by reason of their different effects—as for us, the children of uncreated light, who are accustomed to be led astray and wander by the error of darkness; for us (I say), whose inner and mental eyes were closed because of the sin of our first parents' disobedience, so that we now judge and are accustomed to look at all things with external eyes only as far as the surface; for us (I say), things are therefore thought to be evil, and are believed to work poorly for us, which in truth seem not at all to differ from the single essence and nature (which is absolutely good) of the Monad and Unity, or of the hidden and manifest God. Therefore, He Himself made neither death nor evil, nor did He delight in the affliction and destruction of the living; for He created all things that they might exist, and from His goodness, He imparted to His Creatures that they might be well. Whence He made the nations of the earth healthy, in which there is no medicine of destruction, nor is there a kingdom of the underworld upon the earth. For He Himself created all things living and actually existing by the stretching forth of His own bright property; and among all others, He adorned humans with reason and intellect, so that they, considering themselves to be the children of the bright principle, might walk sincerely in the light, lest they be led away into error by the veiling of the dark principle and be distracted from the paths of true light. Indeed, Adam experienced this difference between light and darkness not at all before his fall; inasmuch as he was kindly snatched up by the life-giving light of the goodness of the eternal monad, so that he was not at all occupied with multitude. But truly, by his disobedience, he fell from the disposition of the Monad into the sphere of the **binary number** <note>The "Dyad" or the state of duality and division.</note>; whence he was made a partaker of the action and passion of both Extremes: namely, of Darkness as well as of Light.

Hence it was, therefore, that the true son of light was first subjected to the passions of darkness and their prince, so that he who previously, without fear, could speak to God—or the Monad and Sole Being—and enjoy familiarity...

# On the super-celestial Origin of Life and Health.

...used to [possess], now struck by the numbness of darkness, he fled the face and voice of God, noticed that he himself was naked, and with a conscience now pricked and wounded, he recognized himself as a sinner, and feeling through experience, he perceived the snares of darkness. From this, therefore, arose the first distraction of the human race from unity into **duality** <note>original: "dualitatem"; the state of being divided into two, moving away from the perfection of the One.</note>; hence (I say) the unique and divine nature of man (insofar as it was made in the image of the uncreated **Monad** <note>The absolute, indivisible divine Unity.</note>) put on the **binary number** <note>The number two; in mystical philosophy, this represents the beginning of division, strife, and "confusion" because it departs from the number one.</note>, the number (I say) of confusion. This happened when the dark body itself—the most vile portion of man, which is nothing but a house of mud and earth for the true man—began to have dominion over its luminous Lord, namely his own Heaven; I mean the most beautiful Soul, which is a true image of the **Unity in the Trinity** <note>The Christian concept of God as three persons in one essence.</note>. And by this means, the foremost among mortals, the son of light or the revealed property of God, confounded himself with that hidden property of God, and thus rendered himself subject to death and evil of both soul and body—he who at first was enriched with immortality alongside the stars and Angels themselves. He became (I say) a partaker of good and evil, of light (I say) and darkness, who previously tasted only of the goodness of the light, or of the luminous fountain.

Hence it is that, although Light and Darkness are the same thing in the most ancient Monad of all—insofar as they were immediately birthed and derived from it, because the Monad is the most fruitful source of both sexes (for from its hidden and dark property, the **universal female** <note>Representing passive matter or the "womb" of the universe.</note> arose, just as conversely from the revealed and luminous form, the **universal Male** <note>Representing the active, shaping force of spirit and light.</note> emerged).

So indeed, after they were brought forth by an ineffable birth, they were made most opposite in nature in every way. For when these two meet, the Light, by strongly illuminating, drives away and resists the dark condition of the other; and Darkness, in turn, by resisting, tries to stain the rays of Light with its obscure gloom. The Light acts and penetrates into the bowels of the Darkness with an ineffable motion; the Darkness, by reacting and resisting, strives to repel its impulses. The Light swiftly pursues those foul shadows; the Darkness attempts to flee to the outermost places of rest, to contract itself within them, and to set itself in opposition against the Light's attacks. The Light strives with its greatest power and effort to prepare, illuminate, and cleanse from its deformed filth the moist matter hidden in the dark mass; the Darkness strives to seize that matter and hold it with a strong embrace. The Light seeks to create, inform, vivify, generate, cherish with heat, and retain things in being; the Darkness seeks to destroy the form by privation, to take away, kill, corrupt, and to hinder life and health with cold, making those endowed with life-giving spirit either languish or succumb to death. The Light brings position, health, and life—both momentary and eternal—and offers blessedness to its children; the Darkness threatens privation, infirmity, eternal death, and a reduction to mere nothingness.

But what are all these things but the one primary Monad, acting either through its Will or its No-Will? Whence neither Darkness nor Light are evil to it, insofar as they are acts of its **Unwillingness** <note>original: "Noluntatis"; the divine act of withdrawal or contraction that allows for "Nothingness" or "Darkness" to exist by the absence of Light.</note> or its **Will** <note>original: "Voluntatis".</note>. For when God does not will all things, it is necessary that all things cease to be, since in the instant of His Unwillingness He contracts Himself—that is, He pulls His Light back into Himself—and all things are converted into a deformed and dark Nothingness. And again, by His willing, in the blink of an eye, they were made by the emission of the **Emanation** <note>The flowing out of divine light to create the world.</note> which He willed to happen. Hence come the "goods" of living things: life, health, joy, love, piety, hope, and salvation. Hence again come the "evils" of those same things: death, disease, pain, sin, fear, and other passions of the mind; namely, from the double and different act of the one Monad: specifically, from its property that is either positive (affirming and willing) or its property that is privative (denying and unwilling). Thus we see this even in the act of the human mind, which is indivisible in itself and always the same in essence (as it is a spark of the indivisible Monad itself). We see that sometimes it wills, and at other times its property is not to will at all; whence it happens that if someone else asks or seeks something from it that is very necessary and convenient for them, and if the mind of the first person denies the petition of the requester...

For to the children of **Light**, the effects of **Darkness** seem evil and intolerable, and vice versa; for just as Light is opposed and most hostile to Darkness in every action, so also Darkness and its children seem to pursue those of Light with hatred in all things. This is clearly recounted in that **War** and fierce battle between **Michael** and the **Dragon**. <note>A reference to the celestial war in Revelation 12:7-9, representing the cosmic struggle between good and evil.</note>

And yet, all these things are truly one in God, and in reality are not nearly as terrible as they seem to us. Instead, it was so ordained by God that just as all things proceeded from one origin through multiplication, so indeed all things should return to that One by being drawn back and diminished. Therefore, nothing is evil in itself, because all things are truly one, which is the **highest good**. They do not belong to truth; they are deceptive and clearly nothing. In this way, **death** itself seems to mortals to be the most extreme of all evils; and yet, if we look at the matter to its very core with the eyes of the intellect, we will perceive that nothing of truth—and consequently nothing of the reality of the thing—is subject to corruption. 

Rather, certain false names disturb men; neither is **generation** <note>The process of coming into being or birth.</note> the creation of life, but the unfolding of a hidden life which is in the **Word** <note>original: "Verbo"; the Logos or Divine Reason.</note> and in God Himself. Nor is **death** a change, but rather a hiding. For this reason, nothing in the world dies; rather, composite things are dissolved. Dissolution, however, is not death, but the resolution of a mixture. The union is dissolved, not as things that perish, but as things that grow old. For imaginary death is, in truth, the beginning of a new life. 

Therefore, what seems evil and most wretched to the sufferer or to those standing by, is in truth a good to God, who works all things and works them well. Mortals, speaking in the manner of mortals, distinguish these two properties of the one stable and most firm **Monad** <note>The Monad represents the ultimate indivisible Unity of the Creator.</note> into "good" and "evil": calling it **good** because it bestows those manifest and bright qualities upon life and health—both of the soul and the body (which are the highest blessings to the living)—and calling it **evil** because that hidden and private property seems to bring death, pain, disease, and sin against the bright precepts of mortals. 

God, therefore, constituted **Man**—the noblest creature among all living things—from both natures: namely, from the dark, corporeal, and earthly nature (and consequently mortal), and from the bright, spiritual, celestial, and immortal nature. He did this so that man, made in the image of the primary **Monad** and participating in both its properties, might satisfy both of his origins: to wonder at and pray to celestial things, and to inhabit and govern earthly things. Thus, he may either adhere strongly to the divine mind—or the bright principle through which he lives—and live through the light, or, by subjecting himself to the dark part and immersing himself in the abyss of death and darkness, he may headlong plunge himself unexpectedly.

### CHAPTER V.

->*On the two foremost qualities of all, arising from those two Principles:*<-
->*And how the two properties of the one God are*<-
->*clearly derived from them.*<-

Although we have spoken quite extensively about the birth and origin of all primary qualities—namely, coldness and heat—in various places in our preceding works (specifically in *Chapter 7, Book 1 of the History of the Macrocosm*; *Chapter 4, Section 1 of the Meteorological Treatise*; and *Chapter 12, Book 1 and Chapter 6, Book 3 of our Cabalistic Discourse* <note>Robert Fludd is citing his own massive encyclopedic works, which sought to link the Bible, science, and the occult.</note>); nevertheless, we think it very necessary to revisit the discussion of them here and to explain their natures a little more accurately. We do this so you may more clearly perceive the immense difference between their natures, even though they flow from one and the same source.

First, therefore, I would have you know that **coldness** itself was the innate offspring—or rather the companion—of the deformed and dark mass. For this reason, that quality is least likely to depart from or leave behind the potential matter from the bowels of the dark **Chaos** <term>Chaos: The unformed, dark state of the universe before God's light organized it</term> unless the opposing quality (namely **heat**, the child of light itself) compels it. And yet, nonetheless, as the effect of heat recedes, coldness returns again by a certain natural inclination into its connatural subject, so that one of these is usually defined by the absence of the other. 

Nor indeed is it a wonder if only one of these qualities requires the absence of the other for its existence in watery matter, since both are most opposed to each other by nature and condition, in the manner of their parents. For it is certain and proven by daily experience that **heat**, the offspring of the bright principle itself, gathers things of the same kind <note>original: "homogénea congregat"</note> and, by dispersing things of different kinds, it warms, expands, refines or thins out, digests, ripens, exalts, fixes, and leads toward the goal of perfection. It fosters and is benevolent to the life of creatures; it is quite fast and lively in its activity, so that by penetrating and refining, it usually consumes, or rather dissolves things into very tiny parts. 

On the contrary, **coldness**, the offspring of the dark principle, is opposed in every thing to that bright lineage. Its role is to gather both things of the same kind and different kinds together, to thicken and make dense, to constrict and contract, to depress and pull to the bottom, to render things raw, immature, and imperfect. It destroys by "mortifying" (killing off), hinders the life of creatures, and, on account of its stupid and dull disposition, is quite slow and most devoted by natural inclination to rest—since it does not move unless it is incited by the impulse of heat.

The reason why there is such a great diversity between these primary natures can easily be drawn from the different conditions of their origins. For since the immediate cause of heat is **motion** (for it is hidden from no one that heat is excited by the liveliness of motion), it is certain that it took its origin from the bright source; namely, the holy spirit of **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientiæ"</note>, or the holy **Emanation**, brighter than the sun and stars, which is more mobile than all mobility, more lively and penetrating than any thing.

For insofar as that eternal spirit, by its bright virtue, acts toward the production of things...

...[generatio]n and preservation, it is likely that it is never idle, and consequently, by its constant action, it produces movement in the Moist Nature. Through the speed of this motion, it stirs up heat, and through heat, it refines, thins, and expands, bringing forth the other things we have mentioned. Conversely, since darkness—or empty and purely potential matter—is the parent and fountain of coldness, and since the primordial point of this dark principle is the **Hidden Monad** <term>Monad: the ultimate unity or "The One" from which all existence stems</term>, or the **Hidden God** (whom the Cabalists <note>Cabalists: followers of the Jewish mystical tradition, whose ideas were heavily integrated into Renaissance natural philosophy.</note> called the **Dark Aleph** <note>original: *Aleph tenebrosum*. The Hebrew letter Aleph represents the number one and the divine source; here, it refers to God in his unmanifested, "dark" state before creation.</note>, because he reflected his rays or acts back into himself in this state), it is therefore necessary that this **Abyss**—over whose face there was darkness for the stated reason—is devoid first of light, and consequently of motion, and finally of heat. It is neither illuminated, nor does it possess activity, nor is it moved, nor is it altered by heat. On the contrary, in its nature, it is alien to light, activity, motion, and heat. Thus, it is quite rightly judged by the leader Moses to be a thing "empty and void" <note>A reference to the description of the earth before creation in Genesis 1:2.</note>. From this, it is made clearer than the midday sun why Darkness and its offspring are accustomed to resist and hinder Light and the children of light with such opposition. A war so savage and lasting has been waged between these two opposites and enemies from the world’s beginning; it is certain that it will continue even until the final end.

But lest you be carried away by further doubt concerning the manifest contrariety between these two natures, I will present here a visual Demonstration, which seems to explain the immense discrepancy between these two qualities.

### A CERTAIN VISUAL EXPERIMENT,
### *by which the opposition of the natures of coldness and heat*
### *is most clearly indicated.*

I would like you to take a matrass <term>matrass: a glass flask with a round body and a long neck, common in alchemical laboratories</term>, or a glass vessel formed with a long neck into this Shape (which you can see on the following page under the letter **a**).

Then, while holding part of the neck **A. C.** of figure **b** in your hand, gradually stretch its head **B** toward the fire, so that it heats up considerably—doing so bit by bit and not suddenly, lest it break. Once this is done, have a certain vessel full of water ready, into which you should submerge or place the mouth of the matrass **A**. Hold it there for a quarter of an hour. You will perceive the water gradually and step by step ascending from **C** toward **D**. It will not stop rising until the heat has been gradually extinguished and consumed, and coldness holds such dominion in the cavity **B** as it had before the heating of the matrass’s head. For then the water will cease to rise further. From this, it is certain that the more intensely **B** is heated, the higher the water will rise before it stops its ascent and upward motion. Nor will it cease climbing toward the upper parts until it reaches the original degree of coldness. But conversely, if any heat is applied again to the head of the matrass **A**—indeed, even if a warm hand is placed upon it—you will immediately perceive the water (which had previously been raised by the effect of cold and the absence of heat) slowly and sensibly flowing back downward.

The reason for this thing can be readily found if we first observe that the nature of heat is to expand by refining <note>original: *subtiliando*, meaning to make "subtle" or less dense.</note>, and that through expansion, it requires a larger space. This will by no means seem vain or foreign to those most skilled in Chemistry <note>original: *Chymiæ*. In this period, chemistry and alchemy were not yet distinct disciplines.</note>, who, for this reason, often see their glass vessels shatter and break apart with a great noise. The reason for this is that when one handful of earth is reduced by rarefaction into ten handfuls of water, and again one of water into just as many of air, ten times as much space is required.

Hence, it follows that the air condensed by cold in the head or region **P**, for as long as the action of heat lasts, will be more refined the more intense the action of heat is. However, the more it is refined, the more abundant a place it naturally seeks for its existence. Therefore, the greatest part of the air formerly [in the]...

Since, therefore, it is the nature of coldness to oppose the nature of heat—dissipating and destroying by thickening <note>original: *incrassando*, literally "making fat" or "thickening," the opposite of refining.</note> what heat has accomplished by refining <note>original: *subtiliando*, making "subtle" or "thin."</note>—it follows that by the very absence or decrease of heat, [cold] gradually approaching and growing contracts the expanded air once more according to its own nature and condition. It binds the air and forcefully attacks it in its own constrictive manner. 

However, because it finds very little air within the cavity **A-B** to fill the space once the contraction has occurred, and because a vacuum or "empty space" (which nature abhors <note>*horror vacui*: the classical belief that nature resists the formation of a void by immediately filling any empty space with surrounding matter.</note>) must be avoided, it draws the water upward due to the water's continuity with the air. It does this all the more as it prevails over the heat: thus, the more the enclosed air is condensed by the styptic <term>styptic: from the Greek *styptikos*, meaning contracting or astringent; here referring to the power of cold to "shrink" matter.</term> power of the cold, the more the water ascends step by step. Finally, as heat gradually returns with its own rarefying <term>rarefying: the process of making something less dense or "thinner."</term> power, the air is refined once more; and the refined air, requiring a larger space, gradually causes that elevated water to descend again, so as to yield the space to the now-expanded air.

### On the super-celestial origin of Life and Health.

Thus, therefore, the World was created: for according to that passage of Saint Peter:
<margin>2 Peter 3</margin>
> *The heavens existed long ago (by **dilating**, that is, and separating the pure from the dark and thick) and the Earth (by **contracting** the impure, dark, and dense)* while the Word stood by: from which it is clear that both the manifest or dilating power of the **Monad** <note>The 'Monad' refers to the Divine Unity or God as the single source of all existence.</note> as well as its constricted and occult power concurred in the composition of the world. Indeed, his end shall also be by such a contrary power; namely, by dilating the worldly matter with light, and purifying it into its true essence: that is, by contracting the shadowy and useless fiction into its primary nothingness. For in this way, all things will be renewed in the final "LET IT PERISH" <note>original: *PEREAT*; a reference to the biblical prophecy that the current form of the world will pass away to be transformed.</note> (as Holy Scripture witnesses). Indeed, by such a rectification, we shall have a new earth and new heavens; nay more, all things that truly exist shall be made new.

With these things properly understood, we see these two qualities openly and clearly disagreeing and opposing one another; and consequently, the nature and property of each clearly indicates the spring from which it flows. For since it is the nature of coldness to condense rare things by its constricting or contracting power, it appears clearly that it belongs to the side of the dark principle, or that property in which God contracts Himself into Himself, by which operation the Darkness draws its origin. Thus, we also observe the rare, clear, and bright Heaven—specifically the luminous air (the work of the Luminous Word)—being contracted and thickened into a dense and dark cloud by the dominion of cold. This is then further contracted into dense water and opaque stones, such as the <term>Ceraunians<note>original: *Ceraunij*, also known as thunderstones. In the 17th century, these were believed to be physical stones formed in the atmosphere during lightning strikes.</note></term> (thickening water into earth and condensing it into something not at all transparent, but obscure: for by condensation, rare and transparent things for the most part become dense, black, and opaque). For just as we see that very deep water cannot be penetrated by the eyes because of the amount of <term>diaphane<note>The "diaphane" refers to the quality of transparency or the "transparent medium" itself.</note></term> present: so indeed, if such a mass could be constricted and coagulated into a smaller size, it must necessarily cease to be transparent and become most opaque, as can be seen in a dense and black cloud. But on the opposite side, we observe the nature of heat is to dissolve and refine those things which the cold has condensed; namely, by reducing Earth through rarefaction into Water in the first degree; Water into vapor first and then into subtle Air in the second; and finally Air into Fire in the third. Consequently, by refining, it reduces Earth back into heaven; the opaque into the transparent, and the dense into the subtle.

Coldness, in turn, by overcoming and undoing that work of heat, is observed to alter fire by condensing it into air, air into a cloud or vapor, a cloud into water, and finally the consistency of water into earth (as we see in ice and hail).

And this is that annual rotation of the Elements into one another, of which the Philosophers so often speak: so that in the winter time the faculty of coldness prevails, and in the summer that of heat. But lest the total destruction of Creatures should occur (which would indeed happen if the cold persisted), the **Monad**, or that eternal Unity (which is the source of these properties), has so ordained that on one side cold should not entirely prevail, but that its numbing and mortifying operation should be mitigated by the rays of the Sun from the South—namely, from the seat of **Capricorn**. Nor on the other side, from the North, should Heat dominate even when the Sun reigns in the palace of **Cancer**, but rather it is tempered in some way by the cold blast from the North Pole, lest by refining the earth and all the waters, it should turn them entirely into smoke.

In this manner, therefore, the vicissitudes of things in this world were established by the Great Architect through a contrary logic, and we observe all things in it to be tempered by contraries: one extreme of which has its beginning from light, the other from darkness; and yet the effects of all these proceed from one single Root and Archetype.

### C H A P T E R V I.

*In which it is proven that either Darkness and Light (and consequently Cold and Heat) arise from a single source or primordial principle; or that two eternal Principles must be admitted in the World, from which it would follow that Unity is excluded from the nature of things. Also, whether Evil as well as Good proceeds from God.*

---

**J**ust as light and darkness concur in the construction of a single world by means of a common moist matter, it is not surprising if those two opposites proceed from one eternal **Monad** <note>The Monad refers to the "One"—the single, indivisible source of all existence, identified here with God.</note>. For if the World was made in the image of the Monad—being not only one in number, but also containing two substances within itself: namely, formal light and the matter or dark abyss, and consequently the twofold properties of these, specifically coldness and heat—it seems likely that those contrary substances and properties were and are potentially in the God-Monad, the single Principle of principles, or the **Ideal and Archetypal World** <note>The 'Archetypal World' is the Neo-Platonic concept of the perfect blueprint of the universe existing within the divine mind before physical creation.</note>. If this were not so, this **Typical World** <note>The 'Typical World' is the physical universe, which serves as a 'type' or reflection of the divine archetype.</note> would by no means be the Pattern and image of God or the Archetypal World. Indeed, if anyone were to thoughtlessly deny this, then this absurdity and impossibility would follow: that there would be two co-eternal principles—one of the power of Darkness, privation, death, disease, and evil; and the other of Light, act, position, life, health, and good. But if duality were everlasting, it would be pointless and vain to believe that it had any principle at all, or that it derived its origin from Unity. For that which exists before all else cannot have a beginning, since a "principle" is considered to be the start of something that did not previously exist. Once this absurdity is granted, an even greater one would immediately follow: that Unity itself would be uprooted from the fellowship of Nature and the company of the mathematical arts. 

But in truth, since the **Dyad** <note>The Dyad represents the number two or the principle of duality/division.</note> is composed of the Monad (or Unity doubled), it is certain that Unity precedes the Dyad in both order and time. It is a most certain truth that simple things must come before things composed of simple parts, just as principles must come before the things they produce. Therefore, the erroneous opinion of the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement that taught a fundamental struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>, which proposes and establishes two eternal principles, is clearly refuted. Likewise, an answer is given to those fables concerning **Demogorgon** <note>A primordial deity in late-classical and Renaissance mythology, often depicted as the terrifying ancestor of all gods.</note>, Eternity, and **Chaos**, which claim these three were uncreated and co-eternal from the beginning, imagining that Chaos was a companion in the eternity of God the Best and Greatest. The Platonists seem to agree with this assertion of the Poets, but with this caution: they acknowledge that Chaos proceeded from Demogorgon by a certain eternal generation. For although they admit that Chaos flowed from the eternal God, they nevertheless wished it to be His companion—as if God and Chaos concurred and "mated" (as a husband with a woman or wife) for the generation or creation of the world and the things within it. Thus, they seem to conclude that just as Chaos was produced by God with no intermediary, so all other things arose and were primarily derived from God and Chaos, as if from primary form and matter. Therefore, they do not seem to have spoken harmfully in calling Chaos the companion of God in this matter.

<margin>Book 2 on Love.</margin>

Indeed, this opinion of the Platonists seems to differ very little from our own. For just as the Word on one hand (the offspring of the manifest and bright God) and the dark abyss or deformed and potential matter on the other (the progeny of the hidden and latent God) are born and procreated from the same Monad or Demogorgon, and under the names of Eternity...

Formation is the constitution of the form itself; whether it is raised up from the outside or from nothing and comes to the things themselves, or whether it is drawn out into the power of matter by divine command. The operation of "making," however, pertains to the mutual conjunction of matter and form.* Thus the omnipotence or unity of God compels, first, the things themselves into their matter or the unity of the individual (whether it be the world or a specific creature), in which world the action of the Father is more eminent than in the Son or Wisdom. Then the disposition of form—according to which the power of the moist nature is most widely diffused—is known to belong most especially to divine Wisdom, which we call the Son and the offspring of the Father. Finally, the highest affection and love proceeds from the primary power and wisdom (or act), which compels the composite of form and matter into one and properly "makes" all things; so that just as it proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son (or from power and wisdom), so also... it joins the union of matter, which is from the Father, with the dilation of form, which is from the Son.

Therefore, the "being" <note>original: "esse"</note> of things is like their matter and origin, while the "essence" <note>original: "essentia"</note> is like the form drawn out from the potential of matter. ### Volume I, Treatise I, Section I, Part I, Book I.

Hence Hermes says: that matter <note>original: "hyle", a Greek term for the fundamental substance or "wood" of the universe.</note> and the divine Spirit were not yet in the service of the world when they had not yet been born from where they were destined to be born; that is, dark matter and the luminous Spirit of Wisdom were both contained within the power of the radical Monad <note>The "radical Monad" refers to the primal, indivisible Unity of God before creation.</note>.

But someone will reply and say: What then? Do you conclude by consequence that God himself, or the radical Monad, is the author of evil—He who is entirely good, indeed the highest Good? Yet truly all evils (as I explained above) have arisen from the darkness and the dark principle, as is declared everywhere in the holy scriptures. What? Do you establish God as the Devil? Or do you believe that God ever ordained or substituted for Himself an evil Angel who could perpetrate evil and crimes in this world against the children of light? Does not the Holy Bible everywhere warn us, the children of light, to abstain from the works of darkness, and to arm ourselves with spiritual weapons against the insults or invasions of the Prince of Darkness? What is it, then, that you can answer to these objections?

To these I do not blush to give an answer, although brief, yet clear and lucid: let it be permitted to me to first seek and ask by way of petition and questioning from the objector himself, concerning the first part of his doubt: *Is anything created evil to the divine and radical Monad?*—He who created all things good, insofar as He created the universal world in general after His own image (which is entirely and only good), and consequently the members of that world, among which man is one of the more excellent? We say, therefore, that insofar as *all things are in God himself*, no differently than number is in unity; and *God is in all things, and Unity in number* (whence He is called the center of any thing whose circumference is nowhere <note>A famous Hermetic definition: "God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere."</note>); therefore it is necessary to conceive that to the divine Monad nothing is evil, since He is all that exists. He is uniquely good, perfect, beautiful, and the Father of all. Wherefore also all His offspring or creatures are established as good by participation: for it follows that those things which have been made such are therefore good, because He who made them is more than such. But the Father and maker of creatures is the highest Good; therefore, those things which are procreated by Him are also good, even if not in equal degree.

It does not follow, then, that those things which seem so to us, the children of light, are entirely evil, foul, and imperfect; for as the Apostle witnesses, those things are held as good by the children of darkness and the worldly which are esteemed as evil by us, the children of light. For the works of light are in every way opposed to those of darkness: hence nothing seems good to one condition that will not appear evil to the other. But in respect to the one God or radical Monad, both Darkness and Light are in an equal relation; as for Him (according to the testimony of the royal Prophet <note>King David, traditionally the author of the Psalms.</note>), darkness is even as the light. For it is as familiar to Him to hide Himself within Himself as it is to emit the rays of His lucid countenance; He is as powerful to harden the hearts of man and besiege him with darkness and lead him into error—*so that, like a drunkard, he gropes in the dark when light fails—as He is to bless and preserve him with the benevolent light of His face.* It is His also in the Macrocosm <note>The "great world," or the universe as a whole.</note> to so withhold the waters that they dry up, and to send them out again so that they overturn the earth. And sometimes He gives them moderately, that they may give fertility to the Earth itself. In His hands it is to make darkness His hiding place, and by the lightning from His face to reveal the foundations of the world; and by His rebuke to send His arrows and scatter men. And again, it is His to act benevolently with and in the elements. It is His to rebuke men sometimes on their bed through pain, making all their bones waste away so that food is abominable to them in life. Sometimes, health and life are preserved for them: For *by His visitation He preserves his spirit: and by lifting up the light of His face over men, He causes them to see light, and makes their darkness shining, so that He leads them in His paths.*

Is not God, then, the Author of both good and evil, in both the Macrocosm and the Microcosm <note>The "little world," or man, who reflects the universe.</note>?

# On the super-celestial origin of Life & Health.

But you will say, according to that frivolous distinction of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages and Renaissance who often made fine-grained logical distinctions.</note>: it is the evil of punishment, not the evil of guilt <note>original: "malum pœnæ, non culpæ". Truly, indeed; what guilt did that good man Job commit—a *Just Man* (as the Text says)—who suffered so many things by divine command? Or who struck him and afflicted him with such a tremendous evil? Was it not his Servant? That Prince in the kingdom of Darkness <note>Referring to Satan.</note>? What then? Was that striker co-eternal with God? For did not that patient man Job allow all these things—whether we call them evil or good—to remain in the will of Him who is entirely good? Nor is it right for men to judge the works of Him who in Himself is just; namely, whether they be good or evil: seeing that it belongs to Him to do whatever He wills, according to His will, as much in the virtues of heaven as with the inhabitants of the earth; *and there is no one who resists His hands, or says: Why have You done this?*

Therefore it is certain that all those things are good which God does, both in the heavens and on the earth: and consequently, in respect to Himself, they are not evil; but in respect to us, who suffer. For example: when a Goldsmith <note>original: "Aurifaber"</note> wishes to purify and cleanse "leprous" gold <note>In alchemy, "leprous gold" refers to gold contaminated with base metals or impurities.</note> or gold contaminated by some impure metal, and wants to test it by the trial of fire, he seems to torture the gold with fire; and yet that work (although full of torture) is good, because it tends toward the best end. No less can also be said of diseases, which pave the way to death or the separation of the parts of the composite—that is, the pure from the impure. According to the pattern of the dissolution and examination of the truth, or the "true animal gold," this process is to us living beings who suffer the worst of all things, and yet to God it seems the best and concerned with a perfect end. From this, it is not for us to judge concerning evil, but for God alone. 

We (I say) living in this life think those things are evil and worst which oppose life and health; but to God the unique Creator, in whose power are both Darkness and Light, "no-will" <note>original: "noluntas," a term for the negative or passive aspect of the divine will.</note> and "will," negation and affirmation, contraction and expansion, death and life, nothing is evil, nothing base, nothing foul. But neither did the blacksmith introduce the rust, nor the parent of the animal body the mud: by the same reasoning, because darkness hides the light from the children of light, therefore this is "evil" to them. So also to those who flee the light <note>original: "Lucifugis", literally "light-fleers," often referring to creatures of darkness or those who reject spiritual truth.</note>, clear light seems an evil; although both Darkness and Light are good.

We say, therefore, that as the two offspring of the radical Monad are entirely contrary in nature, the effect of one predominating and conquering is reputed as evil by the other which suffers: and yet in respect to the original unity, both are of one essence existing in the "will" or the "no-will": not otherwise than we see the same human mind, in number and essence, to be sometimes of a "no-willing" disposition, and sometimes of a "willing" one: sometimes persisting in severity and denying,

From this Hermes says: *that primordial matter and the divine Spirit were not in the workshop of the world when they were not yet born, from which they ought to have been born; that is, dark matter <note>original: "hyle", a Greek term for the fundamental, unformed substance of the universe.</note> and the bright Spirit of Wisdom were in the power of the radical Monad <note>The Monad refers to the "One"—the single, indivisible source of all being in Pythagorean and Hermetic philosophy.</note>.*

But someone will reply and say: What then? Do you conclude by consequence that God Himself, or the radical Monad, is the author of evil—He who is entirely good, or rather, the Supreme Good? Indeed, all evils (as I explained above) have arisen from darkness and the dark principle, as is declared everywhere in the Holy Scriptures. What? Do you establish God as the Devil? Or do you believe that God ever ordained or substituted for Himself an evil Angel, who might perpetrate evil and crimes in this world against the children of light? Are we not, as children of light, everywhere warned by the Holy Bible to abstain from the works of darkness, and to fortify ourselves as children of light with spiritual armor against the insults or invasions of the Prince of Darkness? What is it, therefore, that you can answer to these objections?

To these things, I do not blush to give an answer, however succinct, yet clear and lucid: first, let me be permitted by the way of inquiry and questioning to ask and interrogate him regarding the first part of his doubt: *Is anything created evil to the divine and radical Monad? He created all things good, insofar as He created the universal world in its kind according to His own image, which is entirely and solely good, and consequently the members of the world itself, among which man is one of the more excellent.* We say, therefore, that insofar as *all things are in God Himself*—not otherwise than a number is in unity, and *God is in all things just as Unity is in number* (whence the center of any thing is spoken of, whose circumference is nowhere)—it is therefore necessary to conceive that to the divine Monad itself, nothing is evil, because it is everything that is; which is uniquely good, perfect, beautiful, and the Father of all. Wherefore all His offshoots or creatures are established to be good by participation: for it follows that those things which are so made are therefore good, because He who made such things is more than such himself. But the Father and maker of creatures is the Supreme Good; therefore, those things which are procreated by Him are also good, although not in an equal degree.

It does not follow, therefore, that those things are entirely evil, base, and imperfect which seem so to us, the children of light. For, as the Apostle witnesses, those things are held as good by the children of darkness and worldly men which are judged as evil by us, the children of light. For the works of light are in every way opposed to those of darkness; hence, nothing seems good to one condition that will not appear evil to the other. Yet, with respect to the one God or the radical Monad, both Darkness and Light are in an equal relation; since to Him (as the Royal Prophet <note>King David, referring to the Psalms.</note> witnesses) darkness is even as the Light itself; it is as familiar to Him to hide Himself within Himself as it is to emit the rays of His bright countenance; He is as powerful in hardening the hearts of man and besieging him with darkness and leading him into error, <margin>Job 12</margin>*so that in the manner of a drunkard he gropes in the darkness when the light fails, <margin>Deuteronomy 28</margin>as He is in blessing and preserving him with the light of His benevolent face.* It is His also, in the Macrocosm <note>The great world or the universe as a whole.</note>, to so restrain the waters that they dry up, and to send them forth again so that they overturn the earth. <margin>2 Samuel 22; Job 33:17</margin>And *sometimes He gives them moderately, so that they give fertility to the Earth itself:* It is in His hands to make darkness His hiding place, and by the lightning from His face to reveal the foundations of the world; and by His rebuke to send His arrows and scatter men. And again, it is His to act benevolently with and in the elements: It is His to rebuke men sometimes upon their beds through pain, and He makes all their bones waste away, <margin>Job 10, 12; Psalm 4:7; Psalm 18:29</margin>so that food is abominable to them in life. Sometimes both health and life are preserved for them: For *by His visitation He preserves his Spirit; and by lifting the light of His countenance upon men, He makes them see the light, and makes their darkness shining, so that He leads them in His paths.*

Is not God, therefore, the Author here of both good and evil, both in the Macrocosm and the Microcosm <note>The "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>?

<meta>This page builds upon the previous discussion of the Monad as the source of all things. ### Concerning the Supercelestial Origin of Life and Health.

<margin>Wisdom 16:13</margin>
*The Lord has power over life and death; he leads down to the gates of death and brings back again.* <note>original: "Vitæ & mortis habet Dominus potestatem, qui deducit ad portas mortis & reducit."</note> From these things, therefore, you have it explained more clearly than the noonday sun, first, how contrary the luminous and dark qualities are, and how great is the enmity between them—even though they were brought forth in the same birth—and then, that both nonetheless arise from one and the same root.

<margin>Job 12:22</margin>
The Holy Scriptures best explain the difference and enmity between these two properties in this way. *He reveals* (says Job) *the deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shadow of death, etc.* <note>original: "Reuelat fundamenta è Tenebris, & educit in lucem vmbram lethalem."</note> as if he had said that the formless waters, overwhelmed by darkness and consequently as if dead, were formed and quickened—in the manner of a deadly shadow—by the presence and power of the luminous Word, emanating by the will of the Monad <term>Monad: The ultimate unity or "The One" from which all existence originates in Neoplatonic and Hermetic philosophy.</term>. From this it is argued that, just as the primitive power of the hidden Monad, or the dark Aleph <term>Aleph: The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here used to symbolize the primordial, unmanifested source of God's power before creation.</term>, was to reduce things to nothing and render them empty, void, and plainly dead; so, conversely, His "willing" or positive power brought all things into actuality out of nothingness or potentiality. That is to say, from a formless Chaos <term>Chaos: The disordered state of matter before it was shaped by divine intellect.</term>, He produced a whole world adorned with wondrous beauty; from the void and emptiness, a Spirit filled on all sides with rays of divine Emanation; and from a thing plainly dead and inanimate, a creature full of an immense soul and every power both of quickening and generating, as well as of multiplying and preserving. *By the Word of the Lord* (says the Psalmist) *the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit from his mouth.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note>

<margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin>
From this, it is right to draw out the immense difference between these extremes springing from a single center or point of Divinity; which the Apostle also seems to confirm when he says *there is no communion of darkness with light.* And this is the reason why the Evangelist says: *if we walk in the darkness of unbelief, we have no fellowship with the light of Christ.* For just as Job spoke, in the passage cited before, about the revelation of the foundations of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The universe as a whole, seen as a large-scale reflection of the human being.</term> out of darkness or deadly shadows by means of the emanation of light, so indeed can this same thing be understood concerning the redemption of the foundations of the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: The human being, viewed as a "little world" that mirrors the structures of the entire universe.</term>. <margin>Luke 1:79</margin> For we find it written that *light has dawned upon those sitting in the region of the shadow of death.* By these words it is indicated that just as there are children of light in this world, so indeed there are innumerable children of darkness within it. They are not called so by creation, but through sin and error; for all were born as children of light that they might live: <margin>Wisdom 2</margin> <margin>Wisdom 2:23</margin> *because God created man to be immortal, and made him in the image of his own likeness.* But due to ignorance, some have fallen into the abyss of darkness, and that by the deceits of the Prince of Darkness. *Moreover, those who are on his side imitate him.*

By this speech, the Wise Man seems to imply that those are called children of darkness of whom the Apostle says: <margin>1 Thessalonians 5</margin> *Christians are not children of darkness, but children of light and of the day.* <margin>1 John 1 & 2</margin> And the Evangelist says, *if we walk in the darkness of infidelity, we have no fellowship with the light of Christ.* Furthermore, he is called a child of darkness who hates his brother. <margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin> In their number, the Apostle Paul confesses that he himself once was, in that place where he acknowledges he was snatched from the darkness of errors. Indeed, such men are even sometimes called "Darkness" itself. <margin>Ephesians 5</margin> For the Apostle asserts that the *Gentiles were Darkness before Christ was known, but Light afterward.* For Christ is the Word <margin>1 John 1, John 12</margin> of Wisdom and God revealed; and in His positive property, which is Light, <margin>1 John 1, 2 Samuel 22</margin> *no darkness is in Him.* He came to shine in the world and to give knowledge of Himself, so that we might not remain in the darkness of sin, but walk in Christ Himself and in the Light, that we might have fellowship with Him. For it belongs to God, in His luminous property, to enlighten our darkness, so that by that means, we who by the fall of Adam were cast down from the kingdom of light into that of darkness, might again be numbered among the luminous children of God through the mediation of the True Light.

You see, therefore, how great a difference separates the children of light from those of darkness: since the latter are the children of the hidden God, who remains in His dark property, and are consequently subject to the Prince of Darkness (His chief minister); but the former are subject to the revealed God, who rules in His luminous property, and consequently are under the command of the great Angel, namely Wisdom (whom the Cabalists <term>Cabalists: Practitioners of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition.</term> called Metattron <term>Metattron: A powerful angel in mystical lore, often described as the mediator between the divine and the earthly realms.</term>).
