# Concerning the Super-celestial Origin of Life and Health.

<margin>Wisdom 16:13</margin>
The Lord has the power of life and death; he leads down to the gates of death and brings back again. By these words, you have it explained more clearly than the midday light, first, how contrary the luminous and dark qualities are, and how great is the enmity between them—even though they were brought forth in a single birth—and then afterwards, that both nevertheless arise from one and the same root.

<margin>Job 12:22</margin>
The Holy Scriptures best explain the difference and enmity between these two properties in this way. Job says, *He reveals the foundations out of Darkness, and brings forth the shadow of death into light* <note>original: "Reuelat fundamenta e Tenebris, & educit in lucem umbram lethalem"</note> etc. It is as if he had said that the waters, which were formless and overwhelmed by darkness—and consequently as if dead—were formed and brought to life by the presence and power of the luminous Word, which emanates by the will of the Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the "One" or the absolute unity of God from which all things begin.</note>. From this it is argued that just as the primitive power of the hidden Monad, or the dark Aleph <term>Aleph: The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, used here to represent the primal, unmanifest state of God before creation.</term>, was to reduce things to nothing and render them empty, void, and plainly dead; so, conversely, its "to will" or its positive virtue brought all things out of nothingness or potential into actuality. That is, out of formless Chaos, it produced a whole world adorned with wondrous beauty; out of the void and emptiness, it produced a Spirit everywhere full of the rays of divine Emanation; and out of a thing plainly dead and inanimate, it produced a creature full of an immense soul and every power both of giving life and generating, as well as of multiplying and preserving. As the Psalmist says: *By the Word of the Lord were the heavens established, and all the power of them by the Spirit of his mouth.* <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt Cœli, & Spiritu ab ore eius omnis virtus eorum." See Psalm 33:6.</note>

<margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin>
From here, therefore, it is right to draw out the immense difference between these extremes gushing from a single center or point of Divinity; which the Apostle also seems to confirm when he says that there is no fellowship of darkness with light. And this is the reason that the Evangelist says: if we walk in the darkness of unbelief, we have no fellowship with the light of Christ. For just as Job spoke, in the place cited before, concerning the revelation of the foundations of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or the universe as a whole.</term> out of Darkness or the shadows of death by means of the emanation of light, so indeed this same thing can be understood regarding the redemption of the foundations of the microcosm <term>Microcosm: The "little world," referring to the individual human being as a reflection of the universe.</term>.

<margin>Luke 1:79</margin>
For we find it written that *light has dawned upon those sitting in the region of the shadow of death.* <note>original: "sedentibus in regione umbræ mortis lux orta est."</note> By which it is indicated that just as there are children of light in this world, so indeed there are innumerable children of darkness in it—I do not say darkness from creation, but through sin and error. For all were born
<margin>Wisdom 2</margin>
as children of light that they might live, because God created man to be imperishable, and
<margin>Wisdom 2:23</margin>
made him in the image of his own likeness. But due to ignorance, some have fallen into the abyss of darkness, and that by the deceits of the prince of darkness. Moreover, those who are on his side imitate him. By this speech, the Wise Man seems to suggest that such people are called children of darkness, of whom the Apostle says: the children of darkness are not Christians, but children of light
<margin>1 Thessalonians 5</margin>
and of the day. And the Evangelist says, if we walk in the darkness of infidelity, we have no fellowship with the light
<margin>1 John 1</margin>
of Christ. Furthermore, he is called a child of darkness who hates his
<margin>1 John 2</margin>
brother. In their number, the Apostle Paul confesses he once was, in that place where
<margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin>
he acknowledges he was snatched from the darkness of errors. Indeed, such men are sometimes called Darkness itself. For the Apostle asserts that the Gentiles
<margin>Ephesians</margin>
were Darkness before they knew Christ, but were Light afterward. For Christ, the Word
<margin>1 John 1</margin>
of Wisdom and God made manifest in his positive property—which is Light, and in which there
<margin>John 12</margin>
is no darkness—came to shine in the world and to give knowledge of himself, so that we might not
<margin>1 John 1</margin>
remain in the darkness of sin, but walk in Christ himself and in the Light, so that we might have fellowship with him.
<margin>2 Samuel 22</margin>
For it is the property of God in his luminous state to enlighten our darkness; so that by that means, we who by the fall of Adam were cast down from the kingdom of light into that of darkness, might again be numbered among the luminous children of God through the mediation of the true Light.

You see, therefore, how great a difference stands here between the children of light and those of darkness: since the latter are children of the hidden God who remains in his dark property, and are consequently subject to the Prince of Darkness (his highest minister); but the former are subject to the manifest God who commands in his luminous property, and are consequently under the command of the great Angel—namely Wisdom—whom the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note> called Metattron <term>Metattron: A powerful angel in mystical tradition, often serving as the celestial mediator or the "voice" of God.</term>.

<margin>Psalm 104:29. Job 34.</margin>

Hence, in the passage cited before, it is held: *Good and evil, life and death, etc., are from God.* And elsewhere.

# Concerning the Super-celestial Origin of Life and Health.

<margin>Wisdom 16:13</margin>
*The Lord has power over life and death; he leads down to the gates of death and brings back again.* <note>original: "Vitæ & mortis habet Dominus potestatem, qui deducit ad portas mortis & reducit."</note> By these words you have it explained more clearly than the midday sun: first, how contrary the qualities of light and darkness are, and how great the enmity is between them, even though they were brought forth in the same birth; and second, that both nevertheless arise from one and the same root.

<margin>Job 12:22</margin>
The Holy Scriptures best explain the difference and enmity between these two properties in this way: *He reveals (says Job) the foundations out of Darkness, and brings the shadow of death into the light, etc.* <note>original: "Reuelat fundamenta è Tenebris, & educit in lucem umbram lethalem."</note> as if he had said that the formless waters, overwhelmed by darkness—and consequently as if dead—were formed and brought to life like a lethal shadow through the presence and power of the luminous Word, which emanates by the will of the <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Monad" refers to the singular, indivisible source of all being, God as the ultimate "One."</note>. From this it is argued that just as the power of the primal and hidden Monad, or the dark <term>Aleph</term> <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In this mystical context, it represents the primordial, unmanifested source—the "Nothing" from which all "Something" emerges.</note>, was to reduce things to nothing and render them empty, void, and plainly dead; so, conversely, its "will" or positive virtue brought all things into action out of nothingness or potentiality. That is, out of the formless Chaos, it produced a whole world adorned with marvelous beauty; out of the void and emptiness, it produced a Spirit filled everywhere with the rays of divine Emanation; and out of a plainly dead and inanimate thing, it produced a living creature full of immense power for both giving life and generating, as well as for multiplying and preserving. *By the Word (says the Psalmist) of the Lord the Heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit from his mouth.*

<margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin>
From this, therefore, it is right to draw out the immense difference between these extremes springing from a single center or point of Divinity; which the Apostle also seems to confirm when he says *there is no communion of darkness with light.* And this is the reason why the Evangelist says: *If we walk in the darkness of unbelief, we have no fellowship with the light of Christ.* For just as Job spoke, in the passage cited before, concerning the revelation of the foundations of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Macrocosm" is the "Great World" or the entire universe.</note> out of Darkness or lethal shadows by means of the emanation of light, so indeed can this same thing be understood concerning the redemption of the foundations of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Microcosm" is the "Little World," usually referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. For we find it written that *light has risen for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death.* <margin>Luke 1:79</margin> By which it is indicated that just as there are children of light in this world, so indeed are there countless children of darkness in it—I do not say "of darkness" by creation, but through sin and error. For all were born as children of light that they might live: *since God created man to be undying, and made him in the image of his own likeness: but because of ignorance, some have fallen into the abyss of darkness, and that by the deceits of the prince of darkness. But those who are on his side imitate him.* <margin>Wisdom 2</margin> <margin>Wisdom 2:24</margin> By this speech, the Wise Man seems to imply that such are called children of darkness, of whom the Apostle says: *The children of darkness are not Christians; but children of light and of the day.* <margin>1 Thessalonians 5</margin> And the Evangelist says, *if we walk in the darkness of infidelity, we have no fellowship with the light of Christ. Furthermore, he who hates his brother is called a child of darkness.* <margin>1 John 1</margin> <margin>1 John 2</margin> Paul confesses himself to have been in their number in that passage where he acknowledges that he was rescued from the darkness of errors. <margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin> Indeed, such men are sometimes even called "Darkness" itself. For the Apostle asserts that the Gentiles *were Darkness before they knew Christ, but Light afterward.* <margin>Ephesians 5</margin> For Christ—the Word of Wisdom and God made manifest—comes to shine in the world in His positive property, which is Light, and *darkness is not in him,* to give knowledge of Himself, so that we might not remain in the darkness of sin, but walk in Christ himself and in the Light, so that we might have fellowship with him. <margin>1 John 1</margin> <margin>John 2</margin> <margin>1 John 1</margin> <margin>2 Kings 22</margin> For it belongs to God, in His luminous property, to illuminate our darkness: so that in this way, we who were cast down by the fall of Adam from the kingdom of light into that smoke of the abyss of darkness, might again be numbered among the children of the luminous God through the mediation of the true Light.

You see, therefore, how great a difference stands between the children of light and those of darkness: since the latter are children of the hidden God who remains in His dark property, and are consequently subject to the Prince of Darkness (His highest minister); while the former are subject to the manifest God who commands in His luminous property, and are consequently under the rule of the great Angel, namely Wisdom (whom the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>The "Cabalists" refers to followers of Kabbalah, a Jewish mystical tradition that explores the nature of the divine and the universe, often studied by Renaissance philosophers like Robert Fludd.</note> called <term>Metattron</term> <note>Metattron (or Metatron) is a powerful angel in mystical tradition, often seen as the celestial mediator or the "Prince of the Countenance" who guides humanity toward the light.</note>).

Volume I, Treatise I, Section I, Part I, Book I.

<margin>John 15</margin>
These sons are therefore called the children of the world, of the flesh, and of the devil; those others are called the children of the living God, who created all things and brought them into being. The Light and Savior of the world best describes the opposition between these two natures in these words: *Those of the world are loved by the world, but the world hates me; they are from below; I, and those who follow me, are from above. I proceeded from God; they are of the party of the Devil. If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you,* etc. <note>original: "Mundani amantur à mundo, me autem odit mundus: illi de deorsum sunt; Ego & qui me sequuntur, de sursum. Ego à Deo processi: illi ex parte Diaboli sunt. Si mundus vos odit, scitote, quia me priorem vobis odio habuit. Si de mundo fuissetis, mundus quod suum est diligeret. Quia vero de mundo non estis, sed ego elegi vos de mundo, propterea odit vos mundus,"</note> And the Evangelist says: *The Light came into the world, but men loved darkness more than the light.* <note>original: "Lux venit in mundum, sed dilexerunt homines tenebras magis quam lucem."</note> John 11:9 (by his own testimony): *for their works were evil.* And these are the kind of people who walk
<margin>Isaiah 5:20</margin>
in the night, and the light is not in them; concerning whom the Prophet also says: *Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, putting darkness for light and light for darkness; these (I say) are the children of darkness, etc.* <note>original: "Væ dicentibus de malo bonum & de bono malum, ponentes tenebras pro luce & lucem pro tenebris, hi (inquam) sunt tenebrarum filij &c."</note> It is clear from this how great a dissension exists between the children of light and of darkness in this world; and consequently it is evident that there is an extreme opposition between those two properties, even though they arise from the same single radical spring or divine fountain. What then is to be said? Is it not that the same Unity is the primary principle of the vice and evil of darkness as much as the virtue and good of light? Or why should we have reason for further doubt? Should we doubt whether the Devil (who is called the Prince of Darkness by the Emperor of Darkness—namely, the dark <term>Aleph</term> <note>Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Here, the "dark Aleph" refers to God in his hidden, unmanifested, and terrifying aspect.</note>, or the hidden God) was ordained to perform erroneous, evil, and dark works in any different way than the Prince of Light or Wisdom (whom the Sages hold to be the life and soul of the world) was ordained by the Emperor of Light or the Word—which is the lucid <term>Aleph</term> and the revealed God—to perform the lucid, true, and good works of life everywhere in the world? Were both not created by God, that is, the radical <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Monad" is the philosophical term for the ultimate "One" or Unity from which all diversity emerges.</note>? Do you not have this 
<margin>Isaiah 54:16</margin>
confirmed by infallible demonstration by the Prophet speaking in the person of God? *Behold, I have created the smith who blows the coals in the fire and produces an instrument for his work; and I have created the destroyer to lay waste, etc.* <note>original: "Ecce ego creaui fabrum sufflantem in igne prunas, & proferentem vas in opus suum: & ego creaui interfectorem ad disperdendum, &c."</note>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 39:33</margin>
And the Son of Sirach affirms the same in most eloquent words, saying: *There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they have laid on grievous torments; and in the time of destruction they shall pour out their power, and appease the wrath of him that made them, etc.* <note>original: "Sunt Spiritus qui ad vindictam creati sunt, & in furore suo confirmauerunt tormenta sua & in tempore consummationis effundent virtutem, & furorem eius qui fecit illos, confundent, &c."</note> Therefore, by means of this lethal minister, He destroys and corrupts by way of depriving a thing of its luminous form; conversely, through that lucid minister, He again generates and brings to life by way of removing the dark veil, so that in this manner new things may be produced, according to the saying: *Life and death, good and evil are from the one God, who works by means of his Angels,* as will be declared in the following book.

It was for this reason that the ancient Sages (among whom I name Orpheus, Hesiod, and Proclus), who were accustomed to cloud and hide their divine mysteries in poetic fables, sometimes called this single God of the world and true radical Monad of all things *Apollo*, and sometimes *Dionysius*. I say *Apollo* during the daytime, because they believed it was the role of Apollo to reassemble and restore to their original state those things which had been torn apart by the nocturnal *Dionysius* and divided into seven parts. They called Him *Dionysius* during the night, whose duty they intended to be the destruction, corruption, and tearing apart during the night of that which had been immediately composed and created by the daytime *Apollo*. For this reason, that radical Being of all things was called <term>Apollo</term>: because he generates, gives life, and composes; and this occurs in the number seven <note>The "Septenary" or number seven was seen as the number of completion and the created world.</note>, which is fashioned from the formal number, which is three, and the material number, which is four, which joined together in composition make seven. Therefore, all composition is from the number seven; and also its destruction or dissolution is perfected by retreating through that same boundary. By these things it is clearly shown that all things are created and established by light and the lucid property of God. By His contrary property, however, all things are destroyed and fail. But truly, since they perceived that divine light (which they recognized to be the central Sun) was the author of creation, generation, and composition, they therefore called that property Apollo and Phoebus—

# ->Of the supercelestial origin of Life & Health.<-

...called it a property; the Poets understood this as the Sun, who rules by day, refreshing, generating, and enlivening all things on earth with his life-giving heat. Hence the Ancients called the Sun *Apellin* <note>original: "Apellin," a Greek-derived name for Apollo</note> instead of Apollo, as if he were the "driver away of evils" and the "dispeller of darkness." And the Athenians called him *Alexicacon* <note>original: "Alexicacon," from the Greek *alexikakos*, meaning "averter of evil"</note>, as if he were "expelling evil," and Homer called him the author of health. By these things, we see it clearly declared that this same radical unity—not only according to the sense of Holy Scripture but also the assertion of the ancient Pagan Sages—is a participant in both conditions or properties: namely, the dark property, by which it seems to reflect upon itself and act with a "privative" or withdrawing mind. It does this either by withdrawing the ray of life from the creature little by little and slowly into itself, or by turning its face away from the creature in part, disturbing it and causing it to fall ill; or by absolutely and entirely receiving and contracting the ray of life and spirit back into itself. In this state, it is necessary for the creature to expire or perish. 

<margin>Psalm 104:19 <note>In modern Bibles, this is usually Psalm 104:29-30</note></margin> For every creature has expectation from God; therefore, when He gives, it receives life; when He sends forth His Spirit, it is recreated and enjoys health. But if He should receive or draw back His Spirit and breath to Himself, all flesh would fail and expire at once, and be turned to ashes. <note>original: "nā omnis creatura habet expectationem à Deo... Si vero Spiritum & flatum suum ad se reciperet vel traheret: deficeret & expiraret omnis caro simul, & in cinere conuerteretur."</note> And this contraction or reception of divine goodness is nothing other than the conversion of the bright property into the dark. 

<margin>Job 19:8</margin> Whence Job says: *He has set darkness in my paths.* <note>original: "Semitis meis tenebras opposuit."</note> And elsewhere it is said that *Darkness shall pursue the enemies of God.* And in many places of Scripture, Darkness is held to represent death, the plague and evil of the living, the grave, and unhappiness; but conversely, Light in itself and through itself is esteemed as life, health, form, and supreme happiness.

Therefore, we thought it especially necessary to explain this point to the world; because I have observed many in this world, even those commonly thought wise, who are totally seized by ignorance of this mystery, such that they strenuously defend the idea that there were two co-eternal principles. One of these they made God, whom they called the Prince of Light and the beginning and author of Good. The other they thought to be the Devil, whom they believed to be the Prince of Darkness and the primary origin of evil—not created at all, but co-eternal and equal to God Himself. They fail to understand that the Devil is a creature, formed no differently than the very Angel of the supreme divine light who gives life to all. He was fashioned from a ray of hidden light reflected inward upon itself, becoming as it were obstinate, unwilling, and perverse in form, with a dark external body that is aerial and impure; whereas the Angel of Light arose from a ray of manifest light and the most pure and clear Empyrean Spirit <note>The Empyrean is the highest heaven, traditionally composed of pure light or fire</note>, created before all things.

For by this perverse imagination of theirs, they are not ashamed to diminish the divine omnipotence of the one and only Divinity, who (as the Apostle witnesses) *is all in all, and does whatever He wills in heaven and on earth.* <note>original: "vt omnia in omnibus, & quicquid vult, facit in cœlis & in terra"</note> Nor is it for man to judge whether His deeds are good or evil; nor are they evil simply because they seem evil to the one suffering them. For although the worst of all sins is infidelity <note>meaning unbelief or lack of faith</note>, since it damns just as Faith is said to save, yet our God (as the Apostle witnesses) *has concluded all in unbelief, that He might have mercy upon all.* <note>original: "conclusit omnia in incredulitate, vt omnium misereatur."</note>

<margin>Ephesians 2</margin> But indeed, God did this first in His negative property, through the mediation of His minister—namely, the prince of darkness—whence Paul speaks thus: *You walked according to the Prince of the power of the air, the Spirit who now works in the children of disobedience.* <note>original: "Ambulastis secundum Principem potestatis aeris, Spiritus qui nunc operatur in filiis diffidentiæ."</note> Here and there the Apostle argues that the effects of the negative property are finally to be taken away by the power of the positive property or grace.

Nor is it enough for mortals to say in their own way that this is against the doctrine of Holy Scripture, objecting: Why are we commanded by divine admonitions to embrace faith, if God has concluded all in unbelief? What can we do against God? Or why does God command us to do one thing, when He Himself does another in us? Does not Holy Scripture contradict itself in these express words? To these the Apostle seems to respond, as if seized with wonder, saying: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? Or who has first given to Him, and it shall be recompensed to him? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things.* <note>original: "O altitudo diuitiarum sapientiæ... Quoniam per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia."</note>

Volume I. Treatise 1. Section I. Part 1. Book 1.

## CHAPTER VII.

### *How God is accustomed to work in His property that is absolutely hidden and contractive, to fulfill His privative will.*

We say that the sacrosanct Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to God as the ultimate, indivisible Unity or "The One."</note> has exercised its power in its hidden property, both before the creation of the world, during its construction, and after the completion of that same fabric; indeed, it continues to exercise it diligently to this day. For regarding the time before the age of the world, it was said by Moses, *Darkness was upon the face of the abyss*; and Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed.</note> says: *An infinite shadow was in the abyss*. Now, it was necessary that this unformed matter be exceedingly dark, even beyond the measure of the "palpable darkness" of Egypt, because of the dominion of cold within it—cold being that which has the power to condense. For Light, the parent of heat, had not yet shone forth from the power of the Monad. Hermes seems to give the reason for this: although the Monad had generated a Monad from eternity by the property of emission <note>The outward "shining" or "sending forth" of divine light.</note>, it nevertheless reflected and contracted its heat back into itself through a third property, and thus all things were enveloped in darkness and, consequently, were considered as nothing. 

<margin>Job 26.</margin> Wherefore Job says: *He stretches out the North over the empty space, and hangs the earth upon nothing.* <note>Job 26:7</note> By "empty space" and "nothing," he understood unformed matter, so called because it is not yet "informed" by any presence of light; for it belongs to form alone to give a thing its name and its being. 

<margin>Wisdom 11:27 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Wisdom of Solomon 11:17.</note></margin> And Solomon seems to suggest this same thing when he speaks thus: *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of unformed matter*; where by "unformed matter" he seems to understand Chaos itself, or the crude and undigested mass, which Moses calls *the earth empty and void*; that is, a heap of darkness destitute of divine rays—rays which, when present, caused everything afterwards to be called "full" and "good." In such a state, therefore, did potential matter remain while the Monad was hidden within itself, reserving the essence and act of form in itself. Therefore, that matter is said to exist in potentiality and not by divine act, and consequently is plainly nothing. 

And for this reason it is written that God Himself created the world out of nothing. And although Aristotle seems to assert that *out of nothing, nothing is made* <note>original: "ex nihilo, nihil fit," a fundamental principle of ancient philosophy.</note>, yet in this he does not entirely contradict the Sacred Page. For his assertion is most true if understood as "Absolute Nothing." For as he rightly says, *That potentiality is in vain which is never reduced into act.* But this *Ayin* <note>original: "אַין," the Hebrew word for "nothingness" or "the void."</note> or "Nothing" is so called in a relative sense: namely, insofar as it was not yet endowed with the shining form, and for that reason was entirely destitute of a name. 

But truly, after the Light had shone forth by the expansion of the Monad, that matter—formerly unformed—was immediately imbued with the appearance of waters; hence it is said, *The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters.* Finally, since God is seen and known in His creatures and through His creatures, as the Holy Page teaches, we are accustomed to recognize and contemplate the nature of both His properties through their effects. Indeed, we perceive that cold predominates in the absence of heat, working by its constrictive faculty; by constricting, it thickens, and by thickening, it renders transparent things opaque and dark. Conversely, we see the effect of heat following the presence of light and the sun, whose nature is to move, and by motion to excite heat; and through the mediation of heat, to make dense things subtle by expanding them; to put darkness to flight by refining it; and to make obscure things covered in gloom become transparent and clear.

From these things it is evidently clear that by this method—namely, from the effect, or *a posteriori* <note>Reasoning from effects back to causes.</note>—it will not be impossible to gather and judge the original natures of the Monad's properties which worked *a priori* <note>Reasoning from causes forward to effects.</note>. For nothing is born or operates in the world which this radical Monad does not perfect, mediating through its two aforesaid properties. The effects of these properties are the rare and the dense, the hot and the cold, the bright and the opaque, action and passion, male and female; and finally, everything that the world contains. Wherefore it was said by the Apostle, not without deliberation: *God works all things in all*; and *that God is all, and in all*; and *that from Him, through Him, and in Him are all things.*

Having now recognized the hidden property of God as it existed before His works, and having considered the nature of the primary darkness—so far as the weak capacity of my meager wit allows—deduced from consequence and effect, we shall now take refuge in the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures. Through these, we may more clearly explain the disposition of God's hidden and contractive <note>The "contractive property" refers to God pulling His divine light inward, an act that results in darkness, cold, and the solidification of matter.</note> property at the very act and moment of Creation, so that those things we previously reported may become known to you with a more lucid understanding.

<margin>2 Peter 3.</margin>
<margin>Wisdom 11.</margin>
<margin>Job 12:22.</margin>
<margin>Pimander 3.</margin>
We shall perceive, therefore, with a slightly sharper gaze, that those two Extremes <note>Light and Darkness.</note> emerged from a single, as it were, Central point, and appeared in the primary act of the world's Creation. We see that by their violent action and passion, a third thing—namely, the naked moist nature—was brought forth into the light in a wonderful manner and proportion. This moist or watery nature was the material foundation of the universal fabric which consists of Heaven and Earth. For, as St. Peter testifies: *The heavens were of old, and the earth out of the water and through the water, by the assistance of the Word.* <note>original: "Cœli erant prius, & Terra ex aquis, & per aquas, aſſiſtente Verbo."</note> Therefore, the waters were the foundations of the whole, after they had been brought forth into the light by the presence of light from the womb of the dark Chaos; before which time, they were called not "Waters," but "unformed matter." Hence Job says: *He reveals the foundations out of the darkness, and brings the shadow of death into the light.* <note>original: "Reuelat fundamenta è tenebris, & educit in lucem vmbram lethalem."</note> And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note> says: *There was an infinite shadow in the abyss; water moreover and a thin intellectual Spirit were within the Chaos by divine power: then the holy splendor flourished, which led forth the moist nature from beneath the sand.*

<margin>Pimander 1.</margin>
And in another place, he says: *Pimander <note>The "Pimander" or "Poimandres" is the "Divine Mind" or "Shepherd of Men" in the Hermetic texts.</note> changed his form (that is, his hidden and privative disposition) into one that was open and manifest; which being done, he suddenly revealed the universe. For I beheld (he says) a certain immense spectacle: namely, all things converted into light, exceedingly sweet and pleasant; but a little later, a certain horrendous shadow slunk down with an oblique revolution, and migrated into the moist nature, etc.* By these things, it is right to observe first, that the hidden nature of Pimander—or the Divine Mind—had been changed into that manifest and lucid one. Secondly, that by the apparition or emanation of the divine light, both the dark dwelling of the hidden Pimander (namely, the horrendous shadow or the foul and deformed darkness) and that manifest Tabernacle (namely, the most pleasant Light revealing all things) were made plain. And finally, that the moist nature was revealed by the repercussion of the darkness. Indeed, the contrary actions between light and darkness are here brilliantly explained, and that at the very instant of the creation of the entire worldly fabric.

Now it remains for us to approach more closely to an explanation of the nature and condition of this hidden property, and to speak a few words on its simple disposition, as it exercises itself every hour and moment, both in the greater world <note>The Macrocosm (the universe).</note> since its creation, and in the lesser world <note>The Microcosm (the human being).</note>.

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>
In the first place, therefore, it is written that *the darkness was divided from the light*; whence afterwards both night and day were ordained by the Creator in the orb of the lands. Of these, the former is the privation of light, and the latter is the abolition of darkness; and the one God works toward the diverse effect of each property. When He hides Himself, then the darkness is said to have dominion; but when He dilates and manifests Himself, then the Light is accustomed to prevail over the darkness.

<margin>2 Samuel 22; Psalm 105; 1 Chronicles 6:1.</margin>
*God,* says the holy page, *made darkness His hiding place.* <note>original: "tenebras Deus poſuiſti latibulum ſuum."</note> So also He Himself sometimes spreads out a thick and dark cloud for a covering; indeed, Jehovah Himself said that He dwells in the thick darkness.

<margin>Exodus 10.</margin>
Was it not also by the power of this hidden, contractive property that the three-day punishment of palpable darkness was produced for the Egyptians?
<margin>Luke 23; John 24.</margin>
And was it not darkness that was made over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth?
<margin>Genesis 15.</margin>
Was it not also through the mediation of this property that darkness was placed between Israel and the Egyptians? And that a dark horror fell upon Abraham? Are not the blackest clouds in the air usually procreated by this kind of contractive power, so that the entire surface of the earth seems deformed and obscured by gloom? Indeed, God Himself did these things by that property of His; of which David speaks thus:
<margin>Psalm 104:20.</margin>
*You have made the darkness, and it was night.* <note>original: "Tu tenebras poſuiſti, & facta eſt nox."</note> Do we not observe the very air being changed into hard and opaque ice by the power of this cold and contractive faculty? *He casts down his ice,* says the Royal Psalmist, *like morsels; he sends forth snow like wool, and the frost*

<margin>Psalm 147:16.</margin> "...he scatters the frost like ashes: who can stand before his cold?" And Job says: *By his breath, the mighty God produces ice; by the breath of God, the frost is frozen.* These passages indicate the binding and coagulative power of cold (the daughter of Darkness) <note>original: "striptica & coagulatiua frigoris (Tenebrarum filiæ) potestas"</note>; it acts through a cold breath of the divine property—a constricting force that halts the flowing movement of heat. Conversely, the action of heat, arising from the "luminous word" or the positive, expanding property of God, usually destroys the work of this constricting property. Hence, it follows in the text of the same Psalmist: *Sending forth his word, he melts them; as soon as he blows his wind, the waters flow,* etc. It is as if he had said: that same God, in his cold breath (his hidden and contracting faculty), shatters thin, transparent air into dense, opaque snow, and into frost, ice, and thick rime—substances that do not flow, but remain fixed and immobile. Yet again, by his warm breath (his manifest, expanding, and thinning property), he dissolves those frozen masses and makes them fluid, mobile, and transparent once more. Through these examples, you see the effects of the "hidden God" <note>The "Hidden God" refers to the aspect of the Divine that withdraws light to create form and matter.</note> in the greater world.

<margin>Genesis 15.</margin> The Holy Bible also depicts for us the acts and effects of this power within the "lesser world" (man) in this manner: *A dark horror,* says Genesis, *invaded Abram,* etc. It is as if one were to say: God covered the spirit of Abraham with a horrible gloom and obscurity, leaving him shaken by no small fear. Furthermore, it is clear from these words that darkness <margin>2 Samuel 22.</margin> is radically implanted within man: *You will enlighten my darkness.* And elsewhere it is said: *I will turn the darkness before them into light.* And elsewhere: <margin>Isaiah 42.</margin> <margin>Job 5.</margin> <margin>John 12.</margin> <margin>1 John 2.</margin> <margin>Ephesians 5.</margin> *The crafty shall meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope at noonday as in the night.* Moreover, the Evangelist seems to explain human darkness thus: *He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. He who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness.* And the Apostle says: *You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.* By this speech, he argues for a transition from one divine property to another: namely, from the limit of severity and perdition to that of mercy and salvation. For those who refuse to obey the commands of God’s light are afflicted by the darkness—the "hidden" property of God. For we find it written in <margin>Nahum 1.</margin> that *Darkness pursues the enemies of God.* 

Yet we see that darkness is no more the cause of death and disease than light is the cause of a beneficial life. Hence <margin>Job 23.</margin> Job said: *I did not perish because of the looming darkness, nor did the gloom cover my face.* Indeed, if we consider the matter with a slightly more direct gaze, we shall see that just as the world in its composition carries traces of both darkness and light (being forged from both earth and heaven), so too does man himself. Man, who is the "image and son of the world" as <term>Hermes</term><note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition.</note> says, enjoys his own earth, which we call the **Body**, and has his own heaven, which is his **Soul** or interior. Therefore, it is no wonder if a man devoted to carnal affections is immersed in darkness and clings to the "privative" property of the hidden God. By neglecting the bright heaven (the seat of the "manifest" God) and committing all his delights and joys to the opaque and dark earth, he takes the path of perdition and death, leaving behind the paths of life and salvation. <margin>Wisdom 9.</margin> The Wise Man <note>Solomon, traditionally credited with the Book of Wisdom.</note> seems to confirm this with these words: *The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind that muses upon many things,* etc. 

With these things well considered, we see with open eyes that we and our works are in the hand of God, who does with us whatever he wills. He may either cloud our senses and reason with his gloom and darkness through his hidden property—so that we, walking in darkness, grope at midday like the blind—or, by benevolently sending forth the light of his face, he may lead us in his good paths through enlightenment. Does not Job himself seem to recount this same thing in plain <margin>Job 12.</margin> speech? *Behold,* he says, *he destroys so that it cannot be rebuilt; he shuts a man in so that he cannot be opened. With him is strength and power; both the deceiver and the deceived are his. He leads counselors away stripped and makes judges into fools; he overthrows the mighty. He increases the nations and destroys them; he takes away the heart of the leaders of the earth and makes them wander like drunken men, groping in the dark without light,* etc.

### On the super-celestial origin of Life and Health.

<margin>Psalm 104:29.</margin>
These things, therefore, most clearly explain the effects of both divine properties: one of which leads into error and directs one toward the paths of death; the other, guided by the divine lamp, indicates the right way and instructs in the truth. Did not the Royal Psalmist <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> also clearly explain this when he spoke thus: *All creatures look to God in expectation; when God gives to them, they gather; when he sends forth his spirit, they are recreated and satisfied with good; when he hides his face, they are troubled; when he takes back their spirit, they expire.*

<margin>Job 34:14.</margin>
But Job specifically turns this same discourse toward man himself, speaking in this way: *God established man upon the earth, applying His soul to him; if He were to take back or withdraw his spirit, or breath, or soul to Himself, all flesh would fail or expire at once, and man would be turned to ashes, etc.*

<margin>

Psalm 30.

Through these discourses we are taught, first, that all life comes from the luminous God who emits His **life-giving spirit** <note>original: "spiritū suum viuificum"</note> to every creature through His positive and luminous property. However, by the **contraction** <note>The act of pulling back or withdrawing light/energy into Himself.</note> of their luminous life into Himself through His privative property, they suddenly fail and die. By the mere hiding of His face from a creature, the spirit is immediately troubled, and the creature continues to be sick even unto death, unless God takes pity on him and looks upon him again with a benevolent ray of life and health. Ultimately, in many places in the Sacred Scripture, we find that God makes and gives life to the creature through the emission of His goodness, and brings death through its contraction into Himself. From this also come good and evil, health and disease, generation and decay, and all things in both worlds <note>The macrocosm (universe) and microcosm (man).</note>, whether positive or privative. Indeed, He does all things, and in all these properties of His—namely, by either giving or taking away—He acts in the heavens and on the earth; and *no one is to ask Him, "Why have you done this?" And yet, let impiety be far from God, and iniquity from the Almighty: for it is His property in His wrath or "un-will" <note>original: "noluntate." A technical term meaning the withdrawal of the Divine Will, or the "negative" aspect of God's volition.</note> to be indignant, and in His benevolence or "will" to give life. For He alone is the one who has power over life and death. "I (He says) will kill and I will make to live; I will wound and I will heal; I will strike and I will cure, and there is no one who can rescue from my hand." "If God (says Job) subverts all things and contracts them into one, who shall contradict Him? Or who can say, 'Why do you do so?'"*

<margin>Isaiah 8.</margin>
But sometimes we see Him work through His contractive property—namely, by taking away the light of His face—for the sake of punishing sins. For (says the Prophet), *He who curses his God and does not believe in His word shall look upward and gaze upon the earth, and behold: tribulation and darkness, dissolution and anguish, and a following gloom from which he will not be able to fly away.*

<margin>2 Corinthians 4.</margin>
And the Apostle says, *The god of this world blinds the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ does not shine upon them, etc.* From this it is clear that there are both spiritual and physical, palpable darknesses, with which God is accustomed to darken both the internal and external spirit. Sometimes He affects the righteous man with evil for the sake of testing him, as happened to the righteous Job; sometimes He hardens the hearts of men and causes them to sin so that, by exercising His power over them, He might declare His honor, glory, and omnipotence to the World, and thus become known to all nations upon the earth. And this happened to Pharaoh, from which it came to pass that the fear of the God of the Israelites was held in reverence and esteem among all nations. For the nations were struck with fear by the immense power of the God of the Israelites. But there are also infinite other hidden reasons for divine works, whether tending toward death and disease or life and health, which to inquire into or scrutinize would be not only most vain, but would also savor of the extreme madness of folly and rashness, if we attend to these words of the Apostle:

<margin>Romans 11:33.</margin>
*How incomprehensible are the judgments of God, and how unsearchable are His ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? The Monad <note>original: "Monas"; the divine "One" or ultimate Unity from which all things originate</note>, or the most holy *One*, behaves far differently in this His manifest and open or luminous property than in that which is latent and hidden. For just as in the former He creates, acts, illuminates, forms, gives life, and is accustomed to provide everything that is called "good" by means of His Wisdom; so indeed in the latter He deprives, destroys, and causes failure, darkens, kills, and deforms. Therefore, because of these good effects, that property is called by the holy scriptures *Grace and Truth; the Light of the world and Brilliance, Peace, Delight, or love and charity; Justice, Mercy, Life, Salvation, Goodness, Beauty*, and is named by various other titles following His good effects. But when, conversely, He is named according to His evil effects, He is called *Falsehood, the world's darkness, dissension and contention, hatred and envy, injustice, impiety and cruelty, death, infirmity, malice, ugliness or deformity*, and is named by various other titles following His evil effects. From this it is clear that just as each of these properties is accustomed to produce its effects through a certain wisdom, so the Apostle makes a distinction between one wisdom and another in this manner:

The light things flew up into the high region, and the heavy things settled under the moist sand; so that the moist nature was distinguished and balanced in a symphonic way by the luminous and fiery spirit, in right and orderly number, weight, and measure. First, heaven and earth were made; and then later He adorned the heaven itself with infinite stars by the luminous power of this spirit, He numbered their multitude and assigned them their own names, such as *Arcturus and Orion*, and assigned fixed places to the others, *granting sweet influences to the shimmering Pleiades.* He ordained the Sun *in the manner of a bridegroom, that he might come forth from his chamber, who rejoiced in his motion like a Giant to run his course.* He also turned the whole heaven in its circuit back to its place in one day: *He established the weight for the air, and weighed the waters by measure; for He binds them up in thick clouds, so that they are not torn under them: He makes a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunders.* For it is He who *thunders from heaven and utters His voice; He brings the winds out of His treasuries; He shut up the sea with doors, and makes the wonders of its rising, and calms the motion of its waves as He pleases: He causes the earth to bring forth grass, seed, and fruit* on one hand; and *cattle, creeping things, and beasts* on the other. Finally, by this Wisdom of His, He appointed man to rule over every creature. All these things (I say) were made by His word, and were created by the sending forth of His spirit; by means of which He gave life and breath and all things to all, which for that reason are said *to live in God, to move in God, and to be in Him.* Therefore it is said, *God works all in all, and that all things are from Him*, yet He Himself remains one; indeed, *He who is the Father of all, insofar as He Himself gives life to all, who is over all, and in all, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist.*

...the third property led, born and having emerged from the first two—namely, the **Spirit of Holy Wisdom**—hardly differing in its essential nature from the former ones, insofar as they are all nothing but the one, same, and indivisible Divinity. The subject of the waters therefore emerged from the dark mass; but its form, through which it was made into the shape of waters, proceeded from the bosom of the luminous emanation. The principle of their union consists in the **fiery spirit**, which is therefore said to be *borne over the waters* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2, "The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."</note>, imparting a fiery vigor to them. 

The reason for the consistency of the moist nature is as follows: for this Matter was not moist while it was in the womb of **Hyle** <term>Hyle: a Greek philosophical term for the primordial, unformed matter of the universe</term>; indeed, it abounded in a "styptic" or contracting cold, which made it like a mass congealed by frost and bound by the law of rest. In truth, "coldness" did not even obtain its name before the manifestation of "heat," which leapt forth from the bosom of the luminous extreme; nor did "heat" have a name or being before the manifestation of "coldness." This is because coldness could not be so named except insofar as it was found to be the absolute opposite to the action of heat, nor heat except in that it vehemently resisted the nature of coldness by its action. Just as an "agent" can hardly be considered except in respect to a "patient" (the thing acted upon) on which it acts, so conversely, a thing is not usually called "patient" unless an "agent" is necessarily presupposed. 

When these things are well contemplated, moisture is found in neither extreme on its own; rather, it is produced by the mutual action and passion <note>In this context, "passion" means the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> that occurs between coldness and heat. Consequently, the "Extremes" cannot even be called "dry" except in respect to moisture. For dryness is nothing other than the absence of moisture, just as, conversely, moisture is nothing other than the removal of dryness. Dryness, therefore, is nothing other than the absence of moisture already created, as moisture is the absence of dryness. Whence it is certain that before the appearance of light, the unformed matter from which the world was afterwards fabricated was neither cold nor hot, neither moist nor dry, but existed only in the "potential" for all these things; for which reason it is called by the name ***Nothing***.

Moisture, therefore, is a quality participating in both extremes, which is why it is the middle effect of their action and passion. We observe this in the **Elementary region**, where the Nature or Sphere of moisture—composed of dense and rare water (namely, the sea and the air)—is interposed between the opaque globe of the earth and the luminous sphere of fire. The denser portion of this sphere is situated near the dark orb (as it is closest to the source of cold), while its thinner portion is near the sphere of Light or Fire (as it is closer to the origin of heat). The same logic applied to the production of the universal moist nature in the first creation. For 

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
once the holy Emanation was made—by its own motion, which is more mobile and swift than any other motion—heat was excited within the mass that was originally dark or unformed matter. Acting upon that which was once at rest, and through its action, motion, and the penetration of luminous rays, the darkness (once immobile) now tends downward by the impulse of the light in an oblique revolution. 

<margin>Pimander 1.</margin>
And coldness, now revealed from its depths and forgetting its native sluggish condition, desires greatly to resist the assaults of the heat and to recover the disturbed rest of its unformed matter. By resisting the heat, it seems to react; and leaping forth from its dark source with its deformed matter (which was, as it were, dry and frozen), it wages war against the warm, pursuing offspring of the light. From this it happened that, in the common middle ground, that dry nature—carrying the reacting cold nature—is moistened by the action of the heat (whose nature is to dissolve what is frozen) and is reduced into a moist nature. And the darkness having been driven to the **Center** (which is the place furthest from the circumference in which the light moved), the universe filled the world with its resistance in such a form—either rarer or denser according to the greater or lesser predominance of light and heat within it. Thus, the luminous form that is within it retains it in its moist disposition forever, and prevents it from returning into that dark and deformed matrix of Hyle or **CHAOS**. For ma—

### On Supercelestial Life and the Origin of Health.

...this **primordial matter** <term>original: "hyle"; the ancient Greek concept of the fundamental, unformed substance of the universe</term> having been generated, insofar as it was nourished from eternity in rest and darkness, is by its very nature always inclined and prone to dark desires; always looking back toward that state of rest. For this reason, the more opaque and devoid of the "form of light" matter is in its condition, the more it is devoted to the acts and works of darkness. This is the cause behind why that ray of the mind, granted to humanity by **Divine Wisdom**, is so easily seduced into the error of darkness through the mediation of an opaque body and such an aerial spirit. Being as if blinded, it does not discern those things which are good, and thus it is mocked by the **Prince of the Air** <note>A biblical reference to the ruler of the worldly or demonic realm, from Ephesians 2:2</note>—or of this world, as the Apostle calls him. And this was the reason that the Wise Man broke out into these words:

<margin>Wisdom 9:15</margin>
> The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things; we can hardly guess at the things that are upon earth, and with labor we find the things that are before us; but who shall seek out the things that are in the heavens? Who shall know Your counsel, unless You give wisdom? <note>original: "Corpus quod corrumpitur, aggrauat animam..." from the Book of Wisdom.</note>

By these words, he seems to suggest that heavy matter, submerged in darkness, is the cause of error for the "subtle" or refined matter that is illuminated by only a little light; and thus it seduces the light enclosed with the spirit away from truth and into falsehood. Therefore, we see from these things how prone matter is to cling to its "deformed mother" <note>Referring back to Hyle or Chaos</note>, and to turn itself back from the son of light into that son of darkness. For there is no truth which is not from the Radiant God, who is Truth itself; nor is there any falsehood or false image which is not from the darkness. The opaque subject of darkness may appear to be what it seems, yet it only *seems* to be, since in reality it does not exist by or in itself.

<margin>Pimander 12.</margin>
For this reason, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom these Hermetic texts are attributed</note> concludes that the World is not good except through its participation in divine goodness; since its matter is nothing by itself but a "rude and undigested mass" <note>A classic description of Chaos</note>, which, if it is to be formed, is certainly formed by God. Therefore, he says that the spirit of the world did not exist when it was not yet born, but was already in that place from which it had to be born—namely, in God and from God, who illuminates and gives life to all things.

<margin>Asclepius 7.</margin>
Therefore, just as the moist matter of the world had arisen from **Chaos** as if from a dark mother—which implies deformity and foulness—so, with **radiant Nature** acting as a midwife, it was changed from its deformity and foulness into a beautiful and fair creature. Nevertheless, it cannot acquire any goodness in or by itself, having been born from a "bad and leprous mother"; rather, it acquires all its goodness from the radiant fountain. Hence, it seems to be prone to malice and malignancy in itself, even though its appetite is sometimes tempered and transmuted for the better by its form of light.

<margin>Asclepius 7.</margin>
Hence Hermes says:
> Just as matter is fertile with good quality, so is it equally fertile with malignancy.

Because of this specific portion in the composition of creatures, there is hardly anything to be found in the entire embrace of Nature that is completely perfect and good. Indeed, even in the Saints and Angels there is no complete stability, and the "Dwellers in Heaven" are not pure in the eyes of the Creator.

<margin>Job 15 / Job 5:2</margin>

What, then, should be judged of Man, the prince of sublunary creatures? **Job** called him abominable and contemptible (as one who drinks the water of iniquity) in respect to his darkness and his portion of material perversity. And yet, in respect to the rays of the Divine Mind within him, the **Royal Psalmist** <note>King David</note> declared him to be "a little lower than the angels," insofar as he is adorned with glory and honor. Therefore, in respect to this ornament, he is called the **Image of God**. We say, then, that if the matter of a celestial creature overflows with sacred light, that matter—forgetting its dark origin—directs all its desires toward contemplating the mysteries of divine light. Thus, in this "magnetic" state, it is accustomed to attract so much of the radiant divinity to itself that it is transformed into the divine and eternal nature.

<margin>Job 15.</margin>
But if the disposition of Matter should overcome the disposition of the light-form, it wastes away all the more, and moves backward into its primary nature of darkness with a contrary desire, the more the Light is diminished within it. From this arises the blessedness of the Angels and holy souls, for they are fashioned from the most subtle matter and, being intoxicated by a clear Nectar, they are snatched upward from the abyss of darkness toward the homeland of light. This is also the reason for the incorruptibility of the stars and celestial bodies; their formal substance is governed by a stronger and greater portion of informing light. Thus, they do not look toward the goal of death, destruction, or corruption at all, but long to aspire to the kingdom of eternal life. Conversely, the creatures of the elementary world are subject to corruption and mortality because there is more matter in them than there is a proportion of divine light. Therefore, by its original appetite, this matter tends toward deprivation or corruption, and while "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the active principle that gives shape and life to "matter."</note> hastens toward generation and new life, in this region matter is always in a state of motion, leading to alterations and changes. For this reason, he is called the *Prince of Darkness, the Prince of the air and of the lower world, according to whose ways those who are dead in sin are said to walk. Thus, they are called the children of darkness who are not enlightened; it is their lot not to strive against the principalities, powers, and rulers, the princes of the darkness of this world who dwell in high places* <note>A paraphrase of Ephesians 6:12 regarding spiritual warfare</note>, as the saints and the elect are accustomed to do. Instead, they worship and hold these powers in the highest esteem because, being blinded by darkness, they *take evil for good, darkness for light, and bitter for sweet*, according to the saying of the Prophet <note>Isaiah 5:20</note>; and so, unknowingly, they throw themselves willingly into the abyss of death.

From these things, we see that Matter in itself is evil to us, the children of light. It is so infected by a "maternal leprosy" <note>A metaphorical term for the inherent "stain" or imperfection of unformed primordial matter</note> that unless it is corrected by the power of life-giving light, it is prone to being reduced back into its deformed beginning and into nothingness.

Our **pyramids** <note>These refer to the author’s famous diagrams of two intersecting triangles—one of light and one of matter—representing the balance of spiritual and physical forces</note> illustrate this proportion of life-giving light within the moist matter of the world perfectly: namely, the proportion of the "formal" pyramid adapted to its "material" counterpart, and the "material" to its "formal." Although that monk Marin Mersenne <note>Marinus Mersennus (1588–1648) was a French mathematician and philosopher who famously criticized Robert Fludd’s occult and hermetic theories</note>—armed more with malice and falsehood than with the ray of truth—seems to mock these with such profanity, you will find upon a slightly more careful inspection that they clearly reveal the entire nature of things. For worldly Nature itself is nothing other than the disposition of moist matter springing out of the abyss of **Hyle** <term>original: "hyle"; the ancient Greek concept of primordial, unformed substance</term> by the presence of light, in proportion with the "informing" light. Therefore, from that arrangement of our Pyramids, it is clearly indicated by what proportion form exceeds matter in the celestial and super-celestial regions (which is the source of their greater or lesser incorruptibility and permanence), and by what dimension the mass of matter exceeds the formal power in the sublunary <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earth, characterized by change and decay</note> region, which produces its change and corruption.

<margin>Pimander 14. Asclepius 7.</margin>

But before I proceed further in this discourse of mine, I consider it worthwhile to explain to you a very clear example: namely, the binary Emanation of the **One Monad** <note>The "Monad" refers to the supreme Unity or God</note>—the privative and the positive—as well as their union in the composition of a secondary thing, clearly demonstrating its

### THE DEMONSTRATION OF THIS is explained in the description of the first emblem.

Therefore, from one radical source come the two principles of the world: **Light** and **Darkness**. From darkness, matter arose; from light, the *form* of the world <note>In Aristotelian and Hermetic philosophy, "form" is the active, spiritual principle that gives shape and life to "matter."</note> was born. Without these two, there is nothing in the world, and the world itself is nothing. Therefore, these two make up everything in the world, and yet all things are one; for the two are nothing but the one from which, through which, and in which all things exist. That "One," however, is outside and before all things, for it is the root of all. From the One, then, comes Darkness, from which arises matter, and from matter the *existence* of the world <note>original: "existentia"</note>, with the assistance of the divine act. From that same One also comes Light, from which arises form, and from form the *essence* of the world <note>original: "essentia"</note>. 

The world is thus full of both the subject of darkness and a luminous nature; it is brimming with both will and "non-will" <note>original: "noluntatis." In Fludd's philosophy, this refers to God's power to withdraw His light or creative will, resulting in darkness or "privation."</note>. It shares in both dark error and luminous truth; it is subject to the experiences of life and death, and is endowed with both evil and good—now raining down distress and misery upon mortals, now bringing them joys and happiness. 

By these things it is clear enough that God—the radical <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Monad" is a philosophical term for the ultimate, indivisible "One" from which all mathematical numbers and all of reality originate.</note>—acts in both of His properties: namely, by contracting Himself into Himself (and thus assigning dominion to the darkness of "deprivation") or by expanding Himself and offering His goodness to the world and its creatures. Indeed, He even sometimes does both—partly expanding and partly contracting Himself at once and in the same act—as will be clearly shown in the *following chapter* through the testimony of Holy Scripture.

Here, however, I would like you to understand in passing from the aforementioned demonstration that the logic and property of divine numbers can be gathered from these things, according to the intentions of the <term>Kabalists</term> <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) whose ideas were popular among Renaissance Christian scholars like Fludd.</note>, who attribute **ten names** of God (derived not from His essence, but from His properties) to His ten <term>Sephirot</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> or divine emanations, which flow from the unique <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>Hebrew: "The Infinite"; the unknowable Godhead before creation.</note>, or source of infinity. Some of these emanations tend toward severity, others toward mercy; and some regard both severity and judgment as well as clemency and mercy, as will be clearer below. These ten emanations (I say), along with the names derived from their properties, have allotted their origin from the aforementioned <term>quaternary number</term> <note>The number four (1, 2, 3, 4).</note>. For if you add that quaternary number (1, 2, 3, 4) together, they produce the <term>denary number</term> <note>The number ten (the Decad).</note> when joined. Thus, that quaternary number not only encompasses within itself the number of the ten Sephirot or emanations, but also possesses the same properties within itself. 

For the dark unity brings severity, death, privation, and miseries upon the children of light, just as the unity of light, from its own region, is accustomed to bring them clemency, life, position, and happiness and joy. Finally, the world—which is the fourth unity—is accustomed to participate in both severity and mercy. Furthermore, it also contains within itself the number of composition, namely the <term>septenary</term> <note>The number seven.</note>. For if you add those three unities together after the radical one—namely 1, 2, and 3—they make 6; to which, if the <term>radical Monad</term> <note>The original 'One' or starting point.</note> is added (without which the others are nothing), you produce the septenary number, composed from the number three (the formal) and the number four (the material). Finally, it encompasses within itself the number of confusion (the imperfect) and every number of perfection, and consequently every number. For beyond the number ten, no progression can be made, since all numbers that follow this one derive their origin from it and from those digits contained beneath it. Therefore, this denary number is (as **Hermes** testifies) the *Begetter of the Soul*, because in it Life and Light are united.

> *There he says, the numbers of the unity itself are born of the Spirit, and the unity embraces according to the tenfold ratio, and again the ten embraces the unity.* <note>original: "Ibi inquit, unitatis ipsius numeri sunt ex Spiritu nati, atq; unitas secundum rationem denariam amplectitur, rursusq; denarius unitatem." Therefore, since the world is composed of the union of a dark or material nature and a bright or formal one, there is no doubt that the subject of the world itself is inclined both toward darkness (and consequently toward those things called evils by the children of light) and toward light (from which, in its simple nature, good and beautiful things proceed). They come and are nourished. In this property of His, then (by contracting the invisible air), God covers the heavens with thick and visible clouds, which provide rain for the earth, so that He may cause the mountains to bring forth grass and give food to the cattle. That God does this through His contractive and cold property is confirmed by the fact that He makes thick and black clouds His pavilion <note>original: *tugurium*; literally a hut or booth, referring to God's dwelling place in the storm</note>—or as it is said elsewhere, His chariot. Therefore, because of this property, God is said to dwell in thick darkness. So it is also said that Wisdom was a covering for Israel, or a thick cloud by day and the light of the stars by night. For God worked in both His properties for the protection of the Israelites. So also Job says: *Who has fathered the drops of dew? From whose womb did the ice come forth? Who has made the sapphire clouds by wisdom? And who can tilt the water-jars of heaven?* Has He not also, by His hidden and contractive property, bound the waters in thick clouds so that they are not poured out? But again, in His manifest and expanded property—that is, by the gaze of the bright face of <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible, often used here to denote the active, revealing aspect of the Divine.</note>—*the waters were afraid, and the clouds poured out water.* For Jehovah, flying on the wings of the winds through His hidden property (namely, by contracting Himself into Himself, and the airy creation with Him), set the darkness as His hiding place; around Him was His tabernacle: dark water in the clouds of the air. And then, by His manifest property, expanding Himself out of Himself and sending forth the rays of His face from the darkness, at the brightness before Him, the clouds passed away and were dissolved; the waters or rains were sifted, while at the same time hail, coals, and fire were sent forth. By these things, the dual divine property seems best revealed in the same action: one side is thick, dark, and frozen by contracting, making clouds and hail; the other side thins <note>original: *rarefacit*; to make less dense</note>, breaks, and dissolves His thick pavilion. Indeed, the will of God was so unified in both properties that the hail did not suffer the violence of the fire, nor could the fire act to dissolve the hail.

<margin>Psalm 77.</margin>
Do we not also observe that in the same cloud, once **condensation** has occurred, the nature of the air is forced and contracted into water, stones, and hail? As it seems to be affirmed in the place cited before. Furthermore, elsewhere Job declared the various effects of these properties in the same subject in a more lucid manner: *Behold,* he says, *God is great, surpassing our knowledge; He draws up the drops of rain and pours down showers like torrents.*

<margin>Job 36; Job 12.</margin>
And elsewhere, regarding the punishment of mortals, he says: *Behold, God restrains the waters so that they dry up, and He sends them out so that they overturn the earth, etc.* And He Himself extends both these properties by His Word; by this, the <term>radical Monad</term> <note>The foundational "One" or single source from which all existence springs.</note> contracts and constricts no differently than He expands and dissolves through it; and yet that Word is one and the same with respect to its root, though it is varied in its effect.

Thus we see that from one and the same human soul, a word proceeds that is both negative and privative, as well as affirmative and positive; and yet these words are one in essence, since both are drawn from a single source. In the same way, we see the same flame condense and thin, harden and soften, destroy, and give life with appropriate heat. Or we see the one and same vapor either scattered into the air by **rarefaction** <note>The process of becoming less dense; the opposite of condensation.</note> or changed into drops of water by humid condensation; or converted into snow and hail, frost and hoarfrost (which differ in form from one another). So this one and the same Word, existing in the "will" of the speaker, is accustomed to exercise and carry out whatever He wishes—either according to His negative will, by contracting His power into Himself, or His affirmative will, by expanding and sending forth from Himself the rays of His benevolence—both in God Himself and in man, who is formed in the image of God.

<margin>Psalm 147.</margin>
By His Word (says the **Psalmist** <note>The author of the biblical Psalms.</note>), which runs very swiftly, and by His speech sent to the earth, *God gives snow like wool, and scatters the frost like ashes: He casts forth His ice like morsels; who can stand before His cold? Sending out His word, He melts them; as soon as He blows His wind, the waters flow, etc.* In this thread of speech, it seems to be argued that when the Word is sent to the earth by means of the North winds, a condensation and thickening of the thin occurs. This happens by reason of the cold contracting itself from the Word in its swift, constricting motion, and contracting the previously expanded creature into a thick cloud, and then into snow and hail.

From this, snow, hail, ice, frost, heavy rains, dews, and rain-mists are more frequent at that time: the dark nights are longer, leaves and fruits are destroyed, and the earth seems to mourn, to be harmed by the cold, and to fall ill. Yet, at the same very time, in the Southern region, by His warm and dry property, the air is rendered thinner (rarefied), and the harsh power of the cold seems to be rooted out by the presence of heat; the dark nights are shortened, the earth is brought to life, and it abounds and rejoices with flowers, grass, and fruits.

We conclude, therefore, that God acts through the Word in this world according to the disposition of matter and the time of year, using both His hidden, contractive property and its opposite, and this is done either for punishment and a scourge, or for beneficence—just as we may gather from the express words of the Holy Scripture.

But leaving the subject of the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm</term><note>The 'Great World' or the universe as a whole.</note>, we shall demonstrate that these same effects are produced by these two properties in the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm</term><note>The 'Little World,' referring to the human being as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>.

Since man is made in the image of the world, just as the world is made according to the pattern of the **Archetype** <note>The original model or divine blueprint in the mind of God.</note>, there is certainly no doubt that he is composed of the matter of the world and the divine ray that fills the world's matter. And so that this may appear more clearly to the observer, I would have him notice with what speed the mass of the human body, once the soul has breathed out in death, usually draws earthly coldness to itself and is burdened with great weight. But while the Soul remains and reigns in the body, we perceive that its entire mass or heap is bathed everywhere with heat and imbued with lightness. For the human Spirit is so filled with divine light and heat that, not only in its own nature—by reason of the presence of the rays of divine Wisdom—is it pure, celestial, and incorruptible fire, but it also attracts to itself every hour and moment a power from the heaven and the air similar to itself for its own continuation in the creature. This power is a fire so subtle, kind, and gracious, that it does not destroy and devour the form (after the manner of earthly fire), but rather preserves it and enriches it with life.
