# On the Celestial Origin of Life & Health.

...leading their qualities or virtues through all things: and dispersing darkness and mists.

<margin>Asclepius, 10</margin>
For this reason Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermetic philosophy.</note> says: *Just as the world is everlasting: so also is the Sun: always the governor of living things, or of all vitality: and he is their constant visitor and dispenser.*

Hence it was that the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy.</note> believed the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "anima mundi"; the concept of an intrinsic spirit that animates all nature.</note> had its seat and tabernacle in the Sun: from which creatures, not only sublunary <note>Those below the Moon, i.e., on Earth.</note> but also celestial, have obtained their life, lights, splendors, and glories. For this reason Heraclitus calls the *Sun the fount of celestial light*, and others call it the *heart of heaven*. Therefore, we believe it is hardly well-advised to follow the opinion of Cicero—namely, that a unique light and splendor should be attributed to all stars (excepting the Moon). But this is declared even more clearly because when the Sun is in the signs of the Zodiac, they then emit their own virtues and powers; and when he joins himself to the other wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> either by conjunction or some other aspect, he is observed to alter them in his own manner and to rule them, as it were, by his own nod.

It was for this reason, then, that Speusippus thought the Sun was called **Apollo** for this reason: because his power consists of "many fires" <note>original: "pluribus ignibus"</note>, insofar as he alone contains the power and light of all the stars. For the conjunctions of the stars do not produce effects until they are pregnant with Phœbean seed <note>The influence of the Sun.</note>. And Chrysippus derives the name **Apollo** from *a* and *poly* <note>original: "α & πολὺ"</note>, that is, "from the multitude": as one who contains the powers of all the stars. From this, he is called *Sol* by the Latins: as if he were *shining alone* <note>original: "solus lucens"</note>, and the *shining life*.

Furthermore, with everything being suffused on all sides by his light, power, and heat, he gently warms and cherishes and sweetly dries all lower things. As Ptolemy <note>An ancient astronomer and geographer.</note> testifies, and Averroes <note>A medieval Andalusian philosopher.</note> as well, the origin of life and generation lies with him: insofar as he, with moderate heat, cherishes the **primigenial moisture** <note>The fundamental fluid believed to sustain life.</note> of things, and rouses them every year to generation and growth. And we are taught by experience that this is most certain: for anyone contemplating the order of nature sees the benefits of life poured into all things by the approach of the Sun. From this, Aristotle concluded that *the Sun and man together generate man*, and *the Sun and the plant generate the plant*. Hence it is that he is called **Phœbus**, as if to say *light to life* <note>original: "φῶς τῷ βίῳ"</note>: that is, infusing light and life into all things. Likewise **Apollo**, according to Eusebius, because *he drives away diseases* <note>original: "ἀπαλλάττη τᾶς νόσους"</note>; or called *Apellin* by the Ancients; and by the Athenians *Alexikakos* <note>original: "Ἀλεξίκακος"</note>, that is, the *averter of evil*; and by Homer *Oulios* <note>original: "Οὔλιος"</note>, that is, the *author of Health*; or (as others say) *Apolyon* <note>original: "ἀπολύων"</note>, that is, *washing and purifying*, and consequently curing. By these names it is right to observe that he is not only the Father of life, but also the Author of health, preservation, and purification.

We conclude, therefore, that as long as a person breathes, they are said to live; and therefore Antiquity, with the best of right, ascribed the **Spirits** <note>The vital "pneuma" or breath that powers the body's functions.</note> that move the body, excite the senses, and nourish the thoughts and the mind, to the Sun (who moves and acts upon the universe and is, after God, the cause of all living things).

These **Spirits** (according to Homer) are said to be present in us daily in such a state as the Sun—the Prince and Lord of the Planets—breathes into the Spirit of the World, moves, irradiates, and prepares, refines, and elaborates through the medium of the air. This air, whatever its quality may be, we are compelled—willingly or unwillingly—to breathe in continually and necessarily. With the help of the lungs, we draw it through the mouth and the <term>rough artery<gloss>The trachea or windpipe.</gloss></term>, and receive it into the brain through the nostrils and into the whole body (which is entirely capable of breathing together and flowing together) through the <term>anastomoses<gloss>The connections or openings between blood vessels.</gloss></term> and pores of the arteries, as Hippocrates and Galen <note>Famous ancient Greek physicians.</note> attest. But we are also taught this by experience itself: for according to the motion and temperament of the air, which depends on the Sun and the entire face of the heaven, our Spirits are found to be duller on one day and more vigorous on another. This is especially true of the **animal spirits** <note>Spirits responsible for sensation and movement.</note> and those which flow from them, serving the senses and reason, just as the spirits of the blood serve the body. Hence, such spirits are accustomed to be present in us as the air is, and the spirits are such as the blood is, which encompasses the rest of the humors.

Finally, the Spirit of living things, prepared from the air by the influence of heaven, in a successive...

### CHAPTER V.
->On the healthy properties of the Moon.<-

The Moon is not undeservedly called the *Sister of the Sun* by those investigators more skilled in the mysteries of nature, insofar as these two are held to be the universal Rulers of all things in the world. For as the Sun is the father of native heat and the principal actor in the world, so indeed the Moon is called the ruler of the worldly humors, and the fount, source, and moderator of the radical moisture. Indeed, in the Microcosm, she is the governess of the humors from the moment of birth. For we learn from some Astrologers (among whom we name Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of a major astrological manual.</note>) that it is certain the nature of a composite being is altered by the various positions of the Lunar course. They hold that every living thing—both animal and vegetable—recognizes and feels her powers from the time the vital breath first sustained the perfected man and the spirit of the divine mind infused itself into the body.

Furthermore, it was observed by the Egyptian Astronomers that even in adult age, the Moon can foretell what the coming days will be like, not only for the sick but also for the healthy. Indeed, she declares her power in the heavens and in the sea; she shows herself clearly as the ruler of the ebb and flow of the tides and the damp state of the air. In the humors of all creatures, she proves herself a mother. Therefore, it is clear that in the generation of things, because of the moisture over which she presides, she is held to be the provider of matter—just as her brother, the Sun, is the provider of form because of his heat. One of these can hardly stand without the other, bound by an individual and brotherly bond; for we see that no active force <note>original: "agens"</note> can exist without its destined recipient <note>original: "patiente"; in medieval philosophy, the "patient" is the matter that receives the action of the "agent."</note>.

This star, therefore, according to the doctrine of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century astronomer.</note>, excels in moistening because it is closest to the Earth and near to the rising moist vapors. For this reason, it affects bodies, makes them soft, and is consequently the primary passive element in putrefaction.

Furthermore, just as in the process of Generation the Sun is called the *Father*, so indeed the Moon is named the *Mother*. It is for this reason that the sign or "House" of the Sun is masculine (namely, Leo), while that of the Moon is feminine.

By these things, it can be clearly seen that no generation can occur without the assistance of both. Consequently, without their mutual meeting and presence, nothing in this lower material world can be born or produced.

For this reason, Orpheus <note>The legendary Greek poet and musician associated with mystical hymns.</note> in his Hymns calls these two the *life-giving and prolific eyes of the world*. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, in the passage cited before, calls them the most excellent instruments of divine nature, serving both the birth and growth of things as well as their death and decrease. Therefore, elsewhere he also acknowledges the Sun and Moon as the authors and, as it were, parents of the generation of all things after God. For the Moon [provides the] ma— <meta>catchword: teriam (matter)</meta>

# Of the celestial origin of Life & Health.

<note>original: "[ma]teriam"</note> ...prepares the matter, while the Sun provides the form. By this we are taught that the Moon is the Sun’s companion, representative, and sister. Hence, just as he is called *Phoebus* <note>A name for Apollo, the Sun god, meaning "bright" or "radiant."</note> by the Poets, so indeed she is called *Phoebe*.

Furthermore, the Moon is observed to have such great power over living things that, as she wanes, the marrow of the bones is seen to decrease, as does the wateriness in the <term>ventricles of the brain <note>In early modern medicine, these were thought to be the seat of various mental faculties and humors.</note></term>. Conversely, as she waxes, the quantity of both the marrow and the watery humors increases.

Moreover, the temperament of the body—whether healthy or sick—is noted to vary according to the Moon’s four quarters. According to the basic principles of the <term>Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who classified the physical world through these four qualities.</note></term>, the first quarter is hot and moist; the second is hot and dry; the third is cold and dry; and the fourth is cold and moist.

Has it not also been proven by the infallible observation of Physicians that the <term>crisis <note>original: "crisin" — the turning point of a disease that determines recovery or death.</note></term> of a disease follows the Moon’s quarters, counting from the place or degree in which she was moving at the hour the patient took to their bed? Indeed, I believe it is hidden from no one of the female sex that the monthly cycles of healthy women follow the motion of the Moon in an exquisite manner.

We conclude, therefore, that the entire substance of the earthly body—whether considered in its simple nature or in its composition—is in some way governed by the providence of this light or divinity. Finally, among the parts of the body, she claims for herself the <term>womb <note>original: "matricem"</note></term> in which the fetus is conceived and the conception is nourished, until, at the command of <term>Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth.</note></term>, the birth breaks through the maternal enclosures. Furthermore, she presides over the breasts and the left eye, just as the Sun is said to preside over the right. Among the faculties, she rules the natural and vegetative power. Among the humors, <term>Phlegm <note>original: "Pituita"</note></term> is ascribed to her; for it is found that phlegm increases as the Moon waxes and decreases as she wanes. By her complexion, she renders men <term>phlegmatic <note>A personality type characterized by being calm, cool, and potentially sluggish, associated with an excess of phlegm.</note></term>.

### CHAP. VI.
### Of the healthful properties of Mercury.

This Planet is indeed like a certain *Proteus* <note>A sea-god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape at will.</note>; by its nature and condition, it is remarkably versatile, as all those learned in Astronomy seem to acknowledge along with <term>Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer and astrologer.</note></term>, the prince among them. For his breath or influence is observed to be masculine if he looks upon masculine planets, but feminine with feminine ones. Consequently, he is a <term>Hermaphrodite <note>Mercury was often viewed as gender-neutral or dual-gendered in alchemy and astrology.</note></term>: hot with the hot, moist with the moist, cold with the cold, and dry with the dry. Finally, he is fortunate with the fortunate, especially if he is joined to them in a favorable <term>aspect <note>The angular relationship between planets in the sky.</note></term>. Indeed, in his own condition—for the reasons previously alleged—he is observed to be remarkably changeable, convertible, and common, much like the nature of the Air (which for this very reason can properly be called *Mercury*). For sometimes he stirs up winds in the air and takes on a windy nature, most rapidly assuming the condition now of the Sun, now of the Moon, and sometimes of others.

Furthermore, insofar as he does not wander far from the Sun, he is sometimes believed to have a power almost equal to the Sun itself in drying and absorbing moisture. Yet at other times, because of his proximity to the Moon, Ptolemy testifies that he possesses great power in moistening. Therefore, he says that this *Star* <margin>*Book 1. Apollo.*</margin> *is the bringer of sudden changes in either direction.*

Among the human faculties, he rules the <term>animal power <note>The "soul" or "spirit" responsible for sensation and voluntary movement.</note></term>, and especially the imaginative and rational faculties; he renders the intellect subtle and remarkably penetrating. Among the temperaments, he is said to have power over <term>Melancholy <note>The humor associated with the earth and the planet Saturn, but here linked to Mercury's intellectual depth.</note></term>. This is why Melancholics of this kind are observed to be the most ingenious and most devoted to every branch of Knowledge. Among the humors, yellow and black bile are attributed to him. Among the limbs, there are some who ascribe the gallbladder to him.

We conclude, therefore, that just as this Star is versatile and changeable in the manner of a Chameleon, so indeed it is observed to be good with the good; and then its nature...

### C H A P T E R   V I I.
->*Concerning the healthy properties of Saturn and Mars.*<-

**A**lthough Saturn is generally estimated by the Chaldeans, Arabs, and Greeks—and specifically by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an influential astronomer and geographer.</note> and Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>—as an imbalanced and harmful star, and is consequently held to be the *Greater Malefic* <margin>//</margin> <note>original: "Infortunio maiori"; in astrology, Saturn was traditionally considered the most difficult or unlucky planet.</note>, yet in certain matters, through the diligent observation of a wise and skilled Physician, he is noticed to be quite beneficial. For example, his restrictive power contributes much to the cure of fluxes <note>The abnormal flow of fluids from the body, such as hemorrhages or diarrhea.</note>. Therefore, the Physician ought to wait for the hour in which Saturn holds dominion, and also that time when he is strongest in the heavens, when applying medicine intended to constrict and restrain a flux.

Furthermore, it very often happens that the planet causing the flux is corrected and its malice diminished when it forms a favorable aspect with Saturn. Then, the malignancy of this star is sometimes noticed to be restrained, tempered, and turned toward goodness by the presence of good stars <note>In this context, "stars" refers to planets.</note> that are stronger in that celestial field, as is noted abundantly *elsewhere*. Finally, this star—through the firmness of thought, assiduity of study, and persistent labor—almost everywhere brings with it pleasure and delight, which indeed seems to the mind a certain supreme and peculiar good. For this planet brings with it that desirable kind of <term>Melancholy <note>In the Renaissance, "heroic melancholy" was associated with profound intellectual and philosophical insight.</note></term> that is so pleasing and familiar to Philosophers.

By the same reasoning, the *Martial Planet* <note>Mars</note> behaves in its own condition; he is fiery and burning, just as Saturn is cold and dry. <margin>//</margin> Hence, because of his imbalance or parching heat, he is greatly harmful. But in truth, that immoderate heat is desired in the cure of certain diseases. For in Paralysis, skilled physicians are accustomed to incite a Martial fever <note>A fever associated with the heat of Mars, intended to "burn off" the cold humors causing the paralysis.</note> so that, through its mediation, the disease may be cured. Likewise, in cold and damp imbalances, the Physician must wait for the aid of Mars in his exaltation or dominion for a more refined cure. And also the planet which is the author of that illness is weakened and made more manageable by a benevolent aspect of Mars dominating in the sky, so that it may be subdued by the Physician.

I will say no more of these malevolent planets in this place, because in the *following Treatise*, where diseases are discussed, we shall make fuller mention of them, with the assistance of Divine Providence.

### CHAPTER I.

-> On the healthy properties of the Winds in general. <-

<margin>Pim. 2.</margin> <note>Likely a reference to the "Pimander" (Poimandres), the first tractate in the Corpus Hermeticum.</note>
<image-desc>A square decorative initial box containing the letter 'C' amidst intricate vine and foliage patterns.</image-desc>
Since the air (as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many foundational hermetic, alchemical, and medical texts were attributed.</note> says) is a subtle body, that body indeed penetrates all other things by its sharp rarity; and running to and fro everywhere, it is known to fill and permeate all things. If we consider this carefully, we shall find that the teaching of Galen <note>A Greek physician whose theories of the four humors dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> is by no means to be rejected: by which we are taught that the surrounding air is the foremost among those causes which necessarily alter us, both according to and beyond nature. This is because it is partly drawn in through the pores of the skin by the veins and arteries, and partly introduced through respiration to the joyful chamber of the heart as well as to the ventricles of the brain. This spiritual body, filling the vast cavity of the world, is thought not to exist by itself <note>original: "per se"</note> insofar as it is considered according to its own essence—being neither cold, nor hot, nor moist, nor dry—except in that it held a certain confused participation from its mother, Chaos, from the first creation. It is nothing other than the Mercurial Spirit of the confused and shapeless waters, ordained to receive whatever nature is instilled into it by the uncreated Spirit. Whence it happens that when the North Wind blows—or rather the Angel of that quarter emitting his Spirit—the air is changed into an earthy disposition. But when the South Wind blows, it changes into a damp disposition with warmth; yet by the blowing of the East Wind, it is known to take upon itself a fiery disposition; just as it takes a watery one from the breath of the West.

From these things it is clearly evident that the entire temperament of the air consists in the blowing of the Winds, and that it is continually varied into this or that element according to the dominion of the various Winds. It is for this reason that Air, <term>Spirit</term> <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the "pneuma" or the vital, invisible substance that carries life through the body.</note>, and <term>Wind</term> denote one and the same thing, as is witnessed by that Hebrew word רוח <term>ruach</term> <note>A Hebrew term meaning "breath," "wind," or "spirit."</note>: the meaning of which comprehends those three words—namely, Air, Spirit, and Wind—and indeed even "Angel." Therefore, it is manifest that just as these blasts of Wind are observed to render the air either healthy or contagious and sickly by their breath—and again sometimes making it gloomy and troubled, and sometimes clear and serene—so indeed does this Spirit provide both the food of life and inspiration, as well as the subject for various diseases and infirmities. Since it is accustomed to penetrate all things and surround all living creatures, it is noted for introducing into the bodies of animals breaths that are either favorable to health or those that bring with them infirmities and sometimes death. And this itself seems to differ in no way from the doctrine of Galen and Hippocrates; indeed, in Holy Scripture, God is accustomed to strike the disobedient with corrupted air. Do we not also daily see infinite alterations produced in the air by the various blasts of the winds? Through these, we see even the <term>Microcosmic</term> air <note>The internal "spirit" or atmosphere of the human body, viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>, as well as the body of the earth itself, wonderfully affected for better or worse, as will be seen more clearly in what follows.

## CHAPTER II.

-> In which the healthy disposition of the North Wind and its companions is explained. <-

Although we have argued abundantly concerning the Winds and their causes in our *History of Meteorology* <note>original: "Historia nostra Meteorologica"; likely referring to another of the author's scientific works</note>, we shall nevertheless mention in this place their various powers and dispositions that are favorable to human health—just as we shall discourse at length upon their sickly power in the *following Treatise of this volume*.

To begin our investigation into the Boreal or Northern winds, we say that the principal wind of that region blows directly from the pole of the world through its Axis and is called *Boreas* <note>The North Wind</note>. Its side companion to the East is called *Aquilo* <note>The Northeast Wind</note>, and that situated toward the West is named *Circius* <note>The Northwest Wind</note>.

The Prince of these Winds, namely *Boreas*, is by its own property absolutely cold, dry, earthy, and melancholic <note>In the theory of the four humors, "melancholic" corresponds to the element of Earth and the qualities of cold and dryness</note>. Hence, by its natural action, it is accustomed to take away rains and makes the air subtle, clear, thin, and dry; it purges and purifies the air from the corrupt and pestilential disposition introduced by *Auster* <note>The South Wind, traditionally associated with heat, moisture, and disease</note>.

From this, the most skilled in Medicine conclude that it diminishes the superfluities <note>Excess fluids or waste products</note> of the animal body, and by its coldness it constricts the skin and closes the pores. In this way, it retains the natural heat within the body; for this reason, the natural heat is rendered stronger in performing its duty, and the office of concoction <note>The "cooking" or digestion of food within the body</note> is better perfected. Thus, the natural virtue <note>The body's innate power to heal and function</note> is seen to be strengthened by this means.

<margin>Constantine, Book 5, ch. 4.</margin>
Furthermore, Experience has proven and Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> has taught us that long-lasting blasts of the North Wind render bodies agile and well-colored, and they constrict and harden them; they even render the sense of Hearing clear and easy. And Constantine <note>Constantine the African, a 11th-century physician and translator of Arabic medical texts</note> says that *Boreas*, by its blowing, compresses wicked humors and retains them so they do not fall into other limbs. Similarly, this Wind is said to drive away pestilence and to be beneficial and favorable to Health.

By a similar reasoning, the case is the same with its two aforementioned side-winds, which are also cold and dry, though by reason of impurity. For *Aquilo*, being situated between the pole and the Eastern corner, participates somewhat—though imperceptibly—in the disposition of the *East* wind. Thus it is not as cold as *Circius*; and conversely, *Circius* is not as dry as *Aquilo*, since it turns somewhat toward the position of the West wind, which is moist. From this it is clear that the latter participates more in Western moisture, and the former in Eastern dryness.

<margin>Aristotle, Book 14 on the Generation of Animals.</margin>
Furthermore, it is the nature of these winds to harden bodies, to open their pores <note>Though the author earlier mentioned closing pores to retain heat, the "opening" here likely refers to the "thinning" or "clearing" of the skin's spirit</note>, and consequently to render them more robust and spirited; to purify the humors, to make the spirit clear, to aid digestion, to rectify pestilent air, and to aid the power of generation. Hence Aristotle says: *If the wind be Northern during conception, the infant will be Male; if Southern, a female.* But we have included all of this in the following Distinction.

### CHAPTER III.

->In which the healthy property of the Southern Wind and its side companions is described.<-

Just as we see God (who is the fundamental spirit of all spirits) exercise at times His merciful and healthy property toward mortals, and at other times exercise that wrathful and severe one upon the world: so indeed we believe that no breath proceeds from Him which does not carry with it a property that is sometimes benevolent and favorable to health, and sometimes malevolent and adverse to life and well-being. From this, therefore, it is certain that just as each of the winds sometimes brings with it benefits and healthy effects for both the *Macrocosm* <note>the Universe</note> and the *Microcosm* <note>the Human Body</note>; so indeed they sometimes bring with them very many inconveniences and infirmities: as will be clearly enough explained in the *following Treatise*. For in this place, I have proposed to treat of the benign gifts of the winds suited to the life and health of mortals.

The *Southern* Wind <note>original: "Australis"</note> is therefore opposite in its motion to the *Northern* one <note>original: "Septentrionali"</note>. Wherefore, just as the latter blows from the point of the *Arctic* Pole: so indeed the former is accustomed to send its breaths from the *Antarctic* Pole through the Axis of the world. This wind also claims for itself two side winds serving it, as it were, from each side: of which that which looks toward the eastern part is called *Notus* and *Euro-Auster* <note>the Southeast Wind</note>; that which is placed toward the Western part is called *Auster-Africus* <note>the Southwest Wind</note>. All three of these are hot and moist in their condition. But indeed, *Euro-Auster*, participating somewhat in the heat and dryness of the East, is hotter than the others and not as moist: whereas on the other side, the *South-West Wind* <note>original: "Africus"</note> is not as hot, and is more moist than the other two, inasmuch as it approaches somewhat the Western quarter, whose blast is cold and moist.

The benefits which the South Wind brings are of this sort: It opens the pores of the body which by chance are closed too tightly: and consequently draws out sweats: through which superfluous vapors <note>original: "fumi", literally 'smokes' or 'fumes'</note> retained in the body may depart. It dissolves cold and thick humors, and consequently makes hard things soft.

Of this condition also are its *side-neighboring winds*, which are all warm and moist, and are likened to Spring; in their temperament <note>Latin: "complexione," referring to the balance of bodily humors</note>, they are related to blood <note>the sanguine humor</note>, just as the North Wind has its relation to Melancholy <note>the black bile humor</note>.

The South Wind, with its side-neighboring companions, sometimes acts mercifully. For in the:

**Macrocosm <note>the Great World or Universe</note>:**
* It softens things that are unnaturally hard.
* It produces rains and dews for dry and sterile earth, by which the earth may bring forth herbs, grasses, seeds, and fruits.
* If it be small and brief, it clarifies the air in some measure.
* It is of a sanguine and spring-like nature.

**Microcosm <note>the Small World or Human Body</note>:**
* It opens the pores that were blocked by excessive Northern cold.
* It emits sweats copiously.
* It drives superfluous humors <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health</term> out of the body through sweats.
* It softens and ripens hardnesses that are contrary to nature.
* It relaxes humors that were frozen and thickened in the body by the cold of ice.

But in truth, both philosophers and physicians agree on this: that just as the North Wind is believed to be the healthiest of all winds, followed by the *East Wind*; so indeed the *South Wind*, with its companions, is said to be the most opposed to health of all. Wherefore this wind, with its companions, is accustomed to bring the greatest damage and inconvenience to both Worlds: although in some situations it is favorable, as will be seen more clearly in the *following Treatise*.

### CHAPTER IV.

->In which the healthy property of the East Wind is described.<-

That wind which blows from the Autumnal Equinox <note>the time of year when day and night are of equal length</note>, which is at the middle point of the Eastern Quarter, is called in Latin *Subsolanus* <note>original: "Subsolanus", meaning "under the sun"</note>, because it blows from the rising of the Sun directly under the Equinoctial Circle: whence in Greek it is called Apeliotes <note>original: Απηλιωτης, meaning "from the sun"</note>. This is the prince of the Eastern winds, which with its side-neighbors is hot and dry, fiery, and choleric <note>associated with yellow bile</note>. But indeed, that side-neighbor is called *Eurus* <note>the South-East wind</note>, inasmuch as it turns toward the South and inclines somewhat toward Southern moisture; while the other, namely *Caecias* <note>the North-East wind</note>, being nearer to the North, tends toward its coldness and dryness, though somewhat imperceptibly. 

But the *East Wind* <note>Subsolanus</note>, which participates in a moderate temperament and stands in the middle, is a sweet, lovable, pure, subtle, and healthy wind, and that especially in the morning time, insofar as it is observed to blow under the rays of the Sun then, and in the subtle air tempered by it: whence it happens that it is found to bring nothing of poison with it at that time. Hence it is, therefore, that the Eastern air is so pure, subtle, and only moderately dry: namely because this wind, situated in the middle between the moist and hot South Wind and the dry and cold North Wind, takes on a nature of moderate temperament, which neither exceeds in heat nor seems to surpass in dryness. Wherefore it not only works the aforementioned commendable effects in the air, but also renders the waters healthy, clear, and of good taste. By these things it is indicated that this principal wind, by grace of its temperature, is accustomed to preserve the body in health, and makes the waters healthier, and the flowers and herbs sweeter than the West wind renders them. It follows, therefore, that its blowing conserves health, and is both convenient and favorable to the human body and spirit; namely, because it blows from a place and air that is more subtle and temperate. And hence it is, that architects cause the principal windows of houses to face the Eastern region: because

### CHAPTER V.

->In which the health-giving Power of the West Wind is discerned and explained.<-

From the Vernal Equinox—that is, from the Western corner—blows *Favonius* <note>the West Wind</note>, which is considered a sufficiently healthy wind. For this reason, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar</note> maintains that it is called *Favonius* in Latin because it nurtures <note>Latin: "nutrit," punning on "faveo/favonius"</note> things that are born; furthermore, because of its sweetness, it is called *Zephyrus*.

By its disposition, it is believed to be temperately cold, moist, and phlegmatic <term>phlegmatic: associated with the humor of phlegm and the element of water</term>, since the Sun does not remain long in the West. From this it happens that its nature is, as it were, spring-like, insofar as it is eager to produce herbs, grasses, and fruits.

For this reason, it is judged to be healthiest at the end of the day, because at that time the Sun, passing through the Western region, purifies both the wind and its air. For without the Sun's moderation and breath, that Cardinal point is not so tempered; hence, in this respect, its waters are said to be more turbid and not so healthy.

By these things we can also see that the temperament of the winds—and indeed the power of all things—lies in the power and governance of the Sun, which received its strength from Wisdom itself, who "placed his Tabernacle in it" <note>Psalm 19:4, though the margin notes Job 28</note>. <margin>Job 28.</margin> To Him alone it belongs to "give weight to the air and the wind, and to weigh the waters by measure," etc.
The Ancients also seemed to recognize this, speaking in an allegorical manner of the winds as the children of the Titan Astraeus...

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' within a square woodcut frame, depicting a bearded male figure standing in a landscape with a tree and rolling hills.</image-desc>In my History of the Microcosm <note>Referring to the author's previous work, likely *Utriusque Cosmi Historia*, which explores the human being as a reflection of the universe</note>, I divided the entire sublunary Spirit <note>The vital atmosphere of the earth below the orbit of the moon</note> into three regions: two of these, at the extremes, I made dry, but the middle one I declared to be the Sphere of moisture. This middle sphere I again distinguished into two sub-divided species: the lower and visible sphere I called **Water**; the invisible one I named **Air**. And indeed, not only the authority of the Holy Scriptures but also that of the Philosophers and the Practice of the Alchemists <note>original: "Chymicorum Praxis"</note> proves that this entire region is, in effect, only a single spirit. We are taught that **Fire** is nothing other than thin air; and **Air** is nothing but subtle water; and visible **Water** is nothing but rare earth; and **Earth** is nothing but thick water.

Therefore, proceeding in reverse, we say that **Earth** is nothing other than thick water, and **Water** nothing but thick air, and **Air** nothing but thick fire, and **Fire** nothing but subtle air. Thus, when I spoke of a "single spirit," I understood all of these things. For that sublunary Spirit (which is in truth nothing but that Matter which they call Air) is rendered either thicker or thinner according to the greater or lesser proportions of internal Light, governed by the Spirit that *blows where it wills* <note>original: "Spiritus qui ubi vult, flat"; a reference to John 3:8, playing on the double meaning of "spirit" and "wind"</note>. Thus, Air—or the Spirit when highly ignited—will be so rarefied that it is converted into a fiery disposition, whose master is the **Eastern** breath turning air into fire. But if cold should return, it would gradually and by degrees be stepped back from its fiery faculty, thickening into an air of moderate consistency—a proportion brought about by the **South Wind** <note>original: "Auster"</note>. However, if the cold should press even harder with its condensing power, the spirit is converted first into visible vapor, then into a cloud, and finally into water; in this act, the **West Wind** will hold dominion. Furthermore, we see thick water changed by condensing or freezing into earth: as can be seen in **Salt**, **Crystal**, **Hyacinth** <note>A reddish gemstone, often zircon or sapphire</note>, **Sulfur**, and **Alum**; and also in snow, ice, frost, the **thunder-stone** <note>original: "lapide ceraunio"; prehistoric stone tools once believed to fall from the sky during storms</note>, and other such things. This is usually achieved and perfected specifically by the **Northern** blast.

From these things, it is evident that the same aerial Spirit is divided into Spheres and species, distinct from one another by various degrees of cold in condensing or heat in thinning, through the spiritual operation of the winds.

# On the Elementary Origin of Life & Health,

## CHAPTER II.

### On the Microcosmic Elements, and their Healthful Properties.

That the entire human mass is nothing other than a single Spirit, acting in different ways through the Divine Spirit upon the Elementary Spheres—which are hardly unlike those of the Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or the universe, which was believed to be structured identically to the human body.</term>—will be very easily gathered from Holy Scripture as well as the testimony of ancient philosophers and physicians. However, between the Macrocosmic and Microcosmic <term>Microcosm: The "little world" or the human being, seen as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</term>, we make this distinction: the former are simpler, while the latter arise and are derived from those simple elements.

Indeed, the Macrocosmic elements, gathered into a single mass, are most aptly compared to milk, which contains butter, cheese, and also whey. In the same way, human seed <note>original: "Sperma humanum." In early modern medicine, this refers to the generative substance believed to contain the blueprint and vital heat of the body.</note> functions; in it, the body, the fiery Spirit of life, and the sphere of moisture (composed of phlegm and blood, acting as water and air) are contained. And just as milk in its whole mass is compared to air, so too is the mass of blood in man, and the mass of seed produced from twice-refined blood. For as seed potentially includes the whole man, both internal and external, so blood contains vital air, choleric fire, melancholic Earth, and serous Water; indeed, it even embraces the very life and soul of man himself, as the Scriptures testify. Thus also milk: in its balanced state it is compared to Air; butter to Fire; whey to Water; and cheese to Earth. Hence it was that Job burst forth with these words:

<margin>Job 10:9.</margin>

> *Have you not poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese? You have clothed me with skin and flesh, and fenced me with bones and sinews; you have granted me life and favor...* <note>original: "Nonne sicut lac fudisti me..." This is a paraphrase of Job 10:10-12, used here to show that the body is "coagulated" from fluid elements by God.</note>

In this speech, not only are all human elements clearly explained, but also the Actor <note>The "Actor" refers to God as the primary agent or craftsman of the body.</note> in their arrangement, their preserver, and the one who confirms and binds them in harmonious peace. In truth, these so-called "imaginary qualities" are nothing but the effects of the living God—or of the Spirits of both the macrocosm and microcosm—either contracting and tightening (an action followed by **Coldness**, as was declared before) or dilating, an action followed by **Heat**. Thus we say it is the human Spirit that sharpens a knife by moving it, and not the heat which is stirred up by that motion. So too we say that God—that is, the Divine Essence—works all things in all. ### CHAPTER I.

->*In which it is proven that Wind is, in effect, nothing other than an Element; What a commixture is; and that Temperament is the very proportion of the mixture.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' with scrolling leaf and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Just as no quality can exist unless it resides in the Air, or in some other thing composed of air: so too, Wind cannot exist except in that which is aerial. Therefore, whereas the Ancients accepted hot, moist, cold, and dry as the Elements: We—more essentially and following an even older investigation—can instead list the East, West, South, and North Winds in their place. I say this is "more correct" and based on older observation because the "soul" <note>The *anima* or animating principle that gives a substance its active properties.</note> of any Element arises from those Winds. For the breath of the North Wind, being cold and dry, changes the air into the nature of Earth, and consequently is the origin of Earth. The breath of the West is cold and moist, the origin of Water; that of the South is hot and moist, the origin of Air. And that of the East is hot and dry, the origin of Fire. 

But if anyone should say that the Elements are always present, while Winds of this sort appear only by turns, I respond that the "seeds" <note>original: *Seminaria*; the internal potentials or blueprints of natural forces.</note> of every Wind are mixed everywhere into the "First Matter" <term>Materia Prima: The formless, original substance from which the universe was created before it took specific shape.</term> of the vast world. However, they are mixed in such a way that the fiery power of the East Wind, owing to the lightness of its nature, tends toward the heights; it is followed in nature by the South Wind (aerial), and then after that, by the West Wind (watery). Truly, the constricting power of the North—being cold and dry—seeks the lowest position. 

Indeed, if a portion of these windy powers seems to diminish—whether due to the transformation of one simple nature (or Element) into another, or for the sake of the various compositions of nature occurring every moment—that deficient portion is restored by the mystic breath of God emitted from some quarter of the world. Thus, every windy power is maintained within the Universal Spirit <note>original: *Spiritu Catholico*</note>, which, along with a portion of that Mercurial Spirit <note>original: *Spiritus Mercurialis*; in alchemy and Fludd's philosophy, a subtle, fluid spirit that connects the soul to the body and the heavens to the earth.</note>, animates the element. 

<margin>What an Element is.</margin> Indeed, an Element seems to be nothing other than a portion of the World-Spirit, which by itself lacks quality, but is a certain portion animated by the breath of a certain Angelic wind. <margin>What Wind is.</margin> Thus, we define Wind as an *Angelic Nature informed by the Spirit of Eternal Wisdom, moved and stirred within the vast Mercurial Spirit of the World, where and when it pleases Him.*

Hence, God (according to the Royal Prophet) *made his Angels winds and his ministers a flaming fire.* <note>A reference to Psalm 104:4, reinforcing the idea that natural forces like wind and fire are actually divine messengers or "Angels."</note> These things, therefore, having been rightly considered again and again, we see...

<header>On the Elemental Origin of Life and Health.</header>

We have established that the Winds precede the Elements both in the order of nature and in time, and that they are not only the immediate efficient causes of the Elements—with the divine breath <note>original: *afflatu diuino*</note> blowing within and through them—but they also preserve them. Indeed, within that Spirit which they give form to, the Winds are essentially the Element itself; for the Spirit of the World <note>original: *Spiritus mundi*</note> is, by its own nature, a formless material. From this it follows (as has been stated) that when the Wind blows from the **North**, the earthy Essence reigns; from the **West**, the watery; from the **South**, the aerial; and from the **East**, the fiery. For this reason, we quite deliberately accept the **Eastern** nature as the Element of Fire, the **Western** as Water, the **Southern** as Air, and the **Northern** as Fire. <note>This appears to be a printer's error in the original Latin text, which previously correctly identified the North with Earth (terrea) but here lists it as Fire (Igne) for a second time.</note>

Since this is the case, it will be very easy to demonstrate (in my opinion) that those natures which the Philosophers call **Qualities**—namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—are not "accidents" <term>Accidents: In traditional philosophy, properties that can change (like the temperature of water) without changing the essential nature of the thing itself.</term>, but belong to the Essence and nature of the Angelic winds. These qualities can in no way be separated from the winds, much less do they inhabit them as mere accidents in a subject—which is how the Philosophers, who claim they must exist within some underlying subject, define them. But we shall speak of these things more clearly both above and below.

Now it remains to declare how, from these several "windy natures" (which the Philosophers have called **Elements**), the mixtures or temperaments are formed within the sublunary **Mercurial Spirit**. This occurs not only in the triple Kingdom of composite things—namely the animal, vegetable, and mineral, which are called "perfect mixtures"—but also in the triple **Empire of Meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and clouds.</note>, which are "imperfect mixtures."

We take "commixture" or "mixing" in its general nature to mean the composition of a mixed thing. But in a more strict and proper sense, we call it the mixing of the elements or windy natures with the Spirit in which they reside: that is, the composition of things that have been altered so they can be mixed. From this, a natural composite body is created. The "mixable" substance is the fertile matter of the body to be generated; and since this matter is joined and collected from various parts, one portion is from the Element of Fire (the East), another from Air (the South), another from Water (the West), and another from Earth (the North). Furthermore, of these parts, one portion is Spirit, another humor, another seed, and so on. We say that the "mixable" substance is altered not only in its quality or power, but it is also usually changed by a kind of "corruption" <term>Corruption: The breakdown of an existing form or state of matter, which is necessary for a new form to be born.</term>, so that when the single old form is lost, the new form of the rising body is finally acquired. To understand what truly exists as a mixture, we must consider three things: first, that the things to be mixed are connected to one another and digested into one composite body (such as blood, humors, spirit, flesh, and bones in the human body; or vapor, exhalation, stones, and salts in the composition of a cloud or a thunderous meteor). Second, that the mixable parts act upon and are acted upon by each other reciprocally; from which it follows that they are either opposites or at least diverse. Finally, that they corrupt, transmute, and alter one another from the old form into a new one.

The logic of the mixture is followed by **Temperament**, which is not strictly the mixing itself, but rather the logic or arrangement of the winds and their powers (which they call **Qualities**). It is either absolutely equal, which is called **Temperament by weight** <note>original: *Temperamentum ad pondus*</note>, in which the ratio of the mixture maintains an exact middle point because an equal mass of the mixed elements exists within it—where there is no more heat than cold, nor more moisture than dryness. Or, it is not an absolute temperament, because it is only a moderate balance of the mixed Winds (Elements) within the Spirit, but not a simple equality. This exists in such a proportion as is required for the three kingdoms—animal, vegetable, and mineral—to exist in a state of health and average being. This differs from the "perfection" of the temperament by weight; hence, the ancient Physicians called this **Temperament by Proportion** <note>original: *ad Iustitiam* (literally "to justice"); referring to a functional or "fair" balance needed for life.</note>, insofar as it is sufficient to preserve a creature within the limits of health.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Regarding the absolute ratio of temperaments for things that can be mixed both perfectly and imperfectly; and first concerning those Meteors produced by the blasts of the winds, or by two or three elements.*<-

<margin>A Meteor is anything.</margin>
First of all, before we descend to the exact ratio of the temperament and mixture of healthy Meteors <term>Meteors: In the 17th century, this term referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including clouds, rain, rainbows, and comets, rather than just space rocks.</term>, we believe it is worthwhile to explain in this place what a Meteor is; afterward, we shall clarify its composition. And although we have treated this matter more fully in our *Cosmic Meteorology*, we will nevertheless attempt to briefly revisit the meaning of the words recited there.

A Meteor, therefore, is an imperfectly composed body—not, as some thoughtlessly claim, because it is generated suddenly, or because its generation does not involve a change in substance (as they say) but only in qualities. Rather, it is imperfect because it does not require all the Elements, or the essential blasts of the Winds in the air, for its composition, as animated bodies <note>original: *corpora animata*</note> do. For insofar as it does not consist of all the Elements or the virtues of the Winds—and thus does not acquire a perfect form in its mixture, which is why they are easily generated and suddenly dissolve and vanish—it is called "imperfectly mixed." Thus, from dry air and fire—or the Northern and Eastern Winds—a golden cloud is formed in unequal measure; it arrives suddenly and vanishes again without any unhealthy alteration of the air. Its matter is air agitated by a dry wind; its form is Eastern fire. But conversely, in ignited Meteors, the fiery nature prevails and the Eastern "seeds" <note>original: *seminaria*</note> dominate; from this, hot and unhealthy imbalances <term>Intemperies: An imbalance of the four primary qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) that leads to disease.</term> follow in the Spirit of the Macrocosm <note>The Universe</note>, and from there they are transferred into the Spirit of the Microcosm <note>The Human Being</note>. This is quite clearly demonstrated to us in the occurrence of epidemic diseases that follow the appearance of a Comet.

We say, therefore, that whatever is gathered and mixed in the air from an equal blast of the Winds is exceedingly healthy for both the Macrocosm and the Microcosm.

<margin>Wisdom 11:20.</margin>
From the testimony of the Holy Scriptures, we understand that the eternal Creator composed the entire world from two things: namely, uncreated light and created Spirit. Then, He distinguished it into three regions: the *Empyrean, Ethereal, and Elemental.* Finally, He divided that elemental region into four: the *Elements of Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.* The Founder created the light and the dark Spirit by the breath of His Wisdom, the *Spirit of God* <note>original: *Elohim ruach*</note>, and into three Heavens distinct by nature according to the image of the Trinity. This was done by the breath of the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration the Angelic Race was then created on the first day; blowing from the four corners of the earth, they moved the lowest heaven—the aerial one—into various species according to the diversity of Angelic natures, which operate according to the various properties of God. Thus, *by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit from his mouth.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note> Indeed, God disposed this composition of the world, or rather the ordering of its parts, by an admirable proportion of mixing, according to the saying of the Wise Man: *You have ordered (or tempered) all things by measure, number, and weight.* <note>original: *Omnia mensura numero & pondere, disposuisti*</note> From this it is certainly seen that this temperament, so enduring and immutably persevering, was made "to the weight" <term>Ad pondus: A term in medicine and alchemy meaning a perfect, fixed balance where the qualities are exactly equal and stable.</term> and is absolutely complete.

# On the Elemental Origin of Life and Health

For indeed, through the first ratio of mixing in the world’s structure—which was composed of the matter of darkness and the essence of light—an equal blending is argued for between a Northern <note>Original: *Septentrionalem*. In early modern physics, the North was associated with cold, dry, and dark qualities.</note> force, which has a cold and dry disposition of darkness, and an Eastern force, which has a hot and dry nature of light. Wherefore, through the proportional emanation of divine light into the dark mass (even though both are most opposite in nature), neither the heat of the light (which is the offspring and companion of motion) nor the coldness of the Darkness (which is the child of rest) becomes excessive, or unequal in weight or measure; consequently, they act and are acted upon equally among themselves. And although in the first meeting or mixing, dryness seems to prevail from both principles, yet through the temperament arising from their equal mixture, moisture <note>Latin: *humiditas*</note> seems to be procreated, as you will immediately see.

Hence, therefore, this mixture is first equal, being neither subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" refers to matter that is rare, fine, or spirit-like, whereas "gross" refers to dense, heavy matter.</note> nor gross, even though fiery Light is in itself subtler than anything else, just as Darkness, or Chaos, is grosser than anything else; rather, it exists in the middle, and this is due to the equal resistance of the one and the other.

Furthermore, the vehement appetite of the lucid Fire excites that sleepy, blunt, and stupid state of the darkness into a moderate condition. Moreover, as it is the nature of darkness and earth to constrict excessively, but of fiery Light to open and dilate, it follows that by such an equal mixing, this first composition has neither an excessively constricting nor an excessively dilating or opening faculty, but a moderate one between these two. Indeed, the lightness of the Element of fire—or the Eastern lucid virtue—in the mundane spirit, and the weightiness of that earth—or the Northern earthly virtue—renders such a primary mixture equal, being neither too light nor too heavy; by such an equal balance <note>Latin: *libramento*</note>, it can look toward both lower and higher things. Finally, this mixture or compound, tempered by heat and cold, is found between the subtle and the gross, and is seen to be tempered in constricting and opening, between light and heavy. That it abounds in dryness is certain; for both fire and light are dry, as are Earth and darkness, and this is by virtue of the absence of humor.

But indeed (wonderful to say), by the bond of these two and their moderate action and passion, a certain third thing has arisen or been born from the bowels of Chaos, which is neither Chaos nor can be called Light; it is the *Universal Water*, the mass of the heavens, the lands, and all Creatures, which, when divided from its dark mother or the earth-sea, renders her weak; and by the act of divine light, it is gradually precipitated downward. For an equal mixing has now been made between water and fire. Thus, the Spirit of the Lord <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2: "And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."</note> is now said to be carried over the waters; through this mixture, as through the first, the hands of the Almighty are said to have created the World out of unformed matter.

Through the first meeting of divine light with darkness, there arose (by means of that division which was made of the waters from the dark abyss) *Strife* <term>Strife (Latin: *Litigium*): Robert Fludd uses this term to describe the primal tension or "discord" between opposing forces (Light and Dark) that drives the process of creation and separation.</term>, which is the author of evil and antipathy; by the separation of this, the second creature, namely the mass of Waters, was procreated. Now, I shall say in a few words how the watery or humid nature arose from the equal action and passion of those contrary natures.

For it is indeed necessary that the Medium <note>The "Middle" or "Mean".</note> differs from the two Extremes, since the Medium is of neither extreme's condition, but participates in both. For:

-> A---------B---------C <-

Indeed, B is neither A nor C. Thus it is necessary that B participates equally in the nature of A, the beginning, and C, the end. By the same reasoning, since the fountain of the waters is the dark abyss, but the act through which they are brought into the light is Divine Light, it is necessary to consider the nature of both. And the nature of darkness is to delight in rest, and consequently to enjoy the most intense cold and a gross, heavy, congealing disposition.

By these things it is clear that from a sixfold equal mixing made into pairs of winds, or pairs of Elements, all things were produced primordially and successively: namely, *Heaven and Earth* first, and then afterwards, the four Elements. Hence it is necessary that the whole mundane Spirit, before the division of its own Elemental regions, be exceedingly mobile, yet not so swift in its motion as is Fire itself, or Light.

Next, it is necessary that it be tempered between the intense heat of fire and the moderate coldness of Water. Furthermore, it must also not be entirely moist and slow like Water, because of the dryness of the fiery light; but indeed it follows that it is much more liquid than common water, and consequently, not so slow and sluggish in its motion, but more penetrable on account of its subtlety.

# On the Elemental Origin of Life and Health.

Or if it be permitted to set forth these mixtures according to our reasoning:
From two extremes—namely, divine **Light** and **Darkness** (or the dark abyss)—the **Universal Water** is composed. This is the general matter of the world, having no form or quality in itself, but being an entirely formless thing; from which, as was said before, *God created the world*, as the Wise Man testifies. <margin>Wisdom 11</margin> <note>Fludd refers to Wisdom of Solomon 11:17: "For thy Almighty hand, that made the world of matter without form..."</note> Why a third "moist" thing results from two "dry" extremes, I have declared previously. Then, from the worthier portion of the waters, informed by the presence of divine light, the substance of that "Heaven of heavens" is made, which they call the **Empyrean** Spirit <note>The Empyrean is the highest, most spiritual part of the universe, filled with pure light and fire.</note>; it is so named because it so wonderfully dilates and refines that portion of the waters that it transforms them into a fiery appearance. And this primary mixture of good things is called **Created Light**, from whose density the Angelic species are made; their nature is to receive the light of God abundantly, in the same way that **Stars** are formed from the density of the Ether, or **Meteors** from the density of the air.

Therefore, the dense Empyrean is the central soul of the dense ethereal; and the dense Ethereal is the soul of the elemental.

->*Eternal Wisdom. Spirit.... Darkness.*<-
->*Light ....... Water ........ Chaos.*<-
->*Light........ Empyrean Heaven...... Most worthy water:*<-
->*Then—Empyrean Spirit .... Ether..... Middling water etc.*<-

Finally, the reflection of the **Empyrean Heaven** into the purer part of the lower waters becomes the element of **that Fire**; [the reflection] of the Ether becomes Air; and of these two, the coarsest and visible Water is made. But the seat of all Darkness is the Earth. Wherefore divine Light is the soul and life of the Empyrean spirit. The Empyrean spirit is the soul of the Ethereal; the Ethereal of the Elemental. And as the proportion of temperament stands between the fiery spirit and the ethereal one, so indeed does the element of Fire stand to Air; as the Ethereal to the Elemental, so indeed Air to Water; as Light to darkness, so also heaven to earth.

Thus all created things were made, and arranged in relation to one another by number, weight, and measure, according to the image of the **Archetype** <note>The "Archetype" is the divine blueprint or original idea in the mind of God.</note>, who created them, and from whom all creatures received their form—just as they received their substance from the created waters, or revealed darkness.

Have not the Mathematicians as well as the Mystic Philosophers signified these kinds of mixtures through their five **regular solids** <note>These are the five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>? They made the **Cube** a symbol of **Chaos or the void Earth**. The **Tetrahedron** is the symbol of the **fiery Spirit**; from its depths arose the **Dodecahedron**, which is the symbol of the **Ether**. Next, the **Icosahedron**, which is the symbol of the **Waters**, has the Air hidden in its belly, the symbol of which is finally the **Octahedron**. By these shapes they mystically show how all the regions of the world arose from a single Chaos by the mediation of divine Light.

Indeed, we could publish infinite things in this place concerning the equal and health-giving method of mixing, by which both the world and its creatures arose; but other matters more suitable and harmonious to this work call us away. From these things, however, we can understand how the nature of God exists in every mixture of the world, and that the **universal** <note>original: *Catholica*; Fludd uses this in the sense of "universal" or "all-encompassing," not necessarily the Roman Catholic Church.</note> seat of the world is in the **universal watery spirit**, created through a radical mixture. This, therefore, is the primary formula for mixing in the mundane number. Concerning which Job intends: <margin>Job 12:22</margin> *He reveals foundations out of darkness and brings the horrific shadow into the light*; where by "foundations," he understands the substance from which [things are made]. Concerning this it is said elsewhere: <margin>Wisdom 11 / Job 26:7</margin> *The hand of the Almighty made the world out of formless matter*. Wherefore Job says elsewhere: *God stretches out the North over the empty and void place, and hangs the earth upon nothing*. Where by "empty and void," he denotes formless matter, and consequently nothing in itself; such were those "potential Waters" before the appearance of divine Light. Now indeed, I shall descend to the secondary method of mixing, which is usually completed in the number three.

### CHAPTER III.
### On the mixtures and temperaments in the numbers three and four.

The second degree of mixture <term>mixture (commixtio): the process by which the primary elements combine to form physical matter</term> is that which is made of three: For just as the number two is the first step of numerical progression from unity, so the second degree of mixing arises from three.

The ancients were accustomed to mix the elements equally, three by three, in this manner:

->Table of the Mixture of the three Winds or Elements in equal proportion.<-

<image-desc>A semicircular arc containing the text "Table of the Mixture of the three Winds or Elements in equal proportion" is positioned above a table. To the left of the table are four small circular diagrams, each representing a compass with labeled directions: North (top), South (bottom), East (right), and West (left). In each circle, three points are highlighted and connected by lines, corresponding to the triplets in the table rows.</image-desc>

| WINDS. | ELEMENTS. |
| :--- | :--- |
| East. South. West. | Fire. Air. Water. |
| East. South. North. | Fire. Air. Earth. |
| East. West. North. | Fire. Water. Earth. |
| South. West. North. | Air. Water. Earth. |

We have examined the first of these triple mixtures as follows:

**Fire** is hot and dry; it thoroughly penetrates the other elements. It is mobile, subtle <note>In 17th-century science, "subtle" refers to matter that is thin, refined, or capable of passing through pores.</note>, sharp, and light.

**Air**, however, is hot, but also moist: it penetrates water and earth; it is moderately subtle, and it becomes thinned by the action of fire.

**Water** is also moist, but with coldness: it is mobile, but in a more diminished degree; for it is slow in motion, which is why it moistens more than air does. It penetrates the earth, but not as swiftly, etc.

Therefore, because there are two witnesses <note>original: "testimonia"; here Fludd uses "witnesses" to mean "proportional contributions" or "parts" in a mixture.</note> of heat, the mixed substance tends toward a moderate heat and is quite mobile. This is because its shining soul is more lively than the others; the spirit is more agile than the body, and the body by itself is slow in motion. But by the grace of the soul and the spirit, it is rendered quite agile in motion and action. Moisture also predominates over dryness, because there are two witnesses of moisture. The same applies to coldness, for which there is only a single witness. Therefore, the entire composition consists of evident heat and moisture. 

Yet the heat is not intense, because the heat of the fire is tempered by that of the air, which is indeed dulled and mitigated by moisture. Nor is the fiery heat as violent as that which exists with equal dryness, since its fervor is brought into proportion by both aerial and aqueous moisture. Neither is the moisture of this kind—both aqueous and aerial—excessively aggressive, insofar as it is mitigated in some way by the dryness of the fire.

Therefore, such are the meteors <note>original: "Meteora"; in 17th-century science, this refers to any atmospheric phenomena, including clouds, rain, and wind, rather than just falling stars</note> or bodies, which are not compacted from all the elements. Examples of these are those healthy spring clouds that fertilize the earth with sweet rains and cause it to flower; these are produced by the gentle and steady blowing of the East Wind <note>original: "Subsolano"</note>, the South Wind <note>original: "Austro"</note>, and the West Wind <note>original: "Favonio"</note>. Of this kind also is the mixture of perfect blood, or rather the temperament of the animal seed and that of every other creature, which is composed of winds or life-giving breaths. To these, afterward, in the process of generation and multiplication—in order to bind and harden the rest—the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note> is added. This wind is an enemy to life, as it is cold and dry. By this reasoning, one must proceed with the examination of the remaining combinations: namely, Fire-Air-Earth; Fire-Water-Earth; and Air-Water-Earth.

Finally, the last species of equal mixture consists in the gathering of the four Elements into one—namely, Fire, Water, Air, and Earth—in equilibrium: so that neither Fire attacks Water, nor Air attacks Earth, since all these will be in the same composition with equal strength.

And in this way, you have a description of all the mixtures which are defined by equal portions of the elements, whether they are limited to the number two, three, or finally four. These are accustomed to produce that complete temperament <term>temperament (temperamentum): the characteristic balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines the nature of a thing</term> of a compound which is called "according to weight" <term>according to weight (ad pondus): a perfect mathematical equality of the primary qualities</term>. Now, however, we shall approach the other mixtures of health, which, although they do not exhibit a temperament "according to weight," are nevertheless observed to produce a temperament "according to justice" <term>according to justice (ad iustitiam): a functional balance where qualities are proportioned appropriately for a specific creature's needs, even if not mathematically equal</term>. I say "not according to weight" because they contain some inequality within them, yet not such a great inequality that they exceed the limits of health.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*On the various unequal mixtures, both in the number two and three.*<-

From the unequal mixture of pairs <note>original: "binis & binis"</note>, we can list and recount 12 species, all of which we enumerate in the Tables in this way.

Here, in the unequal mixture of pairs, you see how the Ancients made the Elements the "roots," both in unequal and equal mixtures. I, however, make not only the mixture but even the roots of the elements themselves in the Winds: affirming that the Winds preceded the Elements themselves, both in time and in the order of creation, as we shall soon show more clearly (beyond what was declared before). Now, indeed, we shall declare how the mixtures of things, both unequal and equal, consist in the winds. So that you may understand this better, I would have you seriously observe that the rationale for both equal and unequal mixture exists in the simple winds before it exists in any third thing, because they arise from the meeting of the Winds at a single point. For example: the Winds that possess a natural and equal temperament, both in their simple nature and when mixed together, are the Cardinal <note>The four primary directions: North, South, East, and West</note> winds. For instance: the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note> blowing from the corner of the North is equally cold and dry. It is cold, I say, because it has coldness on one side (the Western side) and heat on the Eastern side: therefore, it consists in the Center (as it were) between these two extremes. Thus, from the Western region, its dryness is gradually diminished as it approaches the moist home of the West Wind <note>original: "Favonij"</note>; but indeed, from the Eastern part, its dryness is strengthened. Therefore it follows that it is equally cold and dry. Conversely, the South Wind <note>original: "Auster"</note> blowing from the Southern pole is equally hot and moist. It is hot because heat is strengthened and reigns from the point of the East Wind <note>original: "Subsolani"</note> toward it; but indeed, the more it approaches the point of the West, coldness prevails. Similarly, the more it approaches the pole of the East, its moisture is weakened, being dulled more and more by dryness; but indeed, if it approaches the West from its own corner—

With these facts gathered, the **temperament** <note>In this context, "temperament" refers to the specific balance or "temperature" of qualities like heat and moisture.</note> of any simple wind, whether equal or unequal, cannot remain hidden from anyone of sound mind. These things standing thus, let us now speak of the mixtures and equal temperaments arising from winds blowing either from opposite directions or transversely.

The **North wind** <note>original: "Boreas"</note>, blowing in an opposite manner with equal force against the **South wind** <note>original: "Auster"</note>, produces that equal mixture and temperament of Air and Earth. In this healthy mixture, the Southern heat does not overcome the Northern cold, nor does the Northern dryness overcome the Southern moisture. From this, a certain mixture is created in the air and from the air, existing between the nature of Air and Earth—namely: **Clouds** that are neither too cold, nor hot, nor moist, nor dry, provided they are mixed perfectly. So also is that equal mixture which is made from equal blasts from the East to the West, and from the West to the East. For example:

If someone takes an equal portion of boiling water and cold water and mixes them together, he will establish an excellent mixture and, consequently, a temperament between extreme heat and extreme cold.

But truly, **unequal mixtures** are formed from pairs, after the manner of the Higher things <note>likely referring to celestial influences</note>, which are described through the connection of two Elements. But these are of a stronger composition than **Meteors** <note>In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon—such as rain, wind, or rainbows—not just falling stars.</note>, and require more blasts of the Winds for their composition: from which first so many **Elements** are procreated, and from the Elements afterwards the **Elemented** <note>original: "Elementata"; things physically composed of the four elements.</note>: namely, the imperfectly mixed things first, and then the perfectly mixed, which are made from the imperfect. For it is impossible for motion to occur from a starting point to a destination unless there is a passage through a middle state. Thus, between the imperfectly mixed and the wind is the **Element**; and between the Element and the perfectly mixed is the **Meteor**, or the imperfectly mixed; in this way, indeed, the seed arises from the elements, from which the animal later emerges.

By the same reasoning, the matter holds true when the **South wind** <note>original: "Auster"</note>, prevailing in its blast over the **North wind** <note>original: "Borea"</note>, brings forth not only rains but also thunder and lightning; and so it is in the others expressed in pairs.

But now I shall reveal a mystery not commonly understood or perceived, which consists chiefly in the power and mixture of the **collateral spirits** <note>The secondary winds that blow from the directions between the four main Cardinal points (North, South, East, West).</note>. For just as the chief power of life and health proceeds from the temperate mixture of the four **cardinal winds**, as the Prophet said: *“Come, Spirit, from the four winds of heaven, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again”* <note>original: "Veni Spiritus à quatuor ventis cæli, & perfla interfectos istos, ut reuiuiscant"; a reference to the Vision of the Dry Bones in Ezekiel 37:9.</note>: and they immediately lived again. So indeed, both the mixtures and the unequal temperaments, whether within or without the limits of health, are for the most part caused by the collateral winds. Hence, just as the **East wind** <note>original: "Subsolanus"</note> is quite friendly to health, so indeed both the **Northeast wind** <note>original: "Cæcias"</note> and the **Southeast wind** <note>original: "Eurus"</note>, its collaterals, are accustomed to harm health because of their intemperate heat or dryness. For the Southeast wind is stronger in heat than in dryness, just as the Northeast is stronger in dryness than in heat. Furthermore, in the opposite quarters of the world, the **Northwest wind** <note>original: "Corus"</note>, which is one collateral of the healthy **West wind** <note>original: "Fauonius"</note>, is unequal and frequently diseased. And the **Southwest wind** <note>original: "Africus"</note> on the other side, which is accustomed to be the parent of superfluous humors and **dropsy** <note>A historical medical term for swelling caused by excess fluid, now known as edema.</note>, produces unequal mixtures through its combinations with its unequal opposites. For the Northwest wind, which is more cold than dry, emitting its blast and meeting that Southeast wind halfway, creates a composition more equally hot and cold, and less moist and dry: because the dryness of the Southeast wind is in diminished proportion to the moisture of the Northwest. But because in this kind of inequality there is the greatest opposition of natures, as between fire and water: therefore the humor of the Northwest wind with its intense coldness is a most suitable subject for corruption, just as the dryness with the fiery heat of the Southeast wind acts toward putrefaction. Hence, the Northwest wind is said to be **pestiferous** <note>Pestilence-bearing or disease-causing.</note>. Such is also the case between the Southwest wind (more moist, less cold) and the Northeast wind (more dry, less cold). Likewise between the **South-Southeast wind** <note>original: "Euro-Auster"</note> (more hot, less moist) and the **North-Northwest wind** <note>original: "Circium"</note> (more cold and less dry); and also between the **South-Southwest wind** <note>original: "Austro-Africus"</note> (more moist, less cold) and the **North-Northeast wind** <note>original: "Aquilo"</note> (more dry, less moist). Furthermore, in the transversal union or convergence of these winds, whether many or few—namely, either the Cardinal with the collaterals, or collaterals with the cardinals—by the various number of their applications, manifold and multiform mixtures and temperaments are produced, tending toward both generation and corruption. For if we observe these mixtures of winds diligently, we shall find far more mixtures in the world than we can derive through observations of the Elements alone. For as the four Cardinal Winds correspond to the four Elements, whose roots they are—namely the North to Earth, the South to Air, the East to Fire, and the West to Water—so indeed the eight collateral winds argue for, as it were, eight other elements, which are interposed between the aforementioned four Cardinal ones.
