### Volume 1, Treatise 1, Section I, Part III, Book V.

...blast. For the nature of the **Northwest wind** <note>original: "Cori"</note> partakes of two portions of water and one of earth; therefore, in the **Expanse** <note>original: "Expanso"; the region of the atmosphere between the earth and the heavens.</note> it brings forth an element intermediate between water and earth. Similarly, on the other side, the essence of the **North wind** <note>original: "Aquilonis"</note> consists of two parts of scorched earth—almost like ash—and one part of fire. For this reason, it breathes into the world an Element that is neither Earth nor Fire, but sits between these two, though it is more inclined toward the substance of earth. In the same way, the **Northeast wind** <note>original: "Cæcias"</note> produces by its blast an Element with a consistency between Fire and Earth, but partaking more of Fire, because it requires two parts of fire for its essence.

By an equal reasoning, the matter holds true beyond the space of the **Equinoctial** <note>The Celestial Equator.</note>. For the **East wind** <note>original: "Eurus"</note> produces by its breathing an Element leaning more toward Fire, yet still partaking of air; hence it is said to produce rains in the end. But the **Southeast wind** <note>original: "Euro-Auster"</note>, conversely, creates by its spirit an Element communicating more with Air and less with Fire. On the other side of the South, the **Southwest wind** <note>original: "Africus"</note> changes the versatile and **Protean** <note>original: "Protei-formem"; referring to Proteus, the Greek sea-god capable of changing shape. This implies the wind is highly changeable.</note> spirit by its blast into an Element having a temperament and nature between Water and Air, but it possesses more of water and less of air. Finally, the **South-Southwest wind** <note>original: "Austro-Africus"</note> generates by its vent an Element that is more airy and less watery. From this it is clear that by this reasoning we can count twelve elements: four of which are **Cardinal** <note>The primary winds: North, South, East, West.</note> and eight of which are **collateral** <note>Side winds located between the cardinal points.</note>. The combinations, therefore, which arise from the mixing of these—whether by twos, threes, or many more—are certainly of a great multitude, as we shall discuss below in its proper place.

<margin>Aphorism II, Book 3.</margin>
However, in these mixtures it is not always required that two or more winds blow at the same time. For the **seeds** <note>original: "seminaria"; a term used in early modern science to describe the hidden "blueprints" or active principles that cause things to grow or change.</note> of a preceding wind, shaping the Protean spirit in their own fashion and mixing themselves with those of the following wind, procreate a new element in the Expanse; and in this way, they alter the nature of the sky from what it was before. This also seems to be confirmed by **Hippocrates** (with whom **Galen** agrees) in these words: *“If winter is dry and Northerly, and spring is rainy and Southerly, in the summer there will occur acute fevers, eye inflammations, dysentery, etc.”* <note>original: "Si hyems est sicca & Aquilonia, ver pluuiosum & australe, æstate facient febres acutas, lippitudines, dysenterias, &c."</note>

By this discourse, he seems especially to argue that the Northern seeds (or **Boreal** seeds) rule in the air secretly from the time of winter until spring, until the South wind, joining itself or mixing its own seeds with those dominant Northern ones, changes the nature of the air—especially when the hot state of summer assists—into a putrid and malignant disposition, because the South wind now prevails and predominates over the North. From this it is manifest that there is no need for two or more winds to blow at once (although this often happens), but the succeeding wind, finding the seeds of the preceding wind in the "great sea" of the **sublunary spirit** <note>The atmosphere below the moon, where all change and decay occur.</note>, performs the same action with them as if it had encountered that wind immediately in its path.

We have spoken before regarding the equal combination or joining of the cardinal winds in pairs. Now, however, we shall demonstrate the unequal mixing of the winds in pairs.

Nor indeed can these types of <term>binary mixtures</term> <note>original: commixtiones binariæ; pairings of two elements</note> be said to arise from simple Elements alone, since each of these winds appears to deviate from the pure nature of the element. For the <term>Circius</term> <note>the West-Northwest wind</note> seems to depart from the exact nature of Earth <note>associated here with the North</note> in proportion to how much it is observed to differ from the position and nature of the Northern pole. For as much as it takes its seat toward the location of the Western pole, so much does it lose some of the dryness of its own pole: for it is necessary that it shares slightly with Western moisture. Therefore, although it is as cold as <term>Boreas</term> <note>the North wind</note>, or pure Earth, it is nonetheless not as dry; and consequently, it is something between earth and water. But it participates more in the earthly nature; indeed, its power is even said to be earthly, not absolutely, but in so far as it clings more closely to that nature. By a similar logic, in its Eastern position, <term>Aquilo</term> <note>the North-Northeast wind</note> loses something of the coldness of its pole, because it inclines toward the Eastern pole: thus, although it abounds in dryness, yet because of an imperceptible lack of coldness, it cannot be called absolutely earthly like <term>Boreas</term> (which blows directly from the pole), but only comparatively so. This same principle applies to all the other collateral winds.

And this is that <term>Mystical Reason</term>, never before this time (to my knowledge) explained by anyone: why species—both in the Meteorological Kingdom <note>atmospheric phenomena</note> and in those three kingdoms of composition <note>the Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral kingdoms</note>—exist in such varied and unknown forms; indeed, they are produced so continually that they are scarcely comprehensible to the human mind. All of these are observed to possess various elemental properties within themselves in diverse ways and in differing proportions to one another, as seen in <term>Opium</term>, in <term>earth-smoke</term> <note>original: fumo terræ; the herb Fumitory, known for its bitter, cleansing properties</note>, in venomous animals, in—

Volume 1. Treatise 1. Section 1. Part 2. Book 5.

...indeed, it results in infinite diversities of human constitution and <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of "humors" or qualities in a person’s body</note>, and also in the hidden and secret natures of other things, for which they cannot provide a clearer explanation; rather they occur because they are such, either from a hidden property, or sympathy, or antipathy, etc.

When, however, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalists, these things happen and produce such effects, it is because such hidden natures—whether bad or good—are imbued by the Angelic winds. The words of the Kabbalists are these:

<margin>Reuchlin, Book 3 of *The Art of the Kabbalah* <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a famous German humanist and scholar who sought to reconcile Jewish mysticism with Christian philosophy.</note></margin>
> *An angel is like a mediating power between God and nature, through which operations are carried out in things that nature either would not do, or would do differently—things which others say come from a hidden property, or simply "because it is so." For there is no need to proceed in an imaginary way as those do who are accustomed to making mixtures of imaginary Elements, fanning them after their own fashion or Fantasy in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, or 4th degree, since it is not within human power to do this so precisely, even if one were able to discern or distinguish the Elements themselves within their composition.*

But in truth, we have winds blowing at every moment from one or another quarter of the world, which show themselves to possess such and such natures, without which no mortal, nor even plants, could long endure; for from them, they undoubtedly receive life, preservation, and the spirit by which they exist. For without their breath, nothing is rained upon or communicated to these lower things.

And likewise, conversely, through corruption, nothing returns to its first principle without them: since contrary winds are most hostile to their opposites. For just as the **South Wind** <note>original: Auster</note> brings warm waters and is accustomed to soften and corrupt; so the **North Wind** <note>original: Boreas</note> drives away the clouds created by it, hardens whatever the South Wind made soft, and resists Southern putrefaction in every way; and so it is with the others.

But now I shall turn my pen to the account of the mixture fashioned from the spirit of three winds.

In the following Table, you will find expressed those unequal mixtures made from three parts, both from the winds—which are the roots of composite things—and from the elements themselves, which correspond to those windy roots from which they arise. For the **East Wind** <note>original: Subsolanus</note> of the Orient with its two "wings" corresponds to **Fire**; the **West Wind** <note>original: Favonius</note> of the Occident, with its collateral companions, to **Water**; the **North Wind** <note>original: Boreas</note> of the North with its assistants, namely the **West-Northwest Wind** <note>original: Circio</note> and the **North-Northeast Wind** <note>original: Aquilo</note>, to **Earth**; and the **South Wind** <note>original: Auster</note> with its consort, both right and left—namely the **South-East Wind** <note>original: Euro-Auster</note> and the **South-West Wind** <note>original: Austro-Africus</note>—to **Air**. For (as we have already said) an Element is nothing other than the transformation of the sublunary <term>Potentiform spirit</term> <note>original: spiritus potentiformis; the raw, unshaped spiritual energy of the world below the moon</note> into the nature of the predominant wind.

But indeed, since no wind is observed to blow absolutely by itself, if the matter is examined a little more accurately as it truly is, therefore no pure Element can be found except by the Wise.

From these types of spheres of unequal mixtures, therefore, you can discern the logic of the three winds: where the top part of any sphere denotes the Northern <note>Latin: *Septentrionalem*</note> region of the world, the bottom the South <note>Latin: *Meridiem*</note>, the right the East <note>Latin: *Orientem*</note>, and the left the West <note>Latin: *Occidentem*</note>.

But a weaker wind is indicated by a single line, which is shown in the Table by **Lesser** <note>Latin: *Minus*</note>.

It would indeed be an infinite task to make a full and complete discourse on the collateral <note>Intermediate directions like Northeast or Southwest.</note> winds and how they move. Therefore, where we have already made mention, or will make mention in the future, of the cardinal winds, there we also include and understand in a general way their two collateral counterparts. Although I confess that I know a discovery <note>The author hints at a more complex system of "wind chemistry" he has devised but chooses to keep the explanation simple for now.</note> which could properly adapt these very things to the natures of their Elements in combination, I will nonetheless omit it in this place for the sake of brevity, so that I may more quickly move on to the matters at hand.

There are also other types of unequal mixtures—namely, from three winds or elements joined equally and unequally: in which, for instance, two are equal and one is unequal, whether it exceeds the equal ones in its blowing (which is indicated by **Plus** in the Table) or is subject to them—that is, it is of less power or efficacy than the equal ones. <meta>This page continues from page 135, which established the symbolic notation for elemental mixtures (three lines for predominance, two for equality/moderation, and one for a lesser portion). Page 136 applies these symbols to the four winds and four elements, transitioning from simple mixtures of two or three components to complex mixtures of all four.</meta>

In these figures (as mentioned above), ≡ signifies Plus: that is, the predominance of one wind over the others, just as in a <term>choleric complexion</term><note>In traditional humeral medicine, the 'choleric' temperament was associated with heat and dryness, linked to the element of fire and the East wind.</note>, the East wind (or <term>Subsolanus</term>) prevails, or possesses more vigor than the other three. In the composition, ═ denotes those that are equal in moderation, and — signifies Minus, or the wind or element that, in the mixture, claims a smaller portion for itself.

We therefore conclude this chapter by saying that you have here a clear description of the <term>Meteors</term><note>original: "Meteororum." In early modern science, 'meteors' referred to any atmospheric phenomena occurring in the region between the earth and the moon, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> which occupy the space between the elements and perfectly composed bodies, formed from both two and three elements; from this, you may more clearly perceive the reasoning behind complete composition—whether it pertains to generation, or to dissolution and corruption.

Now, however, let us descend to the mixed combinations of the four winds or elements—that is, those which have within them winds or elements mixed both equally and unequally.

...than living things; and also in those things which the <term>Saracens</term><note>original: "Saraceni." A term used here to refer to Arabic alchemical and philosophical authorities whose works were foundational to European science.</note> call "congealed," such as <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury.</note>, sulfur, and all metals; also in certain <term>meteors</term><note>original: "meteoris." In the 16th century, 'meteors' referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, snow, and lightning, rather than just space debris.</note>: for some imperfect things mixed from these four elements are sometimes produced in the air: just as is observed in the creation of a certain cloud, in which there is Eastern lightning, Southern wind, Western water, and Northern hail: and also the <term>Ceraunian stone</term><note>original: "lapis Ceraunius." Also known as "thunderstones," these were often prehistoric stone tools or fossils believed to be formed in the air and cast down to earth by lightning.</note>, as if it were a permanent compound mixed from these four.

But where I have here and above made mention only of the <term>cardinal winds</term><note>The four primary directions: North, South, East, and West.</note>, and will continue to do so hereafter, I would have you warned that under their names, we also include their <term>collateral winds</term><note>The intermediate winds, such as Northeast or Southwest.</note>; although any one of them (as said above) does not agree so exactly with the nature and temperament of its Cardinal wind: but because it partakes more of the nature of its Cardinal, we have therefore assigned its temperament to that direction.

<note>The table uses the Latin names for the winds: Favonius (West), Subsolanus (East), Auster (South), and Boreas (North). In this system, each wind corresponds to an element: West to Water, East to Fire, South to Air, and North to Earth.</note>

In this table, therefore, we have the natures of the four Winds (or elements) mixed and balanced in various ways: namely, two equally: as if we mixed together Air and Earth (or the Northern and Southern seeds) ... at a weight of three <term>scruples</term><note>original: "scrupulorum." A scruple is a traditional unit of weight used by alchemists and apothecaries, equal to 1/24th of an ounce or about 1.3 grams.</note>; but Water at a weight of four scruples; and Fire at a weight of two scruples. In such a proportion, Earth and Air will be equal; there will be more of Water, because its proportion exceeds that of the equal ones. Finally, Fire is the "lesser unequal," because its proportion is smaller than that of the equal ones.

# On the Elementary Origin of Life & Health,

From these mixtures, then, which are rooted in the winds and arise directly from the elements, everything in the entire world—whether it is a perfectly or imperfectly mixed substance—derives its beginning and existence. Therefore, there is no animal, nor plant, nor quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, nor any of the "frozen" species <note>likely referring to minerals or metals formed by solidification</note>, nor finally any kind of Meteor <term>Meteoron: in this period, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars</term>, which does not draw or derive its origin from one of the types of mixtures previously recounted. But truly, so that you may more easily understand the logic of these mixtures, I will produce one or two examples.

If anyone, therefore, seeks a more exact understanding of the nature of Milk and its composition, and examines with diligent insight which of these types of mixtures it falls under: I would first want him to understand, and observe in a general sense, that Milk has in its composition something thick, something liquid, and something fatty. He should observe that it is very liquid, less thick than liquid, and in a still smaller degree fatty than thick—as appears in the separation of cheese from milk, and of butter from the cheese and whey.

Its liquid whey, therefore, belongs to the part of the Western wind <note>original: "flatus Occidentalis"; associated with the element of Water</note>, being cold and moist; this portion flows indirectly from the Element of water. Its thick part, however, or the heavy curd, has its root in the Northern wind <note>original: "flatu Boreali"</note> and corresponds to the Element of Earth.

But truly its fatness, being airy, or hot and moist, recognizes a Southern origin <note>original: "Australem... originem"</note>.

Finally, fire is so slight in it that it cannot be discerned except through its effect. For besides the fact that we find the eating of milk warms the body, it is certain that Butter is the "food of fire" <note>meaning it is flammable and provides fuel</note>. Therefore, it is necessary that Butter be of the Southern part, because it is airy; consequently, the fiery power is in Butter in the same way it is in the nature of the Southern wind, which is therefore most fit for producing Thunder.

Therefore, we conclude that this mixture of milk is of that species in which there is more of the nature of the West Wind or Water; less of the North Wind or Earth; still less of the Southern Wind or Air; and truly the least of Fire. Therefore, its mixture relates to the fourth Table of Quaternaries.

But if the thick cheese-part and the Butter were unequal, then we judge its composition should be referred to the final Table. Now we come to the nine Temperaments of complexions; and we shall discuss the *origin of Tastes* in a few words.

# On the Elemental Origin of Life and Health

From these combinations, therefore, which have their roots in the winds and arise immediately from the elements, everything in the whole world—whether perfectly or imperfectly mixed—derives its beginning and existence. For there is no animal, nor plant, nor quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note>, nor any of the mineral species, nor finally any atmospheric phenomenon <note>original: "Meteoron"; in this period, "meteor" referred to any weather event like rain or lightning</note> whatsoever, that has not drawn or derived its origin from one of the types of mixtures previously recounted. But indeed, so that you may more easily understand the logic of these mixtures, I will provide one or two examples.

If anyone, therefore, seeks the nature of Milk and its more exact composition, and examines with diligent insight under which type of these mixtures it is contained: I would first have him understand and contemplate in a general sense that Milk has in its composition something thick, something liquid, and something fatty. He must observe that it is highly liquid, but less thick than it is liquid, and even less fatty than it is thick—as is apparent in the separation of cheese from milk, and of butter from the cheese and whey.

Its liquid or whey-like part, therefore, belongs to the nature of the West Wind <note>original: "flatus Occidentalis," also known as Favonius</note>, being cold and moist; this portion flows mediately from the Element of Water. Its thick part, or the heavy curd, has its root in the North Wind <note>original: "flatu Boreali"</note> and corresponds to the Element of Earth.

However, its fattiness, being airy—or hot and moist—acknowledges a Southern <note>original: "Australem"</note> origin.

Finally, fire is so scant in it that it can only be discerned by its effect. For besides the fact that we find that the consumption of milk warms the body, it is certain that Butter is the "food of fire" <note>meaning butter is highly flammable</note>. Therefore, it is necessary that Butter be of the Southern part, because it is airy; consequently, the fiery power is present in Butter in the same way it is in the nature of the South Wind, which is for that reason most suited to producing thunder.

Thus, we conclude that this mixture of milk is of that species in which there is more of the nature of the West Wind (or Water), less of the North (or Earth), even less of the South (or Air), and truly the least of Fire. Therefore, its mixture relates to the fourth Quaternary Table.

But if the thick cheese-matter and the Butter are unequal, then we judge its composition should be referred to the final Table.

Now we arrive at the nine Temperaments of complexions <note>In Galenic medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors or elements in a body</note>, and we shall discuss briefly the origin of Flavors.

# On the Elemental Origin of Life and Health,

From these mixtures, then, which have their roots in the winds and arise immediately from the elements, everything in the whole world—whether it is a perfectly or imperfectly mixed substance—derives its beginning and existence. Therefore, there is no animal, nor plant, nor quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, nor anything from the "frozen" <term>congelatis: refers to solids like minerals and metals</term> species, nor finally any atmospheric phenomenon <note>original: "Meteoron"; in this period, this included rain, thunder, and lightning as well as meteors</note> of any kind, that does not draw or derive its origin from one of the types of mixtures previously recounted. Its thick part, or heavy curd, has its root in the North Wind <note>original: "flatu Boreali," or Boreas</note> and corresponds to the element of Earth.

But its fatness, being airy—that is, hot and moist—acknowledges a Southern origin <note>original: "Australem," the South wind or Auster</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of elemental mixtures. It moves from the specific example of milk (used on the previous page to illustrate elemental proportions) to the general theory of the "nine complexions" or temperaments formed by the varying balances of the four primary qualities: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</meta>

Volume 1, Treatise 1, Section 1, Part III, Book V.

If we have set aside heat, and wish to dissolve that balance which exists between moisture and coldness, this must be done in two similar ways: namely, by including a larger portion of moisture and a smaller portion of dryness in the composition, which for this reason is to be called **moist**, though it remains tempered in coldness and moisture; or, the proportion of dryness itself will predominate while the same balance between coldness and moisture remains, and then the **Compound** will be called **dry**.

And by this logic, you have four **Complexions** <term>complexiones: the specific "temperament" or chemical makeup of a substance resulting from the mixture of the four elements</term> brought to light. There are also four other **Complexions** which cannot be produced except by the destruction of those four previously mentioned. For instance, in one of these, there is a greater amount of heat and moisture in the composition; for this reason, it shall be named **hot** and **moist**. In another, there is more heat and dryness; thus, the **Compound** will be called **hot** and **dry**. In a third, coldness and moisture will be stronger, and so the **Compound** will be called **cold** and **moist**. Finally, in a fourth, cold and dry will hold dominion; hence a thing so composed or mixed is to be called **cold** and **dry**.

Lastly, that **Complexion** which consists of the four **Elements** in equal proportion occupies its own unique place <note>This refers to the "temperate" or perfectly balanced state, which is the ninth complexion</note>. From this, therefore, it was concluded by the **Ancients** that **nine** (and no more) distinct complexions are to be found in the world.

# On the Elementary Origin of Life and Health,

However, since the mixtures of such primary qualities in flavors might seem not at all clear, or even scarcely believable, I will provide one or two practical examples for the greater certainty of the reader, one of which is as follows.

If we wish to compose a salty flavor, let us boil honey itself, and you will find it becomes salty. But if you strive to bring forth a bitter flavor in it, let the same be cooked again even more; and then we will see that it is reduced to a bitter <note>The Latin text here says 'salsam' (salty), but the chemical logic of the passage and the following sentence suggest it moves toward bitter.</note> nature.

From this experiment, it will be very easy to gather that the fiery power is stronger in a bitter flavor than in a salty one. By a similar reasoning, we shall create a sour flavor if we mix the best wine with water and expose it to the heat of the sun; for in a short space of time, that liquor will be made sour. From this it is clear that there is more water and little fire, because the sun by its heat dissipated the spirit of the wine; but air is present in a moderate amount, because that liquor, after the extraction of the greater part of the fiery portion, is reduced to a nature between fiery and watery. However, it abounds more in water due to the portion of water added and the phlegmatic disposition of the remaining wine, its spirit having finally exhaled.

And it is also certain that something (though little) of earthiness is present in it, because once the spirit of the wine has exhaled, the residue of the liquor—being mixed with its earthy tartar <term>Tartar: the sediment or potassium bitartrate that precipitates from wine, considered "earthy" in alchemy</term>, and at the same time the consistency of the added water having been thickened by the evaporation of the more subtle parts through the sun's heat—inclines somewhat toward an earthy nature.

Similarly, if we wish to create a sharp flavor <term>Acutum: a pungent, piercing, or spicy taste</term>, let the best wine be allowed to rest for a long time without any disturbance, and you will perceive it migrating into a sharp flavor.

Furthermore, the latitude of flavors <term>Latitudo saporum: the range or spectrum of different tastes</term> is best described in this way: We shall represent the two extremes of a single line:

<image-desc>A simple linear diagram illustrating the "latitude of flavors." It consists of three points labeled A, B, and C arranged horizontally. Below the letters are three circles (O) connected by a dashed line: O---O---O.</image-desc>

Therefore, let one extreme **A** be **Oil of Tartar**, which is very bitter; let the extreme **C** be **Oil of Vitriol** <term>Oil of Vitriol: concentrated sulfuric acid, known for its extreme acidity</term>, which is most acidic. If, then, we mix equal parts of Oils **A** and **C** together, they will produce **B**, or a sweet flavor. But if more Oil of Tartar (**A**) is used than Oil of Vitriol (**C**), a clear saltiness will be perceived. And so, in the other degrees of mixing that can come between **A**, **B**, and **C**, we can draw out intermediate flavors, as practice and experience will demonstrate more clearly.

### Volume I. Treatise I. Section I. Part III. Book V.

...nor do they think color is anything else than the varied termination of Light in the transparent <note>Latin: *diaphano*</note> and the opaque, as appears in the colors of the *Rainbow* <note>Latin: *Iridis*</note>.

<margin>2.</margin> Others, however, say that color arises from the multiform mixing of the opaque with the transparent: the active force of which is Light itself, flowing from a lucid source as the first foundation <note>original: *hypostasi*</note> of colors.

<margin>3.</margin> Others deny that the colors of the *Rainbow* are real, since they are produced by the varying reflection or refraction of rays. Nor are they willing to admit that colors are formed by the various mixing of bodies; wherefore they conclude that color itself is a secondary simple quality, produced from the action of the primary qualities. For (they say) we see blackness generated from the action of heat upon moisture, as in charcoal; and again, whiteness generated from the action of heat upon dryness, as is indicated by ashes. And they provide a broader explanation for these colors: because (they say) heat in a moist environment exhales the mixed watery parts of the earth into black smoke and consumes the clear airy parts, but leaves behind the coarse, black, earthy substance. If the heat then consumes that coarseness, the remaining substance will be white. From this they conclude that Cold is the author of *Whiteness*, as is seen in snow and frost, while heat is the author of blackness. Finally, they maintain that intermediate colors are procreated from the mixing of these extremes; thus they establish seven more essential colors in number: namely the two extremes, *Whiteness* and *Blackness*, and the intermediates: *yellow*, *saffron* <note>original: *croceum*</note>, *red*, *purple*, and *green*, which is followed by *black*. Therefore they place *red* in the middle, because the causes of its generation concur equally; then from the mixing of the extreme white with it, *yellowness* and *saffron-color* are generated, just as blackness mixed with redness generates *purple* and *green*.

<margin>4.</margin> Others define color as a secondary visible quality proceeding from the luminous fire, the transparency of air and water, and the opacity of earth, with the primary qualities <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note> cooperating. They say *White* comes from an abundance of light and heat; *Black* from a scarcity of light and an abundance of cold; and *Red* (following the previous opinion) from an equal mixing of white and black, as in charcoal. They say *Yellow* is procreated from more white and less red; *Saffron* from more red and less white; *Green* from more black and less red; and *Purple* from more red and less black.

<margin>5.</margin> *Marius* <note>Likely referring to Domenico Maria Novara or a similar Renaissance philosopher/astronomer</note> (a most learned man and excellent philosopher) denies that color, taste, or odor can be found in the simple Elements. He produces various arguments to confirm this opinion. The first is that although elements seem to have colors—as one earth appears *white*, another *black*, another *red*, and another *saffron*; and water, when one looks at it from afar, appears *green*, and while it falls from a height to the bottom, it seems *bright white*—similarly, the *Air* is diversely colored depending on whether it is closer to the Sun, the Moon, or Fire.

Finally, *Fire* in thick matter is *red*, in a flame *saffron*, in its brilliance *bright white*, etc. Nevertheless, in reality, they participate in no color. For if the true *Earth* is simple and one, and also simply cold and dry, if it were colored, it could only claim one single color. Yet truly, various colors are discerned in the earth; therefore colors are not essentially in it, but present by accident. The same must be judged regarding Tastes and Odors, and so with the rest.

Second: If the Elements had color, then *Earth* would naturally be *black*, *Water* *white*, *Air* *saffron*, and *Fire* *red*; consequently, these colors would appear and be revealed in composite things. Thus, that in which there was more earth would have more *Blackness*; that in which there was more *Water*, more *Whiteness*, and so on.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of contemporary theories on the origin of color. # On the Elementary Origin of Life and Health,

Third: Because all the Philosophers who have treated the Elements made no mention of their colors, and so forth.

Therefore, we will examine all these opinions with a more central inquiry so that we may peel back the husk <note>original: *enucleemus*, literally 'to take out the kernel'</note> to reveal the truth of a thing so internal and mystical as color is; and we shall fish it out from the deep ocean of natural secrets <note>original: *Arcanorum*</note>.

And first, to dwell upon the first opinion: If Light (as is the common assertion) be an *accident* <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist, like the color of a shirt</note>—and an accident is nothing at all by itself, but only insofar as it exists within some subject—how is it possible for "nothing by itself" to produce another "nothing"? Therefore, it is not the varied termination of Light in the opaque or the transparent that produces colors; and yet we admit that the principle of generating colors arises from the source of light, but not in the manner that the first opinion expressed.

Regarding the second opinion, we say: That colors are not even generated from the multiform mixing of the opaque and the transparent, insofar as the transparent is not colored at all by or in itself, as may be seen in the air. Furthermore, the opaque proves nothing but blackness or darkness by itself. But in truth, they add light to the completion of colors, as that without which colors cannot be revealed, but exist only in potentiality. And although they seem to offer something real here regarding the generation of colors, nevertheless, by this description of theirs, they are observed to make public "the unknown through the even more unknown" <note>original: *ignotum quasi per ignotius*</note>, as I shall show more clearly below.

Those who brought forth the third opinion are also mistaken; for in truth, colors are real and follow their own proper subjects with essential necessity, and that especially where they exist naturally and not through a preternatural addition. Consequently, colors are not made by reflection, nor by refraction, nor by the mixing of various bodies; colors exist naturally, not in an adventitious manner <note>i.e., added from the outside</note>, and they mix themselves with things.

Finally, we say that it is even more absurd (the matter having been thoroughly considered) to call color a "secondary quality" arising from the action of primary ones, insofar as we acknowledge that nothing was created except substances, as we will immediately show more clearly. For it is not the action of heat upon the moist that produces blackness, nor heat upon the dry that produces whiteness; rather, it is the degrees of "concoction" <note>an alchemical term for ripening or cooking through internal heat</note> of the different natures of **sulphur**, in which it is necessary that an alteration occurs in the **primary qualities**. We also deny that these qualities are "accidents" (following the common opinion); instead, they essentially follow the nature of the thing according to the degrees of **sulphur**, which are recognized as being various, according to the variation of digestion or the intensity of a single thing.

Finally, that opinion of Marius <note>Likely referring to Domenico Maria Novara or a similar scholastic authority</note>, believing that colors, tastes, and odors are not in the pure elements, will fall in that regard and collapse into nothingness by itself, if we consider that the **sulphur of nature** is radically present in every created thing, both simple and mixed. For how (I pray) is it possible that the conversion or "rotation" of elements from one into another could happen if they did not have the **sulphur of nature** at their root? It is through this alone, in it and by it, that the change from form to form, and from one color to another, occurs. Nor indeed can anyone doubt this matter further if they observe that **Light** was the first creature, and that it is the Root and Origin of the **sulphur of nature**. Therefore, if the mass of the waters is distinguished into the Elements by light, it is necessary that every Element, in its creation, be informed by its own sulphur, and be distinguished from one another and varied in position. Thus, that portion of the waters which is enriched with a greater portion of the **sulphur of nature** is **Fire**; and for that reason, it is elevated above its companions and, in its form and color, approaches closer to light due to the multitude of sulphur within it. Hence, by its natural color, it is saffron-colored <note>original: *croceus*</note> and close to redness.

In **Air**, Sulphur does not overflow as it does in **Fire**; therefore it produces a golden-yellow color <note>original: *flauedinem*</note>. From which, due to the lesser dominance of Sulphur, it is whitish; just as the **Earth**, because of a greater or lesser lack of natural sulphur, appears either blacker or more leaden-colored <note>original: *liuidior*</note>.

### Volume I. Treatise I. Section I. Part III. Book V.

When these things are rightly considered, we will perceive indeed that Earth is properly compared to the nature of **Salt**, while Water and Air—which constitute the sphere of humidity—are compared to that of **Mercury**, and Fire to the condition of **Sulphur**. Consequently, it is clear that the more raw a thing is, the less the grade of its Sulphur is exalted. Yet in every degree of its exaltation, the thing changes from color to color, as is evident in the ripening of fruits. Therefore, we deny that colors arise from mere qualities <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "qualities" (like hot, cold, wet, dry) were often seen as the source of color, which the author disputes</note>; rather, they come from the **Essence of Sulphur** existing in various forms within **Mercury**.

<margin>Pimander, Book 1</margin>
But indeed, so that I may reveal the mystery of this matter from its origin: I pray you consider a thing most worthy of observation. The most lucid Spirit of God (*whose presence, as Hermes says, converted all things into a most joyful light* <note>original: "cuius præsentia (vt ait Hermes) omnia in lumen iucundiβimum sunt conuersa"</note>: that is, produced under the name of "created light," and changed from an invisible thing into a visible one). Light, therefore, from the divine breath upon the Chaos, is the active source and origin of colors. If we were to say that some "accident" <term>Accident: A property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a coat</term> were present in it, we would be entirely mistaken. For the primary Light is a single, most perfect Essence alone, without any adhesion or addition of any foreign thing, in itself and through itself. Nevertheless, it is certain that Light adorned creatures with its flashing splendor and decorated them with all colors. But it is impossible for any thing to give what it does not have. Therefore, it is by no means to be believed that the divine Light, which has no "accidents" in itself, gave accidental colors to the world. Instead, we say that **color is a portion of the Essentifying form**, or a degree of the multiplication or increase of **Sulphur** (or primary Light) within the **Mercury** (or the existing worldly primary matter). For Light, giving life and being to every creature, is seen to grow and increase gradually in any given thing; insofar as its whole effort is to lead the thing in which it dwells, step by step, to the goal of perfection and the completion of ripening. In this motion or action, it is observed to progress from color to color—not because it puts them on like garments or "accidents," but because the natural acts of the Sulphur working upon the Mercurial matter follow the changes of that matter in which the Sulphur dwells; they are found to be present in both in an Essential proportion. For where the fiery Sulphur of nature visibly abounds—as in a gross thing, such as a burning coal—there its form is rendered an intense red. But where the formal substance of the Sulphur is more spread out—for instance, in the smoke of ignited wood—there a saffron <note>original: *croceus*, a deep yellow-orange</note> color is present. If indeed that sulphurous power is spread out even further, as in the air or a more subtle Mercurial matter, there the Sulphur renders itself a paler yellow.

But if anyone should reply that all these forms proceed from light, and therefore it is necessary that they be "accidents"—insofar as Light itself is an accident—I answer thus: If Light were an accident, it would follow that it must exist within some subject, since the nature of an accident is to be *within* something. But since Light was the very first of all creatures, it is not possible for it to actually "inhere" in a thing that did not yet truly exist. Therefore, it is established that Light is a most "Essentifying" creature <note>Meaning it is a substance that gives being or "essence" to other things</note>, existing through itself and in itself, and remaining in itself. It is that most rich divine wisdom, which is one and simple, the source of all essences and virtues, according to the sense of David: *By the breath of his mouth all the host <note>original: *virtus*, often translated as power or host</note> of the heavens were made.* We have here, then, the active source of colors. Now, however, I will turn the discourse to the passive or potential source, so that you may better draw out the reason for the creation of various colors.

As it is manifest, therefore, that Light itself is the formal subject or "act" of all colors—not an accidental one (as some would have it) but an **Essential** one—so indeed we establish for certain that **Darkness** is its passive or material subject. Through the action of both external and central light, this darkness is gradually purified from its deformed foulness; it is worked through the smallest parts and "cooked" <note>original: *decoctum*, a term from alchemy referring to the refining power of heat</note>, changing from Element to Element, from color to color, and from vileness to nobility. And here it must be known that every essential motion of a passive thing toward perfection begins from the color black and moves toward white; from which, finally, it reaches brilliance.

...the transition will be made by the working of super-celestial divine light; as is to be perceived in the superabundant brightness and purity of the Angels and Saints.

But indeed, just as the purest **Sulphur** in nature is nothing other than **Essential Fire**, or a simple tincture originating immediately from the divine light, so truly without its presence nothing in this world can live or exist. *The Spirit* (says the Wise One) *is in every thing* <note>original: "Spiritus est in omni re." A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 12:1, suggesting a universal animating force.</note>. Moreover, the fountain of lucid Wisdom is the **Word** in which there is life. And that Light or fiery tincture is that invisible fire of **Heraclitus** and **Zoroaster** <note>Heraclitus and Zoroaster were ancient thinkers often cited by alchemists as the earliest masters who understood fire as the fundamental element of the universe.</note> from which they claim all things are born. As this fire exists in many forms in various things, it produces infinite species, differing in shape, nature, color, taste, and smell. Thus, one **Element** differs from another by a greater or lesser measure of this Sulphur; and the less of it that is found in a **Mercurial** subject <term>Mercurial subject: The passive, fluid matter that receives the "seed" or action of Sulphur.</term>, the more dark, vile, and ignoble that thing is. 

From this it follows that the more a thing is increased by Sulphur or "tincture"—growing little by little like a fire from a spark into a flame—the more that unformed matter is moved from the deformity of potentiality into the perfection of an act. In every degree of its mutation, it changes its color, not unlike how one Element is changed into another. For black **Earth** changes into whitish **Water**, and whitish Water into snowy and shining **Air**, and snowy and yellowish Air into red **Fire**, as Sulphur increasingly overcomes the common Mercurial body, or the "prime matter" of the Elements. 

For the matter stands differently than some people think, who claim that the color of **Snow** comes from cold; by that logic, black Earth (being the coldest) would be the whitest of all things. Instead, this whiteness happens by grace of the purification of the material subject of the Snow itself. For one may see that Earth, frozen by the Northern cold, does not cease to retain its inherent blackness; yet the ice of water (inasmuch as Water is the Element of Earth exalted and purified by one degree through the "cooking" of Sulphur) is rendered more beautiful, white, and purified. 

But indeed, where Sulphur, by its increase, has worked and purified the matter of water into air, we recognize that by thinning the air itself, it is much to be preferred over the Element of water, both in its fineness and purity as well as the speed of its motion. Therefore, as it is manifest that there is more invisible fiery Sulphur in water than in earth—insofar as water is more mobile than earth (and all mobility comes from the light of Sulphur)—so indeed Air is recognized to excel Water in its sulphurous heat, and consequently is placed above it in purity and perfection. 

Hence it is that cold produces whiter effects in the air than in either water or earth. It is not that cold itself "makes" this or that color, as it only acts upon these Elements by freezing them. Since cold belongs to the potential essence of **Darkness** and is not a mere "accident" <note>An "accident" is a temporary or non-essential quality. The author argues cold is a fundamental part of the "Darkness" that existed before Light.</note> (as the common people suppose), we must believe that by its natural inclination, it tends more toward darkness, gloom, and rest than toward procreating a white color. For that whiteness is the duty of the **Internal Sulphur**, first purifying the water into air by thinning and "cooking" it; and then it is the role of the Cold to alter the purified invisible air into visible frost and snow—the whitest of colors—by freezing it. Only then does the external light reveal that color during the winter time. In the summer, the air is observed to turn more yellow because of the dominion of Sulphur within it, as can be seen in saffron-colored and tawny clouds.

Because of the various ways Sulphur operates in the air regarding the different changes of the seasons—namely in its opaque and less-cooked state, versus its transparent and more elaborated state—various colors are seen and revealed both in the **Rainbow** <note>original: "Iris"</note> and in the clouds, as the Sun shines and uncovers them. Thus, in a lit flame of pitch, the color is seen to tend toward blackness; but the flame of wax tends toward yellowness. <meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s exploration of light, color, and the "Tria Prima" (Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury). ### Volume 1. Treatise I. Section I. Part III. Book V.

the agent in all these things is nothing but one and the same: but because the subjects are concocted <note>original: "concocta." In alchemy, "concoction" refers to the process of ripening or perfecting matter through heat.</note> in different ways and arranged in varying degrees of impurity, they yield variable colors, no differently in mixtures than in the **Elements** themselves. Nor indeed are colors here merely accidents <term>accidents: In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are properties of a thing (like color or size) that can change without changing the thing's essential nature. Fludd argues here that colors are more fundamental than that.</term>; but they are *essential* appearances (as we have said) of the various mixtures of external light within a **Mercurial** subject that has been variably concocted and elaborated.

Hence it is that **Darkness** or blackness in a coal, when equally bathed in the presence of fiery **Light**, produces redness; yet that same light in thick smoke procreates a saffron color. Nevertheless, from that part of the flame closest to the coal or the black wick <note>original: "lichnio." Referring to the wick of a lamp or the center of a candle flame.</note>, a blue color reveals itself, because it has more of the appearance of blackness than of the saffron flame. But if the part of the flame between that purple color and the purely saffron flame is well observed, you will perceive it to be more green, as that color consists of that saffron and blue (or blackness) mixed together.

However, when the fire is completely extinguished, the coal will appear deeply black—not because the moist smoke (as they say) escaping reduced it to such an appearance, but because of the extinction and consumption of the **native sulphur**, or rather because of its hiding within itself. This indeed happens in every destruction of a specific subject, until a new form is introduced: that is, until the second generation of the dead thing occurs. For once their form is taken away, all things will remain dark and formless.

But truly, that this **sulphurous form** is hidden in the center of the thing (for it is more fixed than any other thing and resists the violence of external fire) is declared by the fact that the "species" <note>original: "species." Here meaning the formal essence or spiritual blueprint of a living thing.</note> of things lie hidden in their ashes and in the **Salt** which usually leaps out from the center of the ashes. Frequent experience has taught us this, both in the salt of herbs (which is observed to emit branches in water similar to its own species) and indeed—what seizes us with no small wonder—that which is extracted from **human bones**, if dissolved in a small dish full of pure water and allowed to infuse therein through the night, you will find (marvelous to say) many men like crystals, as if fixed to crosses and hanging in that water. This notable experiment was revealed to me by the Reverend Father and my most worshipful Lord, **John Thornborough**, Bishop of Worcester <note>John Thornborough (1551–1641) was a real English bishop and alchemist who claimed to have discovered the "Philosopher's Stone." This experiment is a form of "palingenesis," the alchemical resurrection of a plant or animal from its ashes.</note>.

-> **Therefore we conclude** <-

that just as the single extreme of all colors is **Blackness** (namely, that inseparable companion of the Shadows; or rather, the formless shadows themselves, destitute of all actual light, for *before the creation of light, darkness was upon the face of the abyss* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2.</note>), so indeed this kind of gloom or extreme color was not an accident (as the common folk say), but was as much of the **Essence of divine power** as **Light** was the act of it. That gloom (I say) was as much of the nature and existence of the formless **prime matter** <term>prime matter: "Materia Prima," the original, undifferentiated substance created by God from which all things were made.</term> as Light was before every beginning or eternity, and from age to age with God and in God. 

Wherefore **Moses** called this kind of real gloom "palpable darkness" <note>original: "Tenebras palpabiles." Referring to the Plague of Darkness in Exodus 10:21.</note> and not accidental darkness. For just as the primary Light could not be considered an accident—since, as it was the first creature, it found no subject in nature existing before it to which it could adhere—so indeed we must think of the primordial shadows and gloom. Similarly, just as it belongs to Light to purify from blackness into extreme whiteness (where every degree of that purification claims an Essential color for itself), so conversely the **Shadows** act by thickening, and by blackness deforming the colors produced by the action of light, hiding them in gloom. 

The intermediate **Mercurial** subject, therefore, upon which both Light (by acting) and Darkness (by resisting, and by that resistance reacting) work, is **Water**, from which (according to St. Peter) the Heavens and the Earth, and consequently all things distinct in both species and color, were made. Wherefore we also consider it to follow that since neither Light nor Darkness are accidents, so neither should **Heat** nor **Cold** truly be reckoned as accidents; for although heat seems to us to be something accidental, it is nonetheless...

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s discussion on the nature of light and color, transitioning from the physical observation of fire (like the candle flame mentioned on the previous page) to the theological and alchemical principles of the "Tria Prima" (Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury). He argues that qualities like heat and color are essential manifestations of the Divine rather than mere superficial "accidents."</meta>

# On the Elementary Origin of Life and Health.

...is nothing other than the turning of light, or invisible fire expanded in the air, into an act, which is so tied to the Essence of light as Light is to God, or a solar ray to the Sun. Therefore, we say that heat is something **Essential**, joined as closely as possible with its luminous source. And the same is true of cold. For who would say that "accidents" <term>accidents: In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the core essence of a thing—like the color of a shirt. Fludd is arguing that these qualities are actually part of the core "essence" of God’s creation.</term> exist in God? Yet truly, in the sacred context we read these things: *By the breath of God, frost is given* <note>original: "Flante Deo, concrescit gelu" - Job 37:10.</note> and *who can stand before His cold?* <note>original: "contra frigora eius, quis consistit" - Psalm 147:17.</note> Similarly, on the contrary, the Scriptures testify that *God is a consuming fire* <note>Hebrews 12:29.</note> and that *He inhabits inaccessible Light.* <note>1 Timothy 6:16.</note> Therefore, to say that any accidents belong to Him would be most absurd and profane. This being the case, what less should be said of the color of the divine aspect? By whose gaze the face of Moses shone so brightly that the Israelites were unable to look upon it.

Furthermore, in the visions of Ezekiel and St. John, many colors were seen in the appearance of the person of God, the Holy Angels, and the Spirits in the wheels: all of which, it must be believed by faith, were **Essential**, and not either imaginary or accidental. For there is nothing in God and His Saints that is not from their pure and sincere Essence and truth; indeed, their purity and simplicity—especially that of God—exceeds all imagination and comparison.

Let us now look at the intentions of the true **Spagyrists** <term>Spagyrists: An early term for alchemists, particularly those following the traditions of Paracelsus who used chemical processes to create medicines.</term> concerning the procreation of colors, so that through their practice we may discern whether those things said by us are true, or at least probable, or not.

One says that the operation in true **Chemistry** is called "the excitation of the four colors." And another says: *that they are changes appearing by their art.* And **Paracelsus** says: *that there are as many varieties of Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt as there are different fruits in the minerals; for one Sulphur and one Salt is held in lead, another in iron, gold, copper, etc.; and in Sapphire, gems, and other stones and marcasites, etc. All colors truly come from the nature of Sulphur and Salt in which they consist; but Mercury exhibits the substance of the bodies.* And **Nicolas Flamel** <note>A famous 14th-century French scribe and legendary alchemist.</note> says: *the Earthy element is black; the Aqueous, shining and white; the Aerial, yellow and citrine; the Fiery, glowing and red.* And **Isaac Hollandus** <note>A 15th-century Dutch alchemist often cited for his practical laboratory instructions.</note> says that there are three various colors which, according to the governance of the Fire and the movement of the natural Sulphur in the matter, present themselves essentially in the work: namely, black, white, and red. And he says that between any of these colors, various colors show themselves—indeed, more than can be devised. By these, he seems to indicate the various kinds of intermediate colors that arise from each extreme and the middle red. 

Elsewhere, they acknowledge that **Whiteness** lies hidden in blackness; **Citrine-yellow** in whiteness; and in that, **Redness**. They denote the reason for these colors to be the **Tingeing and Vivifying Spirit**, which, by gradually drying out the corrupting humidities, passes from nature to nature. In every degree of its change, it transmutes the nature of the compound—the species varying by color—and tinges it in various forms, according to its diverse dominion over the humidity and the increase of the decoction <note>original: "decoctionis." In alchemy, this refers to "cooking" or heating a substance over a long period to mature it.</note> or the fire of nature. 

For whatever is made in this world is made by **Sulphur**, **Mercury**, and **Salt**, which cooperate in the creature in imitation of their roots: namely, **Sulphurous Light**, **Mercurial Water**, and the **Salt** fused from both. Sulphur, as it were, "speaks" and tinges with its habit as it wills; it is the efficient cause from which the Tingeing Light, as if from a mouth, brings forth the aqueous Mercury, through which the heavens are made firm, and its Orbs are distinguished from one another by the operation of Sulphur. From the Salt proceeding from both, every virtue of the heavens is procreated, as it were, to which Sulphur and Mercury are always companions and comforters. Therefore, it happens that when one is altered in the Mercurial matter, it is necessary that (in effect) the remaining two are also altered. And thus we have all things in three; and those three nevertheless result in a single Essence, firm in itself, fixed and everlasting. Therefore it is certain that just as all things are created through degrees from the three, so indeed those three, distinct only by property, consist in a single nature. Thus all are three, and the three are one. 

Colors truly arise from the deeper or more superficial nature of one of the three in another: Thus, the deeper the Light penetrates into a transparent thing, the darker it becomes; and in an opaque thing, it changes the appearance of the object in many forms.

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s exploration into the origins of color, moving from the philosophical and scriptural justifications of the previous page to practical alchemical experiments and a systematic "Ring of Colors." Fludd argues that color is a manifestation of the "formal nature of sulphur" acting upon a "Mercurial subject."</meta>

### Volume I, Treatise I, Section I, Part III, Book V.

Finally, I shall produce a single example proven by our own experience, by which you may perceive how colors are introduced into a transparent subject through the increase or decrease of the formal nature of sulphur. For I extracted from **Wheat** an airy nature, which was nothing other than a certain volatile salt—limpid, fluid, and in its own color very similar to crystal, white and clear. I exposed this liquor to the Sun; and first its natural crystalline whiteness was changed and converted into the form of a **Hyacinth** <note>In the 17th century, "hyacinth" often referred to a reddish-orange gemstone (zircon), rather than the modern blue flower.</note>: then afterward, in the space of three more hours, into the appearance of a **Ruby**: finally, by attracting to itself a multitude of solar sulphur, it took on the darkest color of a **Garnet**: indeed, that liquor, which was previously quite transparent, was now hardly penetrable to the sight because of the multitude of that sulphur.

Therefore, it is evident that color in the substance of all gemstones is **natural sulphur** implanted in any **Mercurial body** <term>Mercurial body: In alchemical theory, Mercury represents the passive, fluid, or metallic "matter" of a substance, while Sulphur represents the active, fiery "spirit" or quality.</term>. For this is the reason that Wheat, only after its putrefaction in the earth, receives so much fire, or light, or sulphurous tincture from heaven: so that by means of it, the wheat can be multiplied infinitely, as if every year. This is more fully declared in our *Anatomy of Bread and Wheat* <note>original: "Anatomia nostra de Pane & Tritico" - a reference to another of Fludd's works.</note>.

Hence, therefore, arises the various tinctures of **Sapphires**, **Hyacinths**, **Rubies**, **Emeralds**, and other precious stones. Hence also the reason for the progression from one color to another in growing fruits: for the more the sulphur grows and grows, the more it changes color according to the condition of the Mercurial subject: as is very easily gathered from the stages of fruits progressing toward maturity.

Now, listen to how these alterations of sulphur in colors usually present themselves even to common sense.

**Blackness** is in unlit charcoal, arguing for the absence or concealment of the sulphurous form within the central salt; wherefore, in the manner of a confused **Chaos**, all things there are overwhelmed by darkness. But if it is slightly ignited into a flame, it brings forth a **Blue** color; in which there is much blackness or black smoke and little flame. But if more saffron-colored flame is present, and less black smoke—or if the smoke is somewhat subtler than in the blue—the color will be **Green**. But if the black charcoal is equal to the sulphurous fire adhering to its body, then a **Red** color will be produced. Where the thinner part of the flame is in the air, a **Yellow** color will come forth; and we shall find **Whiteness** in the illuminated air. You will perceive this more clearly from a candle-wick and its glowing flame; and thus, in the matter of the Mercurial world, with its fiery sulphur acting in various forms, we find the ring or wheel of colors, which we have expressed in this manner.

**YELLOW** | **BLUE**
<note>Equal in whiteness from each side.</note> | <note>More blackness, less light.</note>

<meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s discussion on the nature of color as a manifestation of alchemical Sulphur. Having previously discussed his experiments with wheat, he now expands this theory to the entire mineral and vegetable kingdoms, as well as the cosmic influence of the winds and elements.</meta>

# Concerning the Elementary Origin of Life and Health.

Finally, the Philosophers have confirmed all of this, recognizing and distinguishing **sulphur** <term>Sulphur: In Fludd’s alchemy, sulphur is the active, formal principle that gives a substance its color, smell, and "soul," rather than just the yellow mineral.</term> from sulphur by their colors: that one sulphur is white, such as that in silver; another is yellow and saffron-colored, like that in gold; another is green, like that in copper (which is partly red and partly green, as is evident in green copper-rust <note>original: "ære viridi"; refers to verdigris</note>); another is livid <note>Livid: A bluish-gray or leaden color.</note>, like that of Lead; and so it is with the others. And although these colors in sulphur represent various degrees of its **digestion** <term>Digestion: The alchemical process of maturation or "cooking" a substance through heat to reach a higher state of perfection.</term>, nevertheless there is only one genus of sulphur, which is observed to take on various forms in its action upon **Mercury** and salt.

Thus, in the **Sapphire**, it takes a heavenly form; in the **Turquoise**, a cyan form; in the **Hyacinth**, a yellow form; in the **Ruby**, a red form; in the **Emerald**, a green form; in **Lead**, a livid form; in **Copper**, a red form; in **tin and silver**, a white form; in **Gold**, a yellow form; and so on for the rest. Similarly, in the **cherry**, it appears red; in the **grape**, blue; in the same **apple**, it shows greenness, and with a slightly more mature digestion, yellowness, and sometimes redness. This clearly demonstrates that colors in the same subject are varied according to the increase and growth of the Sulphur within them. And this is the reason for the **transmutation** of one species into another: for every step in the progression from imperfection toward perfection occurs through the increase of the sulphur of that natural thing. Thus, by the mixing of terrestrial blackness (or black sulphur in the earth) in a greater proportion, with the saffron sulphur of the Sun (approaching the Arctic pole) in a smaller portion, there occurs the greenness in plants, foliage, grasses, and crops. And yet, in crops, we see that as the solar sulphur grows, a change occurs from greenness to yellowness, and from that into the redness of the grain; and so it is in other things.

Since these things are so, it must also be understood that since the **Winds** are varied in their operations, the degrees of the nature of Sulphur are disposed in various forms according to their blasts. It will not be difficult to relate all those things we have already said concerning the essences, natures, and degrees of colors in sulphur to the natures of the winds themselves: namely, **blackness** (or the crudest and weakest sulphur) to the **North**; **white** to the **West**; **yellow** to the **South**; and **red** to the **East**. From that fiery degree of the East, a transition is made again into the black charcoal of the North; but in the West, the **Salt** in white ashes melts in water; in the South, it grows into a yellow tincture; and in the East, it is exalted in the **furnace of perfection** <note>The "furnace of perfection" refers to the final stage of alchemical work, often associated with the color red (rubedo).</note> unto redness, in which it stands fixed and remains. 

And because the actions of the **Elements** arise from the natures of the Winds, it must follow that the sulphur of the **Earth** is cruder and blacker than the rest, and more hidden (inasmuch as Earth is cold and dry in its manifest nature); the sulphur of **Water** is more "cooked" than it was in the Earth, hence it is clearer and whitening; in the **Air**, it is indeed more cooked and takes on a yellower habit; but in its **Fire**, in its native home, it is adorned in a golden and purple garment.

And all these mutations Sulphur receives from the single and simple **Source of Wisdom**: which for this reason is called the **Multiple Spirit** <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 7:22, describing the Divine Spirit as "one, yet manifold."</note>, insofar as it changes and alters these multiform sulphurs—which distinguish species by both color and figure—at every moment of time.

### CHAPTER I.

->*On the Super-celestial method of preserving health in general.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'A' (replacing the Latin 'V') featuring a landscape or architectural scene within the letter's frame.</image-desc>
As it is the part of a wise man to look first to the Center before he occupies himself with the Circumference like the common crowd—that is, to search out the internal cause before he passes any judgment on the effect like a reckless worldling—so indeed we consider it the mark of a true Philosopher to explain and investigate the internal and central method of preserving health (as the primary cause), before he thinks about its effects.

But truly, by the Physicians and Philosophers of every age, the matter is held far differently; for it is and has been their habit to take effects for the primary causes in preserving health. They understand very little that God is the acting cause in the world, or the act that is both primordial <term>Primordial: Existing from the very beginning; the first "spark" of action.</term> and final, before all, through all, and in all. For this reason, He is called **Alpha and Omega**, the beginning and the end: as He from whose essence or act, in whose act, and through whose act all things exist. From this it follows that as He Himself is the author of lives, so indeed all creatures endowed with life have the expectation of their life and health from Him. Consequently, it is fitting for every creature to excel in the purity of both Spirit and body, so that it may be rendered worthy to approach the fountain of life—namely God—by the mediation of the ray of life; which ray participates in the divine nature. <margin>Wisdom 7; Wisdom 1:14.</margin> For *the divine Spirit is simple, unique, pure, sincere, undefiled, loving the good, who from His goodness and mercy created all things that they might exist, and made the nations of the earth healthy: and He did not place in them the medicine of destruction, nor the kingdom of the underworld upon the earth, insofar as His bright justice, which He communicated to His creatures (that they might live), is perpetual and immortal.* <note>original Latin quote: "Spiritus diuinus est simplex, unicus, purus...". Fludd is quoting the Book of Wisdom, emphasizing that God created life for health and immortality, not for death.</note>

The cause of diseases, therefore—or the departure from the laws of Health even unto death—is **Unrighteousness**. This is what the wicked have summoned with both their hands and their words, and thinking...

## CHAPTER II.
->In which the purpose of human creation is explained.<-

<margin>Ecclesiastes 12:13</margin> Since the whole duty of man in this life is twofold—namely, to revere God Himself and to observe His commandments (for this is the "whole" of Man, as Solomon testifies)—it is not at all fitting for him to wander from that path. As Christ testified, that path encompasses the entire Mosaic Decalogue <term>Mosaic Decalogue: The Ten Commandments given to Moses.</term>: namely, to Fear God with all one’s heart, and to Love one's neighbor. Of these commandments, the former pertains to the pure spirit and the mystical man, insofar as God is the simplest Spirit; the latter looks toward the body and the external man, by which we are taught to behave toward our neighbors and brothers with sweetness and morality. In this way, through a sweet bond and a peaceful harmony, by uniting earthly things with heavenly ones, we may be able to ascend to the very palace of Eternity and gain entry to the third heaven <note>The "third heaven" is a biblical reference to the dwelling place of God, popularized by St. Paul.</note>. For the doors of Divinity are opened to those who observe the divine mandates, but they are closed to the wicked.

<margin>Psalm 1:2</margin> <margin>Psalm 1:4</margin> <margin>Psalm 34:5</margin> <margin>Psalm 34:8</margin> <margin>Psalm 5:6</margin> <margin>Psalm 14:5</margin> <margin>Psalm 68:3</margin> <margin>Proverbs 11:7</margin>
> *Hence it is that, just as the meditation of the righteous and blessed is on the law of Jehovah <note>original: "Iehouae"</note>, so indeed the unjust are separated from the assembly and judgment of the righteous, and consequently they do not walk in the divine law, nor can they penetrate the seats of the blessed. For this reason, Jehovah is said to be the guardian of the righteous and the pious, and to know their way, while on the other hand, the journey of the unjust and the wicked is delivered to destruction. Therefore, whatever the righteous man does shall prosper; but it is not so with the wicked, who are like the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. Thus, He directs the righteous in the way of salvation and snatches them from all dangers and fears; because the Angels of Jehovah encamp around those who fear Him, and rescue them from evil. But truly, the wicked man shall not dwell near God, nor shall he remain before His eyes. From this it follows that he trembles with fear, because God is present with the generation of the righteous; and he shall perish from the sight of God as wax melts before a fire, and when he dies, his hope and expectation perish.*

We conclude, therefore, that God is a shield and a fortress to the pious and the good, because they strive to perform that for which they were born: namely, to revere God, their salvation and the fountain of their life, with their whole heart, and to observe His commandment with all their effort. Therefore, He preserves them in health through His good Angels and leads all their actions to a happy conclusion; whereas, conversely, He commits the wicked to the cruelty of evil angels, rendering them as wretched in body and soul as they are, for the most part, unhappy in their actions.

<margin>Wisdom 16:13. Job 33:19.</margin> 
Since God has the power of life and death, He leads down to the gates of hell and brings back again. He sometimes rebukes a man through pain upon his bed, and makes all his bones 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:27. Psalm 3:9.</margin> 
waste away; He makes bread abominable to him in his life, and makes his soul loathe food that was previously desirable. And again: *He brings safety and the preservation of health to man, since He alone is the Savior, and there is no other besides Him, insofar as salvation itself is in Him.*

The reason, therefore, for the one or the other—health or sickness—is either the observance or the revocation of that 
<margin>Ecclesiastes 1:15. Deuteronomy 10:12.</margin> 
duty for which man was created and born in continual succession: namely, that he should revere God and observe His Commandment. For according to the testimony of Moses, the Lord Jehovah asked nothing of the Israelites except that they fear Him as their God, walk in 
<margin>Deuteronomy 30:15.</margin> 
all His ways, and love and worship Him with all their heart and all their soul. It is in this sense that these words were brought forth by Moses to the Israelites: *I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, good and evil, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live; for Jehovah your God is your life and the length of your days.* By this speech, he seems to argue that in the observance of the Law and the Commandment there is Life, Health, and length of days; while in the revocation and transgression of it, there arises evil and infirmity, and the shortening 
<margin>Exodus 23:25.</margin> 
of one's natural days. Wherefore it is said elsewhere: *If you serve the Lord your God, I will bless your bread and your water, and I will take away sickness from the midst of you; your land shall not be unfruitful or barren, and I will fulfill the number of your days.*

The condition of these blessings is that men serve the Lord and perform His commandments; if they do not do this, then instead of blessings, curses 
<margin>Exodus 15:26.</margin> 
will follow, just as we read elsewhere: *If you diligently listen to the voice of Jehovah your God, and do what is right in His eyes, if you incline your ear to His precepts and observe all His statutes, I will impose upon you none of the diseases which I imposed upon the Egyptians, for I, Jehovah, will be your healer.* <note>Original: "Iehoua ero curator tuus."</note> These things were said by Him who is the unique life of the world and its health; and He will truly provide these to any pious person, if that person tries to avoid the disposition of his dark or <term>Privative: A philosophical term referring to the absence or "deprivation" of a quality—in this case, the absence of divine light or health.</term> privative nature, and does not resist His luminous laws in the slightest.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Who is the wicked, and the son of darkness: and who is the pious and the Just? Can the just man exactly observe the divine commands? Hear (says Moses) the precepts and judgments which I teach you, so that by doing them, you may live. Keep the commandments of your God, etc. But now it must be asked whether observing these commandments is within human power, or not. We have received this from Solomon himself: that a body infested with corruption burdens the soul, and the earthly dwelling-place weighs down the mind when it is full of many cares; we hardly guess at the things that are on earth, and we find with great labor the things that are right before our hands. 
<margin>Wisdom 9.</margin>
*But who shall investigate the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know the counsel of God, unless God gives wisdom and sends His Holy Spirit from the high heavens?
