The author quotes the Book of Wisdom to argue that human reason alone is insufficient to understand divine law.</note> Thus far the Wise Man. Since this is the case, who can rightly understand the paths and commandments of God by himself and by his own nature, unless God has given him wisdom, by which he may be led into the true way of the luminous Law (the head of which is wisdom itself)?
<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
For it belongs to Wisdom alone to establish the friends of God and the Prophets; for God is said to love no one except the person who dwells with Wisdom. What follows from this? Is no one, therefore, truly just and pious except for the one who possesses mystical wisdom? Who then is secure in this life, since there seem to be so few who have received the living gift of Wisdom?

But if man (*whom God placed in honor, even if he does not understand this himself, as the Psalmist says*)—if (I say) he had rightly understood that Wisdom to have been that eternal light which enlightened every man coming into this world: 
<margin>John 1.</margin>
*by which the world was made, and in which is the life of men;* <note>A reference to the Prologue of the Gospel of John, identifying Wisdom with the "Logos" or Divine Word.</note> he would indeed recognize that this Wisdom is not far from human life and its composition. But because of the deception of the dark body, that Light cannot be discerned by miserable mortals; therefore they do not believe such a divine nature is so near to them. For this reason, they love darkness more than Light, and consequently, they are called "sons of darkness," insofar as they are blinded by darkness and have embraced Error in place of Truth. They are also called "sons of the world," insofar as they contemplate only the visible things of the world and therefore do not believe this Mystical Light exists at all, because it is not subject to their physical senses. In this way they sin and are led astray by the Devil's error, for by holding a dark figment <note>The word "figmentum" here suggests an illusory or false reality created by the senses or the devil.</note> to be the clear truth, they have received death instead of life, according to the aforementioned assertion of the Wise Man: 
<margin>Wisdom 1:14.</margin>
*God created all things that they might exist, and he made the nations of the world healthy; for Justice is perpetual and immortal. But Unjustice is the acquisition of death, which the wicked have summoned with their hands and words; and thinking it a friend, they have wasted away and are worthy of death, etc.* This means: GOD created all things through Justice—that is, through His luminous Wisdom, which is perpetual, immortal, and eternal life itself. From this, His life-giving presence rendered all things healthy, insofar as the Life of the universal World consists in it. But truly Unjustice—that is, that dark, fictional thing or figment which is seen in the true Light but is not truly part of it—has brought diseases, death, sin, and error into the world. It removes and hides that real light from the senses of mortals, just like an ugly rust which the most polished and bright iron has contracted upon itself,

# CHAPTER V.

->By what means access to the divine Presence is made, after God has<-
->hidden his face from sinners: And how Sinners are to be<-
->purged from the filth of sin.<-

In order that the sinner, or transgressor of the divine Law, may be able to behold the benevolent face of **Jehovah**, and return to his former state of health (with the spirit of Grace assisting); three things in particular are to be diligently required of him: namely, *a fit preparation of his spirit to receive mental action, the action of the mental power itself, and finally, the benevolent effect of that action.*

The Sacred Page <note>A traditional term for the Bible.</note> confirms the preparation of the Spirit thus: *Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like a man who tempts God, etc.* And we affirm that this Preparation consists chiefly in three things: namely, in *Repentance, Humility, and Charity*; which three, *Faith and Hope* are accustomed to accompany. We shall therefore discuss these a little more fully in this chapter. The action of the mind, which ought to follow the said preparation, is sincere and faithful **Prayer** <note>original: "Oratio"</note>, through the mediation of which the Spirit is believed to have access to the presence of God and before the throne of the Omnipotent, whose role it is to provide health by his benevolent gaze to both the body and the soul. Just as, on the contrary, his absence is followed not only by the perturbation of the whole composite being through sicknesses and unrest, but even sometimes by **Death** <note>original: "Mors"</note> itself, which is the dissolution of the composite being.

Concerning this action, namely Prayer, we shall discuss at length in the following book. Finally, the **Effect** is the sending of the spirit of Wisdom herself, accompanied by a choir of graces and Angels, into the sinning soul, so that it may be illuminated by her Light, and be cleansed and purged from its darkness and the filth of sin. And by this means, the truly repentant Sinner will be made into a new creature. Concerning this subject, the *third and last Book of this part* will treat.

<margin>Repentance</margin>
As for what pertains to the first part of preparation, Seneca says in *Thyestes*: *He who repents of having sinned is almost innocent.* For Repentance is defined not only as a certain mortification of vices, but also as a spiritual martyrdom of the soul; inasmuch as it is pierced through on every side by the sword of the Spirit (which is the word of God). Hence it is that sincere Repentance cleanses and expurgates, and directs one toward the good: and it is the chief cause why the divine rays, which had turned away from the sinner, return to him again. Therefore, the Poet speaks thus of this part:
> *They often lighten the punishments, and restore the sight that was snatched away,*
> *When they see that one has truly repented of the sin.*

->CHAPTER I.<-
->*Concerning the supreme mystery of Prayer: and concerning its Root, or primary agent.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
The Creator of all universal things, at the moment of His creation, exalted and enriched Man with such dignity and excellence beyond and above all mortal things; the Sacred Scriptures testify that He created him in His own image and likeness. For besides the fact that He infused into him the breath of Life <note>original: "Vitę spiritum"</note> as He did with other animals, He also inspired in him a Divine Mind <note>original: "Mentem diuinam"</note>, by which he was made intelligent and rational above all other living creatures.
<margin>Job 32.</margin> Hence, Job said: *There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding:* <note>original: "In homine est spiritus, sed inspiratio Omnipotentis intelligere facit eum"</note> that is to say, although the Soul of the World <term>Anima Mundi; the Neoplatonic concept of a soul that connects all living things and animates the universe</term> adapted him so that he might live, He nevertheless bestowed upon him a portion of the Angelic life. By this, he might conduct himself wisely and in the manner of a son of God among mortals—that is, in the fear of his Creator, and in love and moral conduct toward his brothers here on earth. This is achieved by penetrating through a mental ray <note>original: "radium siue mentale"; a philosophical concept where the mind acts as a beam of light connecting the individual to God</note> to the seat of God (which is in the highest heavens, insofar as the mind itself, being of the divine essence, cannot be distinguished or divided from the divine source). By this means, he understands the Mysteries of Heaven, modestly investigating all things here on earth and observing them tropologically <note>an interpretive method seeking moral or spiritual lessons behind physical realities</note>, leading a life with his brothers in a social and civic manner, and finally understanding both celestial and earthly things by the power of his God-shaped <note>original: "Dei-formis"</note> mind. For this reason, the voice of the Royal Prophet was not ill-considered when he said:
<margin>Psalm 8.</margin> *That God made man a little lower than the Angels, for He formed him with glory and honor, and for that reason made him Lord over all the works of His hands, and placed all things under his feet: namely, all flocks and herds, the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea, etc.* Indeed, so exalted is that Dignity which he received from the Mind divinely infused, that he even seems to surpass the heavenly inhabitants. For he is not only a partaker and heir of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is even promised that he shall be transformed into the divine image. Wherefore, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetica, a body of mystical and philosophical texts, are attributed</note> breaks out into this discourse with good reason:
<margin>Poimandres 10.</margin>
> Every soul possesses the Good itself from the Mind; for a Soul deprived of the presence of the Mind is able neither to do nor say anything. That divine Job said: *The Spirit of God has made me, and the Breath of the Almighty has given me life.* And elsewhere: *The inspiration of the Almighty has given man understanding, etc.* <note>original: "Inspiratio Omnipotentis intelligere fecit hominem"</note> Truly, this inspiration is the same as the Divine Wisdom <term>Sapientia; the personified wisdom of God often associated with the Holy Spirit or the Logos</term>. Whence it is said elsewhere: *Who has put wisdom in the inward parts or the viscera? Or who has given understanding to the Mind?* And elsewhere: *God made man by his Wisdom.* But Wisdom is always with God, as she who is His counsel and understanding (as the patient man <note>i.e., Job</note> testifies). And yet she is everywhere, insofar as (as Solomon testifies) she fills the world and is present in every thing of this world, but more abundantly in man. Thus, before that Light was obscured by the dark veil of ignorance and shadows in Adam and his descendants because of his disobedience, this Microcosm could do all things and understand all things, and was as if he were God himself, being formed in His image. But after Adam's fall, this Light was so wrapped in the darkness of wrath, and its Omnipotent Virtue so hidden, that it is believed by some worldly people not to exist, or at least to be minimally present to them, because it is hardly perceived by them. ## CHAPTER I.
### *Concerning the supreme mystery of Prayer: and concerning its Root, or first agent.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' within a rectangular woodcut border featuring floral and leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>
The Creator of all universal things exalted and enriched Man at the moment of his Creation beyond and above all mortal things with such dignity and excellence that the Holy Scriptures testify that He created him in His own image and likeness. For besides the fact that He infused him with the breath of Life as He did with other animals, He also breathed into him a divine Mind, by which he was made intelligent and rational above all other creatures. <margin>Job 32</margin> For this reason, Job said: *There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding:* <note>original: "In homine est spiritus, sed inspiratio Omnipotentis intelligere facit eum"</note> that is to say, even though the World Soul <term>Anima Mundi: the vital force that animates the physical universe</term> prepared him so that he might live, God nevertheless bestowed upon him a portion of the Angelic life. By this, he might conduct himself wisely and in the manner of a son of God among mortals—that is, in the fear of his Creator, and in love and moral conduct toward his brothers here on earth. Namely, he does this by penetrating through a mental ray to the seat of God (which is in the highest heavens, insofar as the mind itself, being of the divine essence, cannot be distinguished or divided from the divine source). He does this by understanding the Mysteries of Heaven, by investigating everything here on earth with moderation and observing them symbolically <term>tropologically: interpreting events or texts to find moral or spiritual meanings</term>, by leading a life with his brothers in a social and civic manner, and finally by understanding both celestial and earthly things through the power of his God-like mind.

For this reason, the voice of the Royal Prophet was not without consideration when he said: <margin>Psalm 8</margin> *That God made man a little lower than the Angels, inasmuch as He formed him with glory and honor, and for that reason made him Lord over the works of His hands and placed all things under his feet: namely, flocks and herds, however many there are, and the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea, etc.* Indeed, so sublime is that Dignity which he received from the Mind divinely infused within him, that he even seems to surpass the Dwellers of Heaven in this: for not only is he a partaker and heir of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is also promised that he shall be transformed into the divine image.

Therefore, not without justice does Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed</note> break out into this discourse: <margin>Pimander 10</margin> *Every soul receives the Good itself from the Mind; for a Soul deprived of the presence of the Mind is able neither to act nor to speak anything. For this reason, Man is a divine animal, not to be compared with earthly brutes, but with the celestial Gods. Either, therefore, he is more excellent than the Dwellers of Heaven, or at least he possesses an equal lot with them. For truly, whoever of the celestials descends to the earth leaves behind the limit of Heaven; but Man ascends into Heaven and measures it, nor do the lowest things escape him; he diligently investigates both the sublime and all other things. And what is more, without even leaving the earth, he is raised into heaven. So vast is the power of human nature. Wherefore, we must dare to say, that Man is indeed a terrestrial [God],*

<margin>John 3:19.</margin>

If it takes its refuge in the solace of that divine Light, it will suddenly find that kind, sweet, and lovely Light ready to shine upon it with benevolence. It will make a way and an entrance for the soul, penetrating through the clouds, through the stars, and through the dense Choirs of Angels, to its Father. There, this humbled and repentant Spirit may look upon the face of its Father with joy, and cry out with the prodigal son: *Father, I have sinned against heaven and earth and before you, etc.*

Indeed, the Holy Spirit itself will intercede for them with the Father, so that at last, grace having been granted, they may be reborn and raised anew from the death of sin.

He expresses the desired effect of his prayer, namely that He might grant him the joy of *His Savior* <note>original: "Salutaris sui." This likely refers to Psalm 51:12, where David asks for the joy of God's salvation.</note>; as if he had said: Rain down your Light and Grace upon me. By these words, it is clearly explained that the Spirit which stirred David to repentance was that "Principal Spirit," or that holy Light, by whose action the Gate of the Heavens is opened to anyone: and <margin>Psalm 36:10</margin> is made manifest to the wandering Spirit of Eternity. For He is the Mediator between men and God.*

Since these things are so, we have the mystery of Prayer revealed clearly enough: namely, that it is the Power of the Spirit, or the Divine Mind implanted in every human being, which is accustomed to plead the cause of the sinning Spirit before the face of its Father. This Power ceases from that duty as long as the human Spirit clings to darkness; and as long as it is overwhelmed by darkness, it is called a son of darkness and not of light. Nevertheless, when darkness is left behind and one is clothed in repentance, humility, and hope, the person is transformed again into a son of light through the mediation of the shining Spirit. By its mediation, the person is thoroughly cleansed and purged of sin, and finally exalted to eternal salvation, according to the words of the Apostle: *God has given us eternal life: and this life is in his Son: that is:* <margin>1 John 5</margin> in the eternal wisdom which He gave to man at creation to direct him in his affairs. This wisdom either overflows in clarity according to the will of the Father (the shining fountain) or is rendered darker and more hidden. Whence David says: *If you light my lamp (that is, the ray of life and being which is obscured by the darkness of the body), you will make my darkness shining.*

But since we shall discuss the glorious gifts of eternal Wisdom—which she is accustomed to give to those who repent—more abundantly in the following book, we shall hurry toward the successive explanation of the mystery of Prayer.

---

### CHAPTER II.

->In which Prayer is defined according to the intention of the Scriptures, and then,<-
->a further explanation of the Mystery itself is<-
->undertaken.<-

The Power of Prayer seems to be nothing other than an act of the shining mind <term>mentis lucidæ; the "shining mind" refers to the spark of divine intellect within the human soul</term> stirring the repentant Spirit, leaping forth from the internal hiding places of the human soul, and penetrating and as if knocking at the very seat and throne of the Almighty, so that an entrance may be made for the repentant one to the face of the Creator; so that, as grace shines forth, he may be refreshed in his distress. Hence the Wise Man says: *The prayer of the one who humbles himself will penetrate the clouds, and until* <margin>Ecclesiasticus 35</margin> *it draws near, he will not be consoled; and he will not depart until the Most High looks upon him.* Here, by "Prayer," he understands an outpouring or emission of the ray of the divine soul or mind <margin>Pimander 4</margin> <note>The "Pimander" refers to the *Poimandres*, the first tractate of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> whose nature it is (as Hermes testifies) *to embrace all things that are on the earth and in the sea, and whatever else is above the Heavens*; and thus it raises itself up so that it may gaze upon the Good itself and the shining fountain, etc. Nor is this surprising, since it can by no means be divided from its shining fountain. By "the one who humbles himself," he understands a Spirit led by repentance; by the "penetration of the clouds," he proves the subtlety of that active Spirit, of which the Wise Man says: <margin>Wisdom 7</margin> *The spirit of wisdom is subtle: more mobile than all things, reaching everywhere because of its purity, etc.*

Therefore, insofar as that Mind, or the Breath of Life, inhabits the human Spirit, and the soul is forged by the union of both with each other, we can quite aptly define Prayer as: *The outpouring of the praying soul in the sight of God: which will not be consoled until it approaches Him, and will not depart until the Most High in His kindness refreshes it and hears its petition.*

The first part of this description is confirmed by the response of Hannah to Eli the Priest, who accused her of being drunk: *I have not drunk* (she said) *but I have poured out my soul in the sight of the Lord.* <note>original: "effudi animam meam in conspectu Domini." This refers to 1 Samuel 1:15, where Hannah explains her silent, fervent prayer.</note> And David says: *I pour out my prayer in His sight; I declare my trouble before Him, etc.* Here he shows not only the means by which he prays, but also the reason why. And elsewhere he says: *Let my prayer be directed like incense in Your sight.* And the Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" here refers to John in the Book of Revelation.</note> says: *The prayers of the Saints are fragrances in bowls.*

<margin>
Revelation 5.
Romans 12.
Luke 11.
</margin>
Through the second clause, it is argued that the *Speaker must be urgent in his prayer*, according to the sense of the Apostle. Hence the Evangelist says: *He who prays perseveringly, because of the persistence of his knocking, shall be heard.* <note>original: "propter importunitatem pulsandi." This refers to the parable of the persistent friend in Luke 11:8.</note> Finally, in the aforementioned definition of Prayer or <term>Deprecation</term> <note>A formal prayer meant to turn away evil or seek divine favor.</note>, we find that the "Longing Spirit" is, as it were, the <term>material cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "material cause" is the substance out of which something is made.</note> of the soul, or the formal reason for the outpouring of that same Spirit. The Divine Mind, however—which moves and carries the Spirit, opening a passage for it through the earth, the waters, the clouds, and the air by its own subtlety, and leading its breath like incense to the desired goal or the blessed sight of the Creator—is the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary source of the change or movement.</note>. And finally, the <term>final cause</term> <note>The ultimate purpose or goal.</note> is seen in the granting of the Petition.

Therefore, when these things are considered seriously, though late, we will perceive that the Power of Prayer (contrary to the opinion of common people) does not pull <term>Divinity</term> and Grace down to us, since Divinity is in itself fixed and immovable. On the contrary, through prayers (relying on a secure confidence), we draw and lift our own Spirit up to God.

<margin>
Reuchlin, Book 3, On the Art of the Kabbalah.
</margin>
For neither God nor the Angels (after the manner of mortals) are moved by syllables or words. Instead, we use vocal prayer composed of words so that we may stir our own powers into their fervor, and fix our confidence in them like a <term>sacred anchor</term>. This is just as sailors, when bringing a ship to port, are accustomed to throw out a rope or extend a cable to "pull" the land toward them, even though the land is immovable; by such an effort, they actually pull themselves toward the desired land. By a similar reasoning, through sensible signs, we seem to allure the invisible power of the divine mind to us, when in truth we are drawing our own moving Spirits toward the immovable Divinity.

And this is the <term>Mystical foundation</term> by which not only every genuine petition but also all the Sacraments and the rites of Ceremonies are fundamentally perfected. It is for this reason that in petitions, thanksgivings, Sacraments, and other rites, we use signs, characters, the voice, hymns, songs, drums, and dancing; as well as pipes, cymbals, the lyre, the Organ, and other musical instruments of that kind. We do this not to soften God as if He were a woman, nor so that the Angels might be captured by the sweetness of our Harmony or the charms and flatteries of our prayers and entreaties. Rather, we do it so that by exalting God and divine things, we may acknowledge the smallness of our own condition, most humbly profess our subjection and obedience, and transmute all human pleasure into divine pleasure. Thus, we conceive an intense and burning love toward Divinity, which makes us capable of receiving all graces. For this reason, we stretch our palms toward heaven, spread our arms, and pray on bended knees.

Hence also Abraham and the Israelites were commanded to divide in half a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a turtledove, and a pigeon; to kill with a sword the ram caught by its horns in the thicket and burn it with fire; to mark the <term>Tau</term> <note>The Hebrew letter used as a sign of protection.</note> upon the doorposts of their houses with blood; to look upon the bronze serpent; and to fashion images of <term>Seraphim</term>, <term>Cherubim</term>, and other figures. They were told to speak and vow composed words, to construct a sanctuary, and to build magnificent temples; to look with awe upon their High Priest clothed in such varied and wonderful ornament. Observe: all these things and others like them were done for our own sakes, so that we might be moved and incited by them; that we might be turned away from evil thoughts and converted from visible things to invisible things. By this, our faith is increased, our hope is confirmed, and true Charity, most pleasing to God, is nourished among us.

# On the Super-Celestial Method of Preserving Life and Health.

<margin>
Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*, Book 1.
*The Guide for the Perplexed*, Book 3.
</margin>
This is the doctrine of the Hebrew Doctors and of the Egyptians, who were most skilled in spiritual mysteries, as is affirmed in eloquent words by Johann Reuchlin <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a German humanist and a key figure in bringing Hebrew studies and the Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note>. From him, we have learned what Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Rabbi Moses Ægyptiacus." This refers to Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> handed down: that the intention of such ceremonies is for the sake of frequent memory of God, the fear and love of Him, the observance of divine commandments, and so that the Highest God may be believed in with greater efficacy. And he adds the reason for this quite aptly: namely, because we, oppressed by the heavy mass of the body, lack things that suit our senses, by which our somnolent spirit might be truly and vividly stirred to the veneration of God. It is not unlike the **elephant**, which, when it grows sluggish with laziness, rises up more boldly when fire is shown to it. In the very same way, the power or vigor of our soul—which is, as it were, sleeping—requires such external incitements, whether of voices or figures, to press more robustly into spiritual work. Thus, our contemplation is carried upward into the sublime all the more sharply when we have been previously struck with astonishment.

We conclude, therefore, that the power of **vocal prayer**, and even the sound of **Music**, along with the other ceremonies of the Church, have little or no value in themselves for obtaining grace from God. Rather, it is the internal spirit itself which—incited more sharply by these same syllables, words, sounds, and ceremonies to seek God—is what matters. To God, all these things are dedicated with the greatest reverence and devotion, even though God cares very little for these ceremonies insofar as they are mere human inventions. Instead, He regards only a spirit that is humble, faithful, and confident, as a sacrifice and incense most pleasing to Him; and He is most ready to receive a mental petition, rather than one that is merely wordy.

### CHAPTER III.

->How many things are required for a faithful speaker of prayer: And how he<-
->ought to conduct himself in praying.<-

When anyone girds himself for the mystery of praying, it is necessary that he does not approach it in a crude manner or (as they say) *like a donkey to a banquet* <note>original: "sicut asinus ad cænam." A Latin proverb meaning to be completely unprepared or out of place.</note>—that is, without preparation. Instead, he should be perfectly disposed, both internally and externally, in the ornaments and habits fitting for such a duty, attending to that teaching of the Wise Man:
<margin>Sirach 18.</margin>
> Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like a man who tempts God.

<margin>
2 Chronicles 7.
1 Kings 8:35.
</margin>
As for what pertains to internal preparation, first (as has been declared before), **Repentance** is appropriate for him, whether his petition is for the remission of sins or for any other thing necessary to a sinner. Hence, the Holy Scriptures maintain that Repentance should always precede prayer, accompanied by a turning away from sins.

<margin>
Sirach 35.
Psalm 102:17.
Genesis 32.
Psalm 71:1.
Psalm 91:14.
Psalm 62:8.
Hebrews 6.
Proverbs 28.
</margin>
Next, **Humility** is exceedingly necessary in one who prays. For (as the son of Sirach says): *The prayer of him who humbles himself shall pierce the clouds.* And David says: *The Lord has regarded the prayer of the humble.* Therefore, in his own prayer, he professes his humility with these words: *I am needy and poor, help me.* And elsewhere it is indicated that Prayer ought to be sprinkled with the humiliation of the mind and conscience. Then, afterwards, it ought to be armed with confidence and hope, since without these it can accomplish nothing of importance. Whence the Royal Prophet says: *In You, O Lord, have I hoped, let me never be confounded.* And God Himself says through the mouth of the Prophet: *Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him and protect him.* And elsewhere: *Hope in God, all you congregation of people: pour out your hearts before Him,* etc. By this, he argues that the soul must be poured out in the sight of God with hope and confidence. The Apostle says, *We have hope as an Anchor of the soul,* safe and firm, entering even into the inner parts behind the veil. And Solomon gives the reason: *Because he who hopes in the Lord shall be saved.*

### CHAPTER IV.

->*To whom the duty of prayer is more suited. And what might be the lawful subject of Prayer.*<-

<margin>Psalm 6:10. Psalm 22:25. Leviticus 26.</margin>
Just as God hears the prayers of the righteous and accepts their orations: so indeed He does not despise nor abhor the affliction of the afflicted; nor does He hide His face from him; but when he cries out to Him, He hears. For God is accustomed to show favor to praying sinners: and this especially if the petition is made from the heart and with repentance.

<margin>Isaiah 1. Proverbs 15:8.</margin>
But God excludes the prayers of the wicked that are void of repentance and humility, and He makes them vain and invalid. When you multiply your prayer (says the Lord), I will not hear, because your hands are full of blood. <note>original: "quia manus vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt." A reference to Isaiah 1:15, where the prophet warns that ritual without morality is rejected.</note> In this way indeed the sacrifices of Cain (as being from a root of iniquity) were rejected by the Lord: while on the other hand, those of righteous Abel were accepted. For just as the victims of the impious are abominable to God, so the vows of the righteous are pleasing.

<margin>Psalm 19. Esther 4.</margin>
Therefore, the prayers of the righteous are undoubtedly more effective, and penetrate more quickly into the sight of God than those of sinners or the unjust. For the Lord God is present at the prayers of the faithful: and God will hear the prayers of the pious with ease from His holy Temple.

<margin>Deuteronomy 9. Deuteronomy 4. 1 Chronicles 6.</margin>
David approves of this in this way: *Now I recognize that Jehovah saves his anointed, hearing him from the heavens of his holiness; etc.* <note>original: "Iam agnosco Iehouam seruare unctum suum..." From Psalm 20:6 (Vulgate 19:7). The "anointed" refers to the King or the Messiah.</note> And this was the reason that Esther sought the prayers of the pious, so that her works and words might be directed by the Lord before the King. Furthermore, among pious and righteous men in general, some—by virtue of their office, function, and the sanctity of their condition—are more fit for praying for themselves and for others, and are more effective in their petitions: namely, Priests, Prophets, Apostles, and other holy men of this kind. Hence it is said: *Moses prayed for the people for 40 days and nights, so that he would not destroy them, etc.* <note>Moses' intercession after the incident of the Golden Calf is seen as the ultimate model of the "righteous man" saving the community through prayer.</note> For the people did not pray for themselves, being indeed impious, but the righteous Moses, the greatest Prophet, whose prayers God most easily heard. For the Lord God is accustomed to be present at the prayers of the faithful. And elsewhere (after the time of Moses) we read: That the prayers for the Israelites were made by the priests of the family of Aaron.

Similarly, Solomon—and not the people—prayed to God for the Temple, to be consecrated through God’s presence. Not the people, nor anyone from the people, but he to whom God had abundantly granted His wisdom, by whose help alone we contract a friendship with God.

<margin>2 Chronicles 19. Jeremiah 42. Jeremiah 7. 1 Maccabees 7. Acts 4. Acts 4 & 5. 2 Corinthians 13. Mark 14.</margin>
We read likewise how effective and elegant was the Prayer of Jehoshaphat, through which the Lord fought against the enemies of Israel. So also the remnant of the house of Judah did not pray to God for themselves, but asked Jeremiah to pray to the Lord. And God said to him: *Do not pray, Jeremiah, for this people, do not stand against me, because I will not hear you; etc.* <note>original: "Orare noli tu pro populo hoc..." In this way, although Abraham prayed for the Sodomites, nevertheless his prayers were not accepted by the Lord. Similarly, the Priests prayed against the blasphemer Nicanor, as did Judas [Maccabeus] himself. Finally, Christ prayed for his own. And while the Apostles were praying, *the place where they were gathered was moved, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit.* Furthermore, the Apostles prayed for the Samaritans so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. And Paul: *We pray to God, that you do nothing evil.* And: *That we may not enter into temptation.*

<margin>3 Kings 5.</margin>
Nor yet is any righteous person, or repentant sinner, to be excluded from the duty of prayer: Wherefore we read these things specifically concerning any pious person: *God will hear the prayers of the pious from His Temple.* And elsewhere: *God hears the prayers of the pious—*

# CHAPTER V.

->*How manifold prayer is. Regarding the place and time in which it is fitting to pray; whether we pray more effectively in a congregation or privately; and concerning the proper orientation of the person praying toward the cardinal points of the world.*<-

**P**rayer, by the testimony of the Holy Bible, is divided into Petition and Thanksgiving.

Petition is an outpouring of the soul before the sight of God, either for the advantage and welfare of any matter—be it private or public—or for a curse and disadvantage. For example: Elijah prayed that it would not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and the Heaven poured out rain, and the Earth gave its fruit. <note>Referencing James 5:17–18. Elijah is often cited in Hermetic and alchemical texts as a master of controlling natural elements through divine connection.</note>

<margin>James 5.</margin>
Sometimes both blessing and cursing are the subject of the same prayer, such as the prayer of Hezekiah, Isaiah, and Amos against Sennacherib; in which they blessed their own people, but truly cursed their enemies. So also the prayer of Jehoshaphat was a curse against the Moabites and Ammonites. <margin>2 Chronicles 20.</margin> For he speaks thus: *Behold, the sons of Ammon and Moab who strive to cast us out of the possession which you gave to us, our God; will you not judge them?* <note>original: "non iudicabis eos?"</note> That is to say: *Will you not cast your curse and your wrath upon them?* But indeed, he seeks a Blessing for his people in these words: *We will cry out to you in our tribulations, and you will hear us, and make us safe, etc.*

<margin>1 Maccabees 7:38.</margin>
Similarly, the Priests, in their petition, poured out a Curse against Nicanor before the Altar in this manner: *Take vengeance on this man and his army, and do not let them remain.* And David likewise curses his enemies: <margin>Psalm 34.</margin> <note>In the Latin Vulgate, this is Psalm 34; in most modern English Bibles, it is Psalm 35.</note> *Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me; let them be turned back and brought to confusion who devise evil against me; let them be as dust before the face of the wind, with the Angel of the Lord driving them on; let their way be dark and slippery, with the Angel of the Lord pursuing them, etc.* Yet in that same prayer-hymn, he thus blesses himself: *Lord, when will you look upon me? Restore my soul from their malice; judge me according to your justice, O Lord my God. And so it is in other cases.*

<margin>Tobit 8.</margin>
The other species of prayer, which is thanksgiving for a benefit received, is expressed in many places: see Psalms 143 and 144, etc. Also that prayer of Raguel and Anna <note>Likely referring to Sarah's parents in the Book of Tobit.</note> who said: *We bless you, Lord God of Israel, for you have shown your mercy and have shut out from us the enemy who pursued us.* (Namely, he delivered Tobias and Sarah from the Demon, etc.)

<margin>1 Timothy 2.</margin>
The Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> makes mention of these types of prayer, saying: *Let prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all men.*

And thus far, we have made prayer two-fold according to the subject with which it is concerned.

Now, however, according to its varying nature—and this according to the sense of the sacred letters—we define it as either <term>vocal prayer</term> (spoken aloud) or <term>mental prayer</term> (silent/internal).

We call "vocal" that prayer which is poured out into the open air in syllables and words. The root of this is the "prayer of the mind," which exists in the Spirit as a created thing before it is brought forth by the voice—just as the <term>sensible world</term> (the physical world we see) and the <term>Typical world</term> (the world of symbols) were mystically marked and figured in that <term>Archetypal world</term> (the divine blueprint in God's mind) before they were produced for the senses.

Likewise, mental prayer is no differently sketched out in the human spirit than the mind itself is in the <term>Intellectual Spirit</term>.

By these things it is evident that just as the Intellect is closer to the mind than the <term>imaginative spirit</term> (the *spiritus phantasticus*), so too is the latter closer than the sensitive spirit, which is ex-

...external: just as mental prayer <note>original: "Oratio mentalis"</note>, by its spiritual nature, is that which unites itself with the divine nature and is consequently known to God; more so than **verbal** prayer, which, with respect to the syllables and words spoken by the mouth, is entirely foreign to God. This is true even if it is produced vocally before the face of the Congregation and in an audible sense, so that through it the religious affections of the people and external worship may be drawn to their Center <note>The "Center" refers to God as the focal point of all spiritual gravity.</note>: so that they themselves, truly revering and fearing God and seeking Him in spirit, may approach Him with greater ardor and desire (as we touched upon above); and so that their spirits, praying with Him, may be admitted into the sight of God.

Similarly, one who prays alone is accustomed to pour out vocal prayer so that by the efficacy of that sound and the meaning of the words, his internal spirit may be excited to greater veneration and fervor toward God. This is especially for the unlearned laity, who are entirely ignorant of what the human spirit is, what the "internal man" is, and what the act of the divine mind is within them.

For this reason, therefore, Music is ordained in the Church; precious priestly vestments, lit candles, various craftsmanship of the Cross, and the invention of many wonderfully made Images are established. While these things in themselves may be nothing and perform nothing in divine matters by their own nature, nevertheless, because common people (whose business is more often with sensible things than with intelligible things) are led more by these external objects, even their internal spirits (to whose movements the bodies are moved) are incited through such external objects with a wonderful zeal toward Him in whose honor such things were originally devised.

But let us return to the mystery of prayer. Although every voice is heard by God and the Angels, it is not in the same way that humans hear and understand, or even the way they themselves hear and understand. For even if vocal sounds are perceived by the ears of men, men do not understand everything they hear, but only those things which are subject to their capacity and which they have learned through experience to be such. Therefore, their knowledge of a voice is only from the effect <note>original: "à posteriori"</note>, produced by long practice and experience. But indeed, that whispering which is made in the spirit by the power of the mind is that hidden and mystical sound which is familiar to God and the Angels (as they are spirits), and is in no way hidden from them. Therefore, that internal speech is that which comes from the source <note>original: "à priori"</note>, since it has its origin and its act from the divine mind. And that mystical speech is the foundation of that which is external and vocal. Hence it is that nothing is hidden from God, since His wisdom is the fountain of any spiritual and internal speech, just as that internal speech is the root of the external. Therefore, Wisdom immediately understands whether the voice or the "fruit of human tongues" comes from a good or an evil heart; consequently, God understands those things which are in the intellect and are not yet even uttered. For the intention of the spirit cannot be hidden from God, according to that saying of the Wise Man:
<margin>Wisdom 1</margin>
> *God is the witness of a man's affairs, the searcher of his heart, and the helper of his tongue. And the spirit of the Lord, which contains all things, has knowledge of the voice.*

Furthermore, because a voice that is not meaningful to men is yet known to God—both according to the intention of the internal mind and understood according to the necessity of the creature—<margin>Genesis 21</margin> it is said that the voice of the infant of Hagar, left by his mother and weeping, was heard by God, who granted him the necessities of life. For even though the voice of a crying infant is not "meaningful" <note>i.e., it lacks structured language or vocabulary.</note>, God nevertheless understands his intention before it is uttered. <margin>Matthew 6</margin>
> *Your Father (says Christ) understands what you need before it is asked.*

These things having been established, it is most clearly evident that spiritual petition is to be preferred by many degrees over vocal petition, since the former is the foundation of the latter. <margin>Luke 1:46</margin> Hence the Mother of God <note>original: "Deipara"</note> says: *My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced.*

By these words he seems to imply that words are of no help, except to explain revelations, prophecies, or doctrines to unbelievers through the tongues of the one praying, which is governed by the spirit. Truly, the essence of prayer remains in the mind. Wherefore, the Apostle warns us to pray as much with the spirit by which the tongue is moved, as with the mind, which is the true image of God: since the former prayer is for men, while the latter is closer to God and the Angels. For the voice of God and the Angels is formal and not common; by it they address the Prophets and the Elect in the spirit. That prayer, therefore, is best which is mental, because whether it exists by itself or with vocal prayer, it is always effective insofar as it is closest to God. Therefore, unless vocal prayer is joined with that of the mind, it will achieve nothing.

Therefore, spiritual prayer is most suited to the human temple.

But now we proceed to the second part, in which we shall briefly discuss whether private prayer or prayer performed in a Congregation is more effective.

That prayer in a congregation is more useful for public matters than for private and individual ones is declared by this: just as two things in the realm of bodies are stronger than one; and among reeds, a small portion of them is broken very easily, but a larger combination is not (according to the common axiom, **united strength is stronger** <note>original: "vis unita fortior"</note>); and just as many lights illuminate more than one or two.

As for the place and time in which we might pray more appropriately: it should be known that a Place is either public or private. Scripture mentions public places almost everywhere. It is for this reason that the Tabernacle of God, the Temple of Solomon, all Basilicas, and the Churches of the entire world were built. Concerning the private place, we find that it is chosen according to the circumstances and the necessity of the occasion. Thus, Christ was on the mountain and in the desert. Its spirit is guided toward good or evil in the same way as the <term>Microcosmic spirit</term> <note>The human spirit, viewed as a miniature reflection of the greater universe or Macrocosm</note>. ...why then must we pray at length? Why, therefore, were the prayers of Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Moses—<margin>Matthew 23:14; Matthew 6:7.</margin> and even those of our Savior—so brief and short? Why also does Christ attack those who pour out long prayers, and speak against the Heathens, who use many words when praying?

<margin>Matthew 6:7.</margin> I answer, therefore, that by *continuous prayer*, Christ and his disciples understand something other than vocal prayer—namely, that which is *spiritual* or *mental*. Whence Christ says: *When you pray, do not speak much, as the Heathens do, for they think that by their much-speaking they will be heard.* The Savior would not have said this if vocal prayer were to be used continually. Therefore, in the places cited before, Holy Scripture undoubtedly means internal and mental prayer, or spiritual meditation: namely, that in every business—in eating, drinking, walking, or sitting—we should always lift our minds to God. We should adore Him in our souls with true and sincere worship, look upon Him with spiritual eyes in fear and trembling, and direct all our actions to His glory. In every affliction, we should effectively implore His help and take hold of His saving hand with hope and faith; and finally, we should perpetually commend both our souls and our bodies into His sacred protection and care. And indeed, in this sense—by persevering in meditation upon God—we can truly pray without ceasing. For *he who walks in the way of Truth, and dwells in the Divine Law day and night, is said to pray to God inwardly*: and consequently, he is to be considered a just man. Of such a person the Psalmist sings: <margin>Psalm 64:11; Psalm 37:30.</margin> *The righteous shall be glad in the Lord, and shall trust in him*: and finally, *all the upright in heart shall glory*. For *the mouth of the righteous meditates on wisdom, and his tongue talks of justice: the Law of his God is in his heart, and none of his steps shall slide.* Such a person, therefore, is one who spiritually prays to and reveres God without ceasing.

Finally, the *Position* of the one praying in respect to the quarters of the Heaven is not to be neglected in this place, since the opinions of various men on this matter are diverse.

That the more worthy region of the world is located in the East—contrary to various opinions of the ancient philosophers—we have clearly declared by the testimony of the sacred pages in Chapter 1, Book 1 of our *Mystical Anatomy*. For the Sun is accustomed to visit the earth daily from that place; a creature (I say) flashing with glorious splendor, as it is the place in which the <term>Uncreated Sun<note>A theological term referring to God or Christ as the source of all light, distinguished from the physical "created" sun in the sky.</note></term> is said to have placed His Tabernacle. And for this reason, instructed by divine oracle, I have proved that in the prayers and formulas of several Patriarchs and Prophets, the face of the one praying was turned toward the East. And the Wise Man says, <margin>Wisdom 16:28.</margin> *We must prevent the sun to give thee thanks, and at the dayspring pray unto thee.* <note>original: "anteuertamus Solem," meaning to rise before the sun.</note> Hence, the heads of Temples <note>referring to the apses or altars of churches</note> have always been placed toward the rising sun, so that we might reach toward that region especially while praying.

<margin>Pymander 13; Asclepius 15.</margin> But truly <term>Hermes<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom a vast body of mystical, alchemical, and philosophical writings is attributed.</note></term>, that divine priest, turned his face in his prayers under the open sky toward the South when the sun was setting, but toward the East <note>original: "Eurum seu Subsolanum"</note> when it was rising.

We conclude, therefore, that in prayer at all times, these things must be diligently observed: namely, that after the body has been refreshed by the sober quiet of the night (so that, the digestion of food being completed and the nature of the body now remaining at rest and relieved of its burden, a man might afterward be able to pray with greater zeal and intention), the petitioner ought to rise in the morning to seek the gifts of God, if he desires to find Him promptly. In the morning, I say, at the first hour, stimulated by the irrational creatures. For then *the birds praise God*, as Ambrose testifies. <margin>Proverbs 8; Daniel 6.</margin> *Those that seek me early shall find me*, says the Wise Man. Likewise, other hours after the first are not to be neglected, such as the third, sixth, and ninth, because God is to be praised in them. Whence Daniel (as has been said) *knelt upon his knees three times a day and prayed*.

## C H A P T E R VI.

-> In which the Method of praying is explained, and that vocal Prayer ought to be brief, and not long. <-

**It** is a matter of the greatest importance and value that, in praying, we observe an exact method according to the rites and norms of the Hebrews, both the ancient and the more recent and modern.

In prayers, for the most part, we find these members <note>meaning "parts" or "components"</note>, namely:

First, *is the preparation of the one praying*, indicating their humiliation. Next, *the magnificence of the Lord or the exaltation of His praises*. Then *follows His Power*, which is usually explained through examples relevant to the matter.

Also, Penance with the confession of sins. The remembrance of the divine promise. *The motivating object of the prayer*, or the reason why the request should be granted. Finally, *the vow or covenant* made with God in exchange for such great benevolence.

As for the *effect* <note>meaning the result or answer to the prayer</note>, that is to be confidently expected once the prayer is finished. We do not say that all these members are required for every single petition: rather, more are placed in one and fewer in another, according to the necessity of the subject. The use of these members, however, will shine forth more clearly through various examples of the prayers of holy men.

<margin>Esther 14, v. 1. Humility.

### Volume 1. Treatise 1. Section II. Part 1. Book II. ###

Christ himself testifies that he understands this. For what more can be required by God than what is most exactly contained in the Lord's Prayer? <note>original: "oratione Dominica"</note> Yet that prayer is composed of very few words. It is therefore useless to do with many words what can be done more conveniently with few; we judge it to be vain glory and mere absurdity in those praying to pour out many words to Him from whom nothing is hidden, and to whom the very marrow of the spirit is clearly seen. Such indeed are those babblers who in these times delight to be called <term>Puritans</term> <note>A term used here pejoratively for English Protestants who favored long, extemporaneous prayers over set liturgical forms.</note>, and in past ages the scribes and other sectarians of the same sort, of whom Christ speaks thus:

<margin>Matthew 23:14</margin>
> *Woe to you who, praying long prayers, devour the houses of widows, etc.*

For what (I ask) can be said more in a long prayer, or what can be desired in the heart, that cannot be described in fewer words? For our Father is not so dull <note>original: "stupidus." In this context, the author means "unaware" or "slow to perceive," emphasizing that God does not need long explanations to understand us.</note> (since it is His nature to know our intentions and necessities before they are signaled by voice and words) that He requires so many words for the explanation of a matter. Indeed, these few words, whether expressed mentally or vocally, include within themselves all the necessities of man.

> *O Lord God, most powerful of all, Father most full of mercy, be present with me, a sinner (I pray), by your mercy and kindness, so that I, seeing light in your light, may walk in your paths, now and forever. Amen.*

In this prayer, the speaker first magnifies God, both for His strength and for His mercy, and finally explains the subject of his prayer: namely, that God be present with him by His kindness. In this clause, all things necessary for the health of both soul and body are concluded. Finally, the reason moving God is lawful and honest: namely, *that by seeing light in the light of God, he may walk all the days of his life in the divine way and law, and serve God faithfully with heart and soul.* This perpetual walking in the sight of God is that "continuous prayer" in which the righteous are said to be occupied, which we proved in the preceding sections to be mental and not vocal. In this sense the Evangelist says:

<margin>Luke 18:1; 1 Thessalonians 5; Luke 21</margin>
*It is necessary always to pray, and not to fail.* And the Apostle: *Pray without ceasing.* And again, Saint Luke: *Pray at all times, that you may be held worthy to escape the future evils, etc.*

<margin>Psalm 1:1-2; Psalm 4:4</margin>
The Psalmist also excellently expressed this formula of mental prayer: *Blessed is the man whose delight is in the Law of Jehovah, and who meditates on His law day and night.* And elsewhere more clearly: *Tremble, and do not sin. Meditate in your beds with silence. Sacrifice the sacrifices of innocence, and hope in the Lord, etc.* By these words he understands mental prayer which ought to be continuous; that is, it is fitting to always live in the fear and reverence of God, and to walk sincerely in His ways, according to that which he expressed elsewhere:

<margin>Psalm 15:1-2</margin>
*Who shall dwell in your Tabernacle? He who lives innocently, works what is just, and meditates on the truth in his heart.*

But to return to the proposal. In our vocal prayers, let us especially imitate Christ our Lord, saying:

> *Our Father, who art in heaven: hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. For thine is the Kingdom, and the Power, and the Glory, forever and ever. Amen.*

In this formula of praying, two things are to be noted: namely, the *Quantity* and the *Quality of Prayer*. Regarding its *Quantity*, he argues that it ought not to be long but brief and vigorous, without any superfluity of words. Its *Quality* consists in an exact method.

### On the Supercelestial Method of Preserving Health ###

->In which are observed<-

<margin>Connection or Relationship.</margin>
The connection and relationship between the one praying and the very One whom he entreats is explained in these words: *Our Father who art in heaven.* <note>original: "Pater noster qui es in calis."</note> Wherefore it follows that if He who is prayed to is our Father, then we are the children of Him whom we pray to. And just as a Father is inclined toward compassion for his son, so indeed, if he is accustomed to chastising his children for their sins, he nevertheless does this moved by paternal kindness and mercy, just as a Father does to a son. Hence, our Savior most appropriately began his prayer with "Father": a name indeed full of piety and clemency. And truly, Christ revealed to the flesh that God is indeed our Father, because that <term>Central Light</term> <note>A Neoplatonic and Hermetic concept referring to the divine spark or the Logos that illuminates the soul from within.</note>—which illuminates every man coming into this world, and through which and in which we move and have our being—proceeded from that luminous source in the manner of a son from a father. Yet He is nonetheless one with the Father. Wherefore we are said to be fashioned in the image of God.

<margin>Matthew 26; Mark 14:36; Luke 23:34.</margin>
For this reason, Christ always placed the word *Father* before his prayers, such as: *My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me, etc.* <note>original: "Pater mi si, non potest calix hic transire"</note> and elsewhere: *Abba, Father, all things are possible for thee;* and *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, etc.*

By the same reasoning, since we are the brothers of Christ, Christ himself warns us to pray in the same formula: *Our Father who art in heaven, etc.* And the prodigal son says: *Father, I have sinned against Heaven and against thee; I am no longer worthy to be called thy son, etc.* This, therefore, is the method of the one praying's introduction to God: that God ought to lend His ears because the one praying is His child, and consequently He is that person's father. Thus, He is greatly moved to be kind and merciful by that word "Father."

For whoever is ignorant that God is his Father, God—as a Father—will not wish to hear his prayers.

<margin>Magnification.</margin>
In the second place, the speaker extols and magnifies the praises of his Father in these words: *Our Father who art in heaven: Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, etc.* In this portion, he suggests that he regards Him with all praise and sanctity in his heart and Spirit, and attributes to Him all dignity and glory, and desires the coming of His Kingdom so that His presence may be made manifest.

<margin>Humiliation. Luke 22.</margin>
Then he proves his humility in these words: *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven,* that is: as much in my earthly body, fashioned from mud, as in my spirit. So Christ said of himself: *Father, if thou wilt, remove this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but thine be done, etc.* That is: I most humbly subject myself to thy will.

<margin>Subject.</margin>
Next, he proceeds to the general subject of his prayer, which he seems to distinguish into a threefold condition. For in the first place, he seems to ask for the nourishment of his body and the sustenance of his life; then for the remission of his past sins; and finally for his liberation from future evil and sin.

<margin>Charity.</margin>
Afterward, in that clause, he indicates a most necessary duty of the one praying: that remission of debts from God, the Father of mercy, is not to be expected by the one praying unless he himself remits the debts to any of his brothers. For the compassion of the one praying attracts to itself its like from the heavenly Father—who is most merciful—through <term>sympathy</term> <note>In early modern philosophy, "sympathy" refers to a natural resonance or "likeness" between things that allows them to influence one another across distances or dimensions.</note>.

<margin>Power.</margin>
Finally, he expresses His power and dominion in these words: *For thine is the Kingdom and the Power and the Glory forever, etc.*

### Volume I, Treatise I, Section II, Part I, Book II ###

From this, he argues that it belongs to Him alone to make man blessed, and again to curse him with the effects of the greatest unhappiness, and to lead him into error and temptation.

<margin>Psalm 104:29.</margin>
I say "to make blessed": since it belongs to Him alone to forgive sins and to give us our daily bread, and to restore and preserve us by the presence and kindness of His face, according to that saying of David: *All creatures look to God to give them their food in due season; when God gives it to them, they gather it up; when He opens His hand, they are satisfied with good things, etc.* <note>original: "Omnes creaturæ à Deo habent expectationem..."</note>

<margin>Job 12.</margin>
He is also accustomed to curse and to make men unhappy when He wills. Whence we pray, *Lead us not into temptation.* <note>original: "Ne nos inducas in tentationem."</note> According to that saying: *With Him is strength and power; the one who errs and the one who leads into error belong to Him. He makes counselors go mad and makes judges fools. He makes them wander like drunkards, groping in the dark where there is no light.* <note>original: "Apud illum est robur & potentia... palpent in tenebris deficiente luce."</note> Therefore, the Heavenly Father (in whom we move and have our being) is primarily to be prayed to, so that He might not lead us into temptation but deliver us from all evil—since His is the Kingdom, the Power, and the Glory, and consequently, He is the one who works all things in all people, now and forever.

Furthermore, I think it should by no means be omitted here that the Jews, in prayers for health and in giving thanks for benefits, used certain Names of God which signify clemency and kindness from a most favorable aspect. See <term>Iah</term> <note>original: יה, Iah. One of the shorter forms of the Divine Name in Hebrew, often associated with joy and praise.</note> and <term>El</term> <note>original: אל, El. A primary Hebrew name for God, often signifying might or the source of all power.</note>; but they are used in different respects. For in giving thanks, they call God *Iah*, as can be seen in many Psalms of David. For example: *Praise Iah, who heals the brokenhearted.* And: *If you, Iah, Lord, should mark iniquities, who could stand?* <note>original: "laudate Iah qui sanat fractos animo... si iniquitates obseruaueris Iah."</note> However, one uses *El* when one wishes to acquire grace from His Fortitude. Here he says: *O most Mighty God of the spirits and of all flesh; if one man sins, will your wrath rage against all?* <note>original: "Fortissime & Deus spirituum & carnis; num vno peccante..." Referring to Numbers 16:22.</note> And Moses, praying for the restoration of health for the leprous <term>Mary</term> <note>The Latin "Maria" refers here to Miriam, the sister of Moses, who was struck with leprosy in Numbers 12.</note>, spoke thus:
> <gloss>O God, please heal her now.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "אל נא רפא נא לה" (El na rapha na la). El: God of grace. Rapha: heal. Na: please. La: her.</note>

Wherefore, if we wish to seek a thing of grace, such as the Salvation and Kindness of God required for the protection of health, we are advised by the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Scholars of the Kabbalah, a mystical Jewish tradition that explores the divine nature through the symbolism of names and numbers.</note> to invoke the Name *El*. They also call the Name *Iah* the *Mirror of Clemency* because of His benevolent effects—just as, conversely, they call *Adonai* <note>original: אדני, Adonai. A Hebrew name for God translated as "Lord," here associated with the attribute of Judgment.</note> the *Mirror of Severity*, as the book *Porta Lucis* <note>The "Gates of Light" (Sha'are Orah), a foundational 13th-century Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note> states.

If someone, however, in a more imprecatory manner, desired the influence of judgment and justice, let him invoke the name <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים, Elohim. A name for God often associated with the creation and the rigorous exercise of justice and natural law.</note>. For He himself (as the Archangel testifies) is the minister of all those exercising power. For just as the name *El*—which we translate as "God"—nourishes all things and succors all with the highest piety and clemency, which is His own nature (and for this reason, grace is attributed to Him), so indeed in the nature of the name *Elohim*, God is said to exercise His power, and for this reason is called a *Man of War* and like a *Strong Warrior*. Wherefore, from this influence come severe punishments, as we shall discuss more fully in the following Treatise on the causes of diseases.

Therefore, it should be noted here that in blessing-prayers for the protection of health, and in cursing-prayers for the confusion and scattering of enemies, it will be sufficient to use the names *Iah* and *El*, or *Adonai* and *Elohim*. That is: by the title of a Father most full of piety and of a merciful God, kind and overflowing with the fullness of grace; or by the title of the most mighty God and most powerful Lord, who is accustomed to subdue rebels, like a terrible and most robust Warrior, etc.

By these words, the properties of those Names—both the kind and the unmerciful—are indicated.

**S**ince no one can extend their vow or desire further than to the Highest Good—which is the subject and Goal <note>The Latin word "Meta" refers to a turning point or goal-post in a race.</note> of all Magi, true Philosophers, Kabbalists, Alchemists, and indeed Theosophers, and toward which they are accustomed to aspire and aim with their greatest effort (since in its most August Sanctuary is contained whatever can be desired by man)—it is necessary that the acquisition of that very Good crowns the desire of the faithful person who prays. What that Highest Good truly is, the Wise Man <note>Refers to King Solomon, the traditional author of the Book of Wisdom.</note> seems to suggest:
> *The body (he says) infected with corruption weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind full of many cares: so that we hardly guess the things that are on earth, and we find with labor the things that are at hand. From these words it is evident that the Highest Good is the Spirit of Wisdom, which God is accustomed to pour out and liberally rain down from the holy heavens upon those who pray rightly and faithfully—as much to wash away sins and illuminate the darkened mind, as to obtain all the comforts of human life and to preserve health. For this Spirit is the salvation of men, the root of life, the fount of truth, and the author of all good.

<margin>Psalm 17:1</margin>

We conclude, therefore, that Wisdom is that holy spirit which alone produces the desired effects of the one praying: Wherefore it is necessary that the one praying has the Image and as it were a ray of Wisdom herself in his heart, if he wishes to have good success <margin>Wisdom 7.</margin> through the pouring out of his soul before Jehovah. For the Wise Man witnesses that *God loves no one except him with whom wisdom dwells.*

With equal success, by the virtue of wisdom, the effects of a curse are produced in prayer against the impious and adversaries. For when that spirit looks fiercely upon the impious, they are suddenly drained of life: as happened to the sons of Aaron, who offered the strange fire of Jehovah— <note>The text cuts off here, referring to the biblical story of Nadab and Abihu from Leviticus 10.</note>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:1.</margin>

# Volume I. Treatise I. Section I. Part I. Book II.

...ordained and consecrated, and named above all by the divine mouth after Creation. Then it was desired by the Patriarchs and ancient Fathers, later prophesied by the Prophets, at last proclaimed by the Most Blessed Virgin, and finally bestowed upon Him by Joseph. In the following centuries, it was spread abroad by the Angels, magnified by the Apostles, testified to by the Martyrs, confessed and praised by Christians, poured out like oil by Holy Virgins, and venerated by all the faithful throughout the whole world.

We conclude, therefore, that this is that universal and saving name which Jehovah acknowledged was within that Great Angel <note>Refers to the "Angel of the Lord" who guided the Israelites in Exodus, interpreted here as a manifestation of the Divine Name.</note> whom He sent before the Israelites for their salvation during the journey through the desert. And this name is so great, ample, and magnificent that it encompasses within itself all the names of God proclaimed by the Cabalists <note>Students of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) who analyzed the various names of God for their hidden powers.</note> and the Teachers of the Hebrews—namely, the power of the names *Ehieh, Iah, Elohim, El, Shaddai, Adonai, etc.* <note>original: "Ehieh, Iah, Elohim, El, Sadai, Adonai." These represent different aspects of God in Hebrew, such as "I Am," "The Lord," and "God Almighty."</note> For just as all things are made and ordered by the One as Father, so indeed through this single, luminous, and Essential name (and by no other) are all things brought into action; according to that passage: <margin>1 Corinthians 8:5–6</margin> *For although there be those called gods in heaven and on earth... yet for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through Him, etc.* Where we also see that as "Jesus" by itself signifies the Divine Wisdom and the Word, which is the Seal of the Almighty; so "Christ" is added to it, insofar as through the incarnation of Jesus (the divine light), the creaturely incarnation is called "Christ," or "The Anointed."

Hence Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, a central figure in Western theology.</note> holds that the difference between these two names is this: the Name JESUS is the name proper to the Divinity; but that other name, CHRIST, is common and pertains to the Sacrament. For it was not the Divinity by itself, but the body joined with the Divinity—the anointed flesh—which was offered in the true Sacrament.

The name CHRIST, therefore, is the Name of Grace, as He is a Man anointed through grace; but the name JESUS is the name of Glory, since He Himself is the Divinity in His glorified nature. For just as through the grace of Baptism—which is accomplished in truth through the Anointing performed with the Spirit and fire—men are called "Christians" after CHRIST; so in heavenly glory, we shall be called true "Jesuits" <note>In this mystical context, the author uses "Jesuit" in its literal etymological sense: "those belonging to Jesus" or "the saved ones," rather than referring strictly to the religious order.</note> after JESUS himself—that is, those saved by the Savior. In short, as great as the discrepancy is between Grace and Glory, so great is the difference between "Christ" and "Jesus."

Moreover, JESUS was that supersubstantial <note>original: "supersubstantiale," meaning a name that exists beyond or above all physical substance.</note> name by means of which the Angel of God, whom He sent before the Israelites, performed so many wonders and stupendous deeds; and without it, the inhabitants of Heaven can do nothing. This is that name which gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, speech to the mute, life to the dead, health to the sick, terror to demons, and the remission of sins.

We say, therefore, with the Apostle: <margin>Romans 10:13</margin> *Whosoever shall call upon this name shall be saved.* Concerning this name, the Lord Himself says: *Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.*

We have treated this most sacred name at such length so that the reason why Christians use it so frequently in their prayers may be understood: whether separately or joined with the name Christ, and why they usually close their prayers with these words: *Through Christ Jesus our Lord,* or some similar formula.

Therefore, once your faithful prayer is made and the Jesuitical <note>Here meaning the "saving unction" or "salvation-bringing oil."</note> unction is obtained from on high, you—having finally been chosen for the number of the "Christs" <note>Meaning "the anointed ones."</note> and surrounded on all sides by good Angels through the power of that wonderful name (JESUS), who is the head of the Angels—shall tread the way of health and the path of salvation, and you may obtain your wishes from God in an admirable manner.

And so much for the method of Prayer.

Now, however, let us return to the effect of Prayer, which, through the mediation of the Angels...

### On the Super-celestial Method of Preserving Health.

...angels, both the good, who are engaged in preservation; as well as the evil, who plot ruin, infirmity, and destruction. We say that this works swiftly, whether in the person praying for themselves and their neighbors or friends by blessing, or against their enemies and foes by cursing. For through this wonderful and most divine Word JESUS, or through that name CHRIST—which also encompasses JESUS—the good Angels are appointed and ordered for the protection or defense of the health of the righteous. <margin>Genesis 48:16.</margin> *That Angel (says Jacob) who delivers me from all evil, bless these boys.* And David, having offered his prayer, declares its effect thus: *God sent from heaven and delivered me,* <note>Refers to Psalm 57:3. In this tradition, God's "sending" is interpreted as the dispatching of an angelic messenger.</note> where by "sending," he implies an angelic action. Hence, it is said elsewhere: <margin>Psalm 90, verse 10. <note>In modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 91.</note></margin> *No evil shall come to you, and the scourge shall not approach your Tabernacle: for He has given His Angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. They shall bear you in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone. You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon. Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him: I will protect him because he has known my NAME: he shall cry to me, and I will hear him: I am with him in tribulation: I will rescue him and glorify him. With length of days I will satisfy him, and I will show him my salvation, etc.* In these words, truly golden, the following points are most worthy of note.

<margin>Wisdom 16:13.</margin>
First, that life and health, as well as death and infirmity, are in the hand of God. Whence it is written: *He has power over life and death: and leads down to the gates of hell and brings back again.*

Second: that He is accustomed to bring about life and health, as well as death and infirmity, through the mediation of good or evil angels. *No evil shall come to you (He says) and the scourge shall not approach your Tabernacle:* that is, the effects of the evil Angels. And in the preceding verse He seems to confirm this: *You shall not fear (He says) the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the plague that walks in darkness, nor the noon-day demon.* <note>original: "Dæmonio meridiano." This "Noonday Devil" was historically associated with sloth or sudden heatstroke-induced illness.</note> And in the following verses He says: *For He has commanded His Angels (the good ones, clearly) concerning you, etc.*

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
Third: He demonstrates that this is not to be obtained from God without faithful prayer. For He says, *Because he has hoped in me, and cried to me, therefore I will hear him.* And there He also denotes the reason why He hears him, and is more ready to deliver him. *Because (He says) he has known my name, etc.* The Name (I say) of Omnipotence; which is JESUS, in whom those who believe and acknowledge Him shall be heard and preserved by God: *for God (as said before) loves all those with whom Wisdom dwells:* <note>Refers to Wisdom of Solomon 7:28, "For God loveth none but him that dwelleth with wisdom."</note> which is the virtue of the sacred name JESUS, whom all Angels, both celestial and infernal, obey and bow their knees to (as to the supreme Commander). In Him, therefore, is salvation itself: and he who enjoys it must necessarily <margin>Psalms 4:9, 6:9, 118:6, 27:1. <note>Psalm 4:8 in English versions.</note></margin> *both lie down and sleep in peace: according to the words of the Prophet. For if God be with us, who can be against us? I will say therefore with the royal Psalmist: The Lord Jehovah, or JESUS, the power of the highest Jehovah, is my Light and my Salvation; whom shall I fear? Jesus is the strength of my life.*

By these things, therefore, we can perceive how the prayers of the faithful are heard, and who are the righteous and faithful whose petitions God is accustomed to hear mercifully: namely, those who trust in Him, and in whom the fire and light of grace dwell, or those who are refreshed by the Jesuitical Baptism <note>original: "Baptismo Iesuitico." This does not refer to the Jesuit Order, but to the "Baptism of Jesus"—specifically the baptism of fire and the Spirit mentioned in Matthew 3:11, contrasting with the water baptism of John.</note>—namely, by fire and the Spirit. For with these, Wisdom dwelling makes them beloved by God. Hence, the ancient Sages said in a symbolic manner: *Do not speak of God without light.* For this reason, both the Pagans and the Jews placed lights before their altars. And the Roman Church does so to this day in its churches. Indeed, the ancients even placed lights near dead bodies, for their protection (as they imagined) from the tearing of witches, <note>original: "veneficarum."</note> or rather from the frequenting of light-shunning and evil demons. These lights, however, are in truth symbolic; leading to that true and mystical light which is familiar to God (having originated from Him).

A petitioner is not required to be long and tedious in his prayers, for the reasons we have brought forward previously. ## Prayer of Sarah.

<margin>Tobit 8.</margin>
> **H**ave mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, and let us both grow old together in health.

This is her entire prayer, and yet it is sufficient. For first, it proves her humility and poverty, and also her repentance for sin: for where sin is not present, there mercy is not required. Then, in one word she reaches the subject of the Prayer: Which is, that God might preserve both Tobias and herself and keep them within the bounds of Health until old age.
