# On the Celestial Method of Preserving Health.

...the rays of Saturn [♄] and Mars [♂], who are the "malefics" <note>In traditional astrology, Saturn and Mars were considered "infortunes" or malefics, often associated with hardship or disease.</note>. Therefore, if the aforementioned planets are the **Significators** <note>The planets that represent or "point to" a specific area of life, such as health or career.</note> when they appear in the Birth Chart, and they are afflicted in these two ways at once, the effect will be all the more intense; but if they are afflicted in only one way—namely, by their own weakness or by the mere aspect <note>The geometric angle or "gaze" between planets.</note> of the malefic planets— the harm will be less severe.

Now, the **Significators** of health and illness are the **Lord of the Horoscope** <note>The planet that rules the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, the **Luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, and especially the **Moon** [☽], the **Sign** and the **Lord of the Sixth House** <note>The 6th house is the section of the astrological chart traditionally associated with physical illness and the body’s weaknesses.</note>, and whatever planet or planets are found in the sixth house, whether in the original birth chart or in the annual revolution <note>A chart cast for a person's birthday each year to predict themes for the coming twelve months.</note>. In any of these Significators, two things must be considered: first, whether the planet is strong or weak; and second, whether it is free from the malignant rays of the two aforementioned planets, Saturn [♄] and Mars [♂]. If, therefore, all the said significators are strong and free from such rays, they indicate good health; if not, they indicate no small number of infirmities.

Once these things have been considered with diligent insight, and the nature and condition of the future disease is understood from the nature of that Sign and Planet, it will be the task of the **Skilled Physician** to meet such an evil and prevent it through contrary medicines and nourishment. These can be applied at the proper times while the person is still healthy: because **opposites are usually cured by opposites** <note>original: "contraria contrariis curari solent." This is a fundamental principle of Galenic medicine, where a "hot" disease is treated with "cold" remedies.</note>. Thus, if future celestial influences are fiery and bilious <note>Associated with yellow bile, one of the four humors, which was thought to cause heat and irritability.</note>, threatening a healthy person with fevers and inflammations, these influences can usually be made ineffective—or at least mitigated, softened, and blunted—through a regulated diet and medicines that partake in the nature of the **Moon** [☽] and **Venus** [♀] <note>Astrologically, the Moon and Venus were considered cool and moist, providing a balance to the heat of Mars or the dryness of Saturn.</note>.

And up to this point, I have judged that it would not be useless for students of Medicine for me to measure out my discourse on the method of preserving health through the observation of the heavens. Now, however, we shall descend with a light leap to the **Elemental** <note>Referring to the terrestrial method of health based on the four elements (Earth, Air, Fire, Water) and the four humors, rather than the stars.</note> method of preserving health.

->PREFACE.<-

<margin>Elementary things.</margin>
Now indeed, we have arrived at the non-natural things <term>non-naturals: A traditional medical concept referring to six external factors—air, food/drink, exercise, sleep, excretion, and emotions—that are not part of the body's nature but are essential for health and causes of disease.</term> contained within the sublunary region <note>The realm below the moon, meaning the Earth and its atmosphere, which was thought to be subject to change and decay.</note> which are often harmful to health. Although these things truly depend upon divine nature, the actions of Angels, or (as the Astrologers would have it) the influences of the Heavens, we have now left behind the super-celestial and celestial realms. I have proposed to myself in this place to examine those Elementary things with greater diligence, in the manner of ordinary Philosophers and Physicians. However, I do so under this law: that we recognize in our hearts that all these things—whether air, Winds, Elements, or accidents whether internal or external—do not happen by their own essence, but by the power of God, who works all things in all, as much on earth as in the heavens. And although we say in common speech that this or that is done by Angels, or by Stars, or by the Elements, or by Action, or Motion, or food, or drink, or exercise, and other such things, yet in truth, with the Wise Man and the Apostle, we recognize that all these things have their rise and origin from the divine act essentially and radically innate in every creature.

<margin>Wisdom 12:1</margin>
The incorruptible spirit, says Solomon, is in every thing; and Saint Paul says: "There are indeed those who are called gods in heaven and on earth, yet for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him."

<margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin>
By arguing from this, every formal act and motion in a creature is to be attributed to God the Father, from whom [it comes], and immediately through the Word, through which [it exists].

<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin>
Wherefore he concludes elsewhere, that God works all things in all. And elsewhere: "From him, through him, and in him are all things."

<margin>
Romans 11.
Acts 17.

But let this be forever established in my heart: that in him and him alone, we live and move and have our being; in him every creature consists, and without his life-giving act, it returns to its own earth, as the Royal Psalmist <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> affirms. And yet (I say) let it be permitted to me to speak in the common tongue, and to imagine subordinate acting causes alongside the Heathens, who made heat and cold the active principles, and made fire, air, and water their dwellings; when in truth heat and cold are only Effects—the Essence of the one divine being in varied properties, hiding itself through contraction...

### CHAPTER I.
### *On the Universal Nature of Air.*

In the first section of this first treatise (Part 2, Book 2, Chapter 2), we established that the Air, in its universal mass, is the universal substance or "patient" <note>In philosophy, a "patient" is the passive recipient of an action, as opposed to the "agent" who performs the action.</note> of the **World Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus mundanus"; a vital, subtle substance thought to permeate the entire universe, linking the physical and spiritual realms.</note>. In one region it is called **Empyrean** <note>The highest, most refined level of the heavens, associated with fire and light.</note>, in another **Ethereal**, and in a third **Elementary**. And although we have made it a single and simple substance in itself, we have said that it varies throughout the world by its thinness (rarefaction) or thickness (density), and according to these variations, it takes on different names. Thus, it is sometimes called Earth, sometimes Water, Air, Fire, Ether, and the Empyrean Spirit—which we have declared to be the furnace of fiery perfection. And just as we recognized the universal substance of this Spirit as the universal "passive" element of the world, so too have we shown that the **Eternal Wisdom** <note>The Divine Mind or Word of God.</note> is its active principle. According to Wisdom's will, the air becomes either thinner or more subtle, faster or slower, heavier or lighter, hotter or colder, wetter or drier, purer or more corrupt. Consequently, it becomes either healthier or more sickly, darker or clearer, more turbulent or more peaceful. Sometimes it is more ready to produce comets, and at other times more apt to bring forth simple rains, or rains with thunder, or snow, ice, frost, or a serene appearance. In short, this Spirit is like passive wax, which, according to the will of a man, can receive any impression—

...it is suited to receive a form, even though in itself it has no shape, but is like a formless mass. In this way, the **Mercurial Spirit of the World**, <term>Spiritus Mundi: In Renaissance philosophy, this is a "world-soul" or subtle substance that connects the physical world to the divine, acting as a medium for life and celestial influences.</term> while by itself it has no shape or image, is nonetheless usually brought into whatever figure or image is impressed and worked upon it by the **Great Seal of God**, whose character is **Truth** itself. From this, the vain assertions of both Philosophers and Physicians are swept away—those who have posited secondary, tertiary, and quaternary causes in the world, and other such fictions. These "efficient causes" cause even Christian men to vanish into their own imaginations, so that they are falsely forced to place a discrepancy between true Philosophy and Theology. Do we not see the ethnic <note>Non-Christian or pagan.</note> Philosophers themselves, the inventors of these fictions, wavering in their opinions on this matter? For **Aristotle** firmly established that air is hot in its own property; and his reason, as **Galen** testifies, is that Air does not thicken and congeal like Water. But in my opinion, this assertion of his is false, because we see air frozen into frost and snow without the water itself freezing. We also see that, without any preceding rain or mist, trees are weighed down with heavy ice from the gathering of frozen air.

On the other hand, the **Stoics** made Air cold, and they judged this because of the rapid freezing of oil (which they believed has an airy nature). But if they had considered the matter well, they would have found that, just as this mundane Spirit is by itself of no form or image but like raw wax, they would perceive it as being neither hot nor humid, nor cold nor dry by nature. Instead, it becomes hot, humid, cold, or dry according to the greater or lesser action of the **Divine Wisdom** working within it. For example: where it acts swiftly and with vehemence, it is converted into a fiery nature, as in lightning and other ignited Meteors. 

<margin>

Galen, *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, book 2, chapter 15.
</margin>
But if it acts moderately and more temperately, then we call this Spirit the **Breath** <note>original: "Ruach" - a Hebrew term meaning breath, wind, or spirit.</note> or **Air**. If it works even more slowly and sluggishly within it, then its parts are gathered and coagulated together to form the appearance of water. Where that divine Light contracts itself more into itself, there an element that is more opaque, dense, solid, and cold is procreated. By this, one may see that all things which are called **Elements** are nothing but a single passive or created Spirit, altered into various species; and that the forms of those species are nothing other than the various acts of the one simple, uncreated, acting Spirit, who (as the Apostle testifies) "works all in all." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:6.</note> Hence it is that Galen himself seems to be confused in this: for although he acknowledges that Air is temperately hot, elsewhere he acknowledges it to be extremely hot, where he calls it the **heat of the air** <note>original: "Aeris feruorem"</note> or "burning heat," arguing from that that Air is sometimes of the nature of the element of fire rather than Air. Similarly, in another place he says, *"Hot air warms us in one way, temperate air in another."* In this, he seems to acknowledge that one kind of Air is of the nature of Fire, and another is of the nature of that Element we call Air. And from this it must follow that Air itself, by the consensus of both Philosophers and Physicians, is versatile, changing into the nature of one element or another. Consequently, it is like the **universal and Catholic Mercury of the Philosophers**, <term>Mercury of the Philosophers: Not the common metal, but a "First Matter" or universal substance in alchemy that can take on any form or quality.</term> which behaves like the celestial planet Mercury. For just as that planet turns and changes into the nature of whichever planet it is joined with (so that it is sometimes **Saturnine**, sometimes **Jovial**, and occasionally of a **Martial** or **Lunar** nature), so indeed the Air sometimes takes on a Northern disposition (subject to Saturn), an Eastern one (subject to Mars and the Sun), a Southern one (subject to Jupiter), and a Western one (appropriated to the Moon).

But just as all the Stars in heaven have their power from the Sun, so indeed all the winds have their power from Him who "placed his Tabernacle in the sun" <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4.</note>; who, as He is One, so indeed He is everything that is—as will be explained more widely below.

<margin>Galen, *On the Medical Art*, chapter 85.</margin>
Having considered these things—that Air is the sanctuary of God, by means of which and through which God either blesses the creature and preserves it in health, or makes it unhappy by cursing the air and rendering it corrupt—we see that according to Galen's doctrine, Air can in no way be avoided, as it must necessarily surround our bodies; for in...

## CHAPTER II.

### How the Air follows the motion and disposition of the four Winds: and that the four Elements are generated from the mass of Air by the mediation of the winds.

In the second chapter of the first section of the second part of the second book of this Treatise, the reason is explained as to how the Winds alter the nature of the aerial mass into the condition of the four Elements. For the Eastern Winds produce the nature of Fire. The southern wing of the East Wind, <note>original: "Subsolani," referring to the wind blowing from under the sun, or the pure East wind.</note> which blows from the Winter Solstice and is called Eurus, <note>The Southeast wind.</note> is moderately hot and very dry; although it participates somewhat in Southern humidity, by its blast it alters the nature of the Air into the fiery condition of the Element. This is especially true at the start of its blowing, although very often—for the reason we alleged previously—it becomes rainy toward the end. This happens particularly if, from the opposite side, the Circius <note>The North-Northwest wind.</note> blows secretly. For by the mixing of the congealing blast of the Circius with the dissolving blast of the Eurus, a moist and cloudy disposition is birthed in the middle of the Air from the proportion of cold and heat, sometimes mixed with thunder. For when two opposing winds blow at once, even though the name is assigned to the stronger one, it is still necessary that the intervening Air be condensed into clouds, which are easily dissolved into rains by the predominant fiery heat. But truly, if Circius or some other wind does not blow transversally in an opposite manner, the Eurus will wonderfully heat the Air and reduce it into the fiery Element by thinning it. Furthermore, on the other side of the East Wind is the Caecias (or the Hellespontine wind), which abounds in dryness because it participates in the dryness of the North; for this reason, it is said to dry everything out. However, it is not as vehemently hot as the Eurus, and thus it is suited to receive such a quality or impression from the Eurus upon the Air, rendering the air itself quite dry and hot. And if its opposite blows secretly—namely the Africus or Lybs <note>The Southwest wind.</note>—it is accustomed to gather clouds, but mostly dry ones. By this reasoning, the Air takes on the nature of the fiery Element, not just according to the summer season, but contingently; this is what Galen understands when he provides an exposition on these words of Hippocrates:
<margin>Aphorism 7. 13.</margin>
> "But in strong heats, convulsion occurs, etc." where by "heats" (Galen says), Hippocrates understands the fervor of the surrounding Air, etc.

In such a case, there are various precepts for preserving health, such as these:

->Wholesome precepts pertaining to the Air when it takes on an excessively hot nature.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
When the air necessarily surrounding our bodies is disseminated everywhere by an excessively hot blast, it brings forth weakness of the body, and by opening the body's pores, it extracts excessive sweat and causes the native spirits to expire. <term>Native Spirits: The "spiritus" or subtle vapors believed to animate the body and maintain life; their loss was thought to cause exhaustion or death.</term> The manual correction of this is explained in this verse: *If it grows hot, let Rose, Myrrh, and Willow change it.* <note>original: "si caleat, mutent hunc Rosa Myrrha, salix."</note>

Furthermore, the operation of the sweltering Air is resisted by the drinking of ptisan <term>Ptisan: A medicinal drink or herbal infusion, most commonly made from barley water, used to cool the body.</term> and the use of a cold diet.

A healthy person should position themselves toward the naturally cold regions of the world; for it rarely happens that the Spirit <note>The "Spiritus Mundi" or divine breath mentioned on the previous page.</note> does not blow at least a little from those quarters; for this reason, one must frequently visit that...

<margin>Water.</margin>
That part of the house which faces the North or the West should be used: and let the dwelling have various air vents. Furthermore, visit cooling groves and thickets, and frequently look upon the outlets of clear springs and murmuring waters, as long as a wind of that quality blows.

Let your clothing be well-arranged for this purpose: for choleric and sanguine people <note>Choler and Blood are two of the "four humors" thought to govern the body; these types were considered naturally warm and required cooling.</note> in this case, a garment of linen or silk lined with cotton is best: and let it be cut mostly in the long French style: for such clothes will not inflame the blood or allow one to swelter, and they will even somewhat hinder the entry of the sweltering Air.

But indeed, the opposite winds—namely, the servants of the West Wind <note>original: "Favonij"</note>: specifically the Southwest Wind <note>original: "Africus"</note> on its Southern wing and the Northwest Wind <note>original: "Corus"</note> on its Northern wing—usually produce phlegmatic effects. The effects of the Southwest Wind will tend more toward Southern heat and be quite moist, which is why they bring phlegm-inducing rains with them. But indeed, the Northwest Wind has a relation to Northern dryness, and because of this, its effects will not be as moist, but far colder, since it claims one influence from the West and another from the North. Therefore, just as these Winds are entirely opposed to those of the East—namely, the Northwest to the Southeast <note>original: "Euro"</note> and the Southwest to the Northeast <note>original: "Cæcio"</note>—so indeed, when these blow, they transform the Air from the disposition of the Element of Fire into that of Water. Since the Northwest Wind somewhat condenses and freezes, while the Southwest Wind somewhat dissolves (though not excessively), they return the air to a watery condition; and thus the Element of Water is said to have its dominion. In this case, I advise Phlegmatic people to observe the following precepts.

->Precepts.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Since Phlegmatic people are by their nature more dull and filled with watery juice: therefore it is necessary to consider that if such Air surrounds their bodies, they must necessarily participate in its nature, and for this reason, they are more burdened and oppressed by phlegmatic humors. Hence, it is necessary that this Air be corrected partly by art—namely, by lighting fires, taking baths, and using fumigations, and by the method of diet—and partly by nature—namely, by frequenting that part of the house which faces the opposite wind or region, and also by choosing a naturally dry and sandy place for a dwelling.

<margin>2.</margin>
The second is that herbs, grains of corn, and other such things that are opposite to the nature of phlegm should be gathered during such weather in which hot winds have blown for a longer time; also with a good aspect of the "ignited" <note>fiery or heat-producing</note> planets—namely, with a strong or well-disposed Sun or <term>Mars</term> <note>The symbol ♂ refers to Mars.</note> taking the lead.

<margin>Air.</margin>
But where the Wind blows from the Southern Point, the sublunary Spirit <note>The vital force existing in the earthly realm below the moon.</note> takes on a moderate nature, which has the temperament of the Element of Air—namely, hot and moist. But if its Eastern wing blows—namely, the Southeast Wind <note>original: "Euroauster"</note>—heat presses more strongly because of its relation to the Eastern angle or cardinal point. If indeed its Western wing blows, the nature of the breeze will be more inclined toward a cold disposition. From this, it follows that the Elemental Spirit, now changed into an airy disposition—namely, either more or less hot and moist—alters the bodies it necessarily surrounds, and makes them more fit to receive its impressions, which also infects and changes the airy Spirit within man. But indeed, this wind is "diaphoretic" <note>A term for something that induces sweating.</note> and usually weakens one through an excessive flow of sweat, because it breathes out the beneficial Spirits of life. Furthermore, it is pestilential, harmful, and corrupts the world spirit <note>original: "Spiritum mundanum," the vital force permeating the universe.</note>; it fills bodies with superfluities, so that sometimes it makes them swell; it is the mother and procreator of rot. Therefore, where these Winds blow too much, I advise those who are healthy but prone to difficulty of hearing, or heaviness of the head, or catarrhs <note>Inflammation of the mucus membranes, such as a head cold.</note>, or flux of the belly <note>Diarrhea.</note>, or putrid fevers, or weakness and sweating, and such things, not to despise these precepts.

On the Elementary Method of Preserving Health.

### Precepts.

1.  The first is that, since southern effects <note>Referring to illnesses caused by the warm, moist South Wind, often associated with decay or "putrid humors."</note> are usually cured by a Northern breeze—for the North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note> compresses putrid humors and holds them back, hardens bodies that the South Wind <note>original: "Auster"</note> makes soft, purifies humor, and rectifies pestilential air—I therefore advise that anyone subject to Southern blasts should inhabit that part of their house which faces the Northern winds. They should breathe in these blasts long and freely when the North Wind blows, for by the mixing of these with the spirit and blood of the creature, the person will be seasoned, corrected, and changed from a fluid nature into a firmer nature, so that they can afterward long resist Southern attacks.

2.  That one should gather and preserve herbs and grains for their own use in that very year when Northern winds are more frequent, provided a good celestial aspect is considered. This is because such simple medicines will retain the nature of the Air from which they received their hidden life, and they will communicate that nature to the blood, whether it be for nourishment or medicine.

3.  I advise that the surrounding Air be improved and corrected by art—namely, by fire or by fumigations—and also by a diet that should be contrary to the Southern blasts. This diet should be capable of altering the corrupt Air for the better. Furthermore, it is not at all fitting to agitate the body with excessive exercise into heavy sweats, due to the diaphoric <note>tending to induce sweat</note> disposition of the surrounding air.

<margin>Of Earth.</margin>
Finally, the blast of the North Wind brings the air back into a terrestrial nature and condition; for we see the air itself transformed everywhere into frost, snow, and ice by means of this blast. This may also be seen in the winter time by looking at the decoration of trees and herbs with a white seasoning of frost. The Western wing of this wind <note>likely referring to the North-Northwest wind</note> is not as dry as the Eastern one, specifically the Northeast wind <note>original: "Aquilo"</note>, which partakes of the dryness of both the Eastern and Western quarters. Nor indeed is the Northeast wind as intensely cold as the North-Northwest wind <note>original: "Circius"</note>, because the latter partakes of the cold of both the Western and Northern quarters. Therefore, when these blow, the earthy nature dominates in that vast Mercury <note>Here, "Mercury" refers to the volatile, spiritual essence of the atmosphere.</note> of the sublunary region; for which reason it is harmful to several temperaments. For while it benefits Cholerics and those whose constitution is prone to corruption, such a blast is unpleasant to those of a Sanguine temperament and quite oppressive to Melancholics, because it increases their humor <note>Melancholy was associated with the element of Earth; more cold/dry air would exacerbate this.</note>. Because of its extreme coldness, it is not easily endured by anyone; for just as the life of a creature consists of heat and moisture, so blasts of this kind are opposed to it in every way, being cold and dry and of a Saturnine nature <note>Related to the planet Saturn, traditionally associated with cold, dryness, and decay.</note>, which tends to destroy human nature. Therefore, these things being considered, these precepts for preserving health in such a case are by no means to be despised.

### Precepts Pertaining to Health.

1.  The first and general precept is contained in this single verse:
> Though it be cold, let it be warmed by coals without a hearth. <note>original: "Et gelidus cum sit, tepeat prunis sine foco." This likely refers to using portable braziers or heaters rather than an open fireplace to maintain a steady, dry heat.</note>

Second: That if a person's constitution cannot tolerate the cold, they should betake themselves to that vent of the house which faces the southern breath, and meanwhile let there be fires and moist fumigations.

If anyone who is currently healthy is nevertheless susceptible to "Northern" diseases—namely, ailments of the lungs such as a cough, consumption <note>original: "phthisi"</note>, roughness, contractions of the nerves, melancholy, and others of this sort (which we shall review in the following Treatise)—I warn them above all to correct the Air by art. They should also gather suitable herbs, grains, and other such things while the Southern blasts have a stronger and more lasting dominion in the sublunary spirit.

### CHAPTER II.

#### *How the Air is governed annually by the Solar power, and reduced into the nature of the Elements according to the four quarters of the year; And concerning the healthful precepts to be observed in each of them.*

<margin>Ecclesiastes 1:5</margin>
Solomon excellently describes that obedience which the Air, or the world-spirit <note>original: "spiritus mundanus"</note>, is accustomed to offer to the sun, just as Psyche <note>The personification of the Soul</note> does to a worldly Cupid. *The sun rises (he says), and sets, and returns to its place; and being reborn there, it wheels through the south and turns toward the North, and the spirit—that is, the air—goes about surveying all things in its circuit, and returns to its cycles:* etc. From this speech, we can gather not only the daily motion of the sun but also its annual motion through the Zodiac: namely, from Libra to the Tropic of Capricorn, and from there through Aries to the Tropic of Cancer. It also denotes the passive medium in which it moves, namely the world-spirit, which it seems to alter according to its greater or lesser presence. From this, therefore, the four different Quarters of one year are produced, according to the varied disposition of the air in which the Sun moves and which it moves itself. Nor indeed is the temperament of the air changed by the operation of the sun alone, but also by the winds. Yet the winds can do nothing unless they are stirred by the sun and variously animated according to the will of God. This, then, is the reason why the winds are called by the Poets—and not at all unwisely—*the infants of Titan, Astraea, and Aurora:* <note>In mythology, the winds were often said to be the offspring of the dawn (Aurora) and the stars/titans.</note> inasmuch as they are fathered by the heat of the sun, which makes the properly condensed air subtle and thin, especially at Dawn. And Aristotle himself supports this opinion. Hence the winds are said to receive the commands of Juno, for they are never accustomed to blow except in the Air (which is called Juno). And if we ascend by a higher ladder to God, we shall say in the same sense as the Revelator <margin>Revelation 7</margin> that *that great Angel who descended from the East*—that is, the presiding governor of the Sun—has command over *those four angels to whom was given dominion over the four cardinal winds.* Thus we have the Sun as the soul of the world, governed by God, and the universal air moved and quickened either by the sun itself or through the mediation of the winds it stirs up.

And yet this is certain, and proven by experience, that sudden and chance winds sometimes produce operations in the open air which are in every way opposed in quality to the fixed seasons of the year. Such winds are observed to be created against the Sun's decrees by some violent planet predominating in the heavens: for example, on the hottest days of Summer, rains with hail—indeed, even hailstones in abundance—are generated in the air, which are most often produced when Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄</note> is ruling in the sky. Similarly, in the depths of winter, lightning or flashes of light sometimes occur under the dominion of Mars <note>original symbol: ♂</note>. But I will conform myself in this place to the natural and customary constitution of the year: namely, to the four quarters of the year.

Concerning their quality, quantity, property, and variety, therefore, we shall speak very briefly in their proper order.

<margin>SPRING</margin>

### Healthful Precepts.

1. In Summer, whatever is of a cold and moist complexion is beneficial, such as veal with vinegar, porridge made from barley flour, pomegranates, plums, cherries, cucumbers, melons, lettuce, and other things of this sort. Because they blunt the fiery disposition of the internal air breathed in by the body and hinder the onset of diseases caused by heat.

Let the quantity of food be small, because in Summer the Digestive Faculty <note>original: "Virtus digestiua"</note> is weak: but let one eat more often, and let the food be of good digestion: let one drink often and largely of wine diluted with much water, or beer.

2. Let things that move the bowels <note>original: "alium suauitate cientia"; literally, things that move the belly</note> be taken if necessity compels it, and it will be better to move them upward <note>i.e., by vomiting</note> than downward <note>i.e., by purging</note>, according to the sentiment of Hippocrates. But let the belly not be urged at all, unless where reason persuades. Similarly, let the body not be moved too much by exercise; and let baths be used sparingly.

And yet, in summer, it is fitting to wash with cold water: for this constricts and retains the heat of the body and consequently aids Digestion.

Let the heat of the air be corrected by open vents, irrigations, and cooling herbs and leaves: namely, willow, roses, foliage, etc.

<margin>Autumn.</margin>
Next, in the successive progress of the year, the Air changes into a Melancholic temperament <note>Associated with black bile, being cold and dry</note> and constitutes the Autumnal Season. In this, as in the preceding states or changes of the Air, we think three things must be considered: its quantity extends from the point of the Autumnal Equinox or Libra [♎︎] until the Tropic of Capricorn, that is, from the 10th day of September until the 10th of December.

In quality, however, this season is cold and dry: in its temperament, it is unequal; and for that reason, it is in every way contrary to the Spring disposition, which is of an equal temperament. Wherefore Hippo-
<margin>Aphorisms 3.9.</margin>crates, with the consensus of Galen in the place cited above, wishes that in Autumn, the most acute and largely fatal diseases arise: namely, because of its unequal temperament.

The reason why Autumn is so unhealthy is because its Air participates in two contrary qualities: namely, the heat of the preceding Summer and the cold of the following Winter. By fighting among themselves, with coldness eventually winning, it harms the animal nature, which consists chiefly of innate heat.

Furthermore, in this season, the dryness of Summer meets the humidity of Winter, and eventually humidity prevails more as Winter approaches more quickly. Hence, we know by the effect that in the Microcosm, almost all things hasten toward Autumnal corruption after their Summer maturation. This is why leaves fall from the trees, fruits tend toward decay, and the entire spirit of the sublunary Heaven seems to incline toward the laws of old age; likewise, diseases are observed to happen to creatures naturally through corruption, as will be seen more clearly in the following Treatise.

<margin>Aphorism 3. 10.</margin>
In the Microcosm, it also produces and draws out black bile <note>original: "choleram nigram"; in humoral theory, black bile was associated with melancholy and the autumn season</note>, and for that reason, it is harmful to those of a Melancholic temperament. Indeed, the unlucky and unhealthy Autumn air is very prone to such humors. Furthermore, phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> and thin fluxes are said to abound in it because of that meeting between the summer heats and the winter colds.

Therefore, we believe it will be necessary to observe these precepts for the correction of this Autumnal Air:

### *Precepts for the preservation of health during the Autumnal season.*

1. Since this Autumnal Air is cold and dry, as physicians and Astrologers maintain, they advise using a dietary regimen <note>original: "victus ratione"</note> tending toward heat and moisture, such as chickens, lambs, sweet grapes, old and light wine, and the like. Similarly, sweet things that moisten and cool, and which smell pleasant, are very beneficial. And Diocles <note>Diocles of Carystus, a 4th-century BC Greek physician</note>, in his letter to King Antigonus, seems to highly approve of the sharpest and most succulent foods, and those that oppose thin flows—that is, those that block the passages by constricting them and prevent the descent of thin humors.

Some describe the time for eating thus: Since Autumn is of an unequal temperament, they advise eating around the noon hour when it has grown warm, not otherwise than in Summer when one does not eat much at one time. But in the morning and evening, due to the dominance of cold, the quantity of food becomes larger, in the manner of winter, because the external coldness of the air aids digestion through Antiperistasis <term>Antiperistasis: the intensification of a quality (like internal heat) when surrounded by its opposite (like external cold)</term>.

2. But since corruption and putrid humors tend to gather in the Microcosm just as they do in the Macrocosm, this time is most suitable for the evacuation of the worst humors. Wherefore, even a healthy person should be purged more often as a precaution.

<margin>Diocles to King Antiochus.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle's letter to Alexander.</margin>
Others seem to praise vomiting; but Diocles advises that vomiting should be done as little as possible in this season. Aristotle, on the other hand, in his letter to King Alexander, asserts that vomiting should be provoked more often in this season. Baths may also be used where reason requires, as well as Phlebotomy <term>Phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, used to balance the body's humors</term>, specifically from September to December.

3. Intercourse <note>original: "Coitus seu Venus"</note> should be used no less sparingly than in summer; indeed, it should be avoided as much as possible, unless fullness <note>likely referring to a buildup of semen or bodily tension</note> urges it. But it is useful for health to stir the body with exercise.

<margin>Winter.</margin>
Finally, the last Quarter of the year, at the end of which the Dragon is said to eat its own tail: for just as the head of the natural and autumnal Dragon is in Aries <note>♈︎</note> or the Vernal Equinox, so indeed its tail ends in Pisces <note>♓︎</note>. This fourth part, I say, is called Winter; in which the Air in the Macrocosm converts itself into a watery quality and sometimes an earthy and styptic one.

From this we should observe in passing that any Quarter of the year—whether it be Spring, Summer, Autumn, or Winter—is changed into various elemental natures by the force of different blowing Winds. For example: when the South Wind <note>original: "Austro"</note> blows in winter, the air becomes watery; from the North, it becomes constrictive and earthy; from the East <note>original: "Euro"</note>, it becomes more fiery, and so on.

The *Quantity* <note>In this context, "quantity" refers to the duration or span of the season</note> of this season extends from the Tropic of Capricorn (the Winter Solstice) to the Vernal Equinox; namely, from Capricorn to Aries <note>original: "à ♑. ad ♈"</note>, which is from the 10th of December to the 10th of March.

Furthermore, the natural quality of this season in the **Macrocosm** <note>the Great World or Universe</note> is cold and moist, being watery and rainy. In the **Microcosm** <note>the Little World or Human Body</note>, it is <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>associated with the "phlegm" humor, which was believed to be cold and wet</note> and pituitous; indeed, the pituitous humor increases during this time. It follows, therefore, that this season is beneficial to those of a **Choleric** temperament <note>who are naturally hot and dry</note>, but harmful to those of a **Phlegmatic** temperament, as it makes them overfilled with watery humors and more sluggish in their disposition.

Its *Effect* in the Macrocosm is to fill the sky with clouds, to submerge the lands with a multitude of waters, to cover the face of the fields and mountains with snow, and to cloak the surface of the waters with ice. It adorns the grass with frost and dew, yet it renders trees and herbs as if they were lifeless. In the *Microcosm*, it tends to produce moist and sometimes putrid diseases, generating coughs, dizziness, and <term>apoplexy</term> <note>a sudden loss of consciousness, often associated then with an excess of cold, thick humors</note>. So that evils of this kind may be prevented, let these rules be observed:

->*Salubrious Precepts against the Assaults of Winter.*<-

1. Since Winter is harmful to those who are cold and moist (that is, the phlegmatic), even those within the limits of health, the dietary regimen must be considered first, as it can correct the winter air. At this time, a diet tending toward heat should be used, such as young pigeons or mutton; roasted meats are more beneficial than boiled. This Quarter requires more abundant food in a single meal than any other, because the internal <term>native heat</term> <note>the vital warmth believed to be centered in the heart</note> is strengthened and made more powerful by the external cold, and thus the digestive faculty becomes stronger. However, drink should be more sparing, though it ought to be of a stronger effect: such as wine not as diluted with water as in summer, or a beer of better and stronger composition.

2. One should abstain from purging the belly unless necessity compels it. But if a purgation is required, **Hippocrates** <note>the famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> seems to blame vomiting in this season if the healthy person is slender. Elsewhere he says: *In summer, treat the upper parts [of the body] more; in winter, the lower.* <note>original: "Medicari æstate ſuperiores magis, Hyeme vero inferiores."</note>

3. If the cold assails the body greatly, it is fitting to heat the air of the room well; let the fire be without smoke. The body should be comforted with warm ointments where weakness is present.

4. At this time, one need not abstain much from sexual intercourse. Much physical exercise is beneficial; and sufficient food will not be harmful, because digestion is now strong.

5. Fumigations <note>cleansing the air with medicinal smoke</note> of Juniper wood, Aloes, Cypress, and Frankincense contribute to health. We conclude, therefore, that by these observations, a healthy person can preserve their natural heat and <term>radical moisture</term> <note>the essential fluid believed to act as the "fuel" for the body's life-force</note>; while these remain unharmed, health will remain intact.

# On the Elementary Method of Preserving Health.

Creatures (of which man is the leader) were intended to live and not be corrupted in any way. For as Solomon witnesses, *God created all things that they might exist, and they did not place in the world a means of corruption or destruction.* <note>original: "Deus creauit omnia ut essent, & non ponebant in mundo modum corruptionis, aut exterminij." This refers to the Wisdom of Solomon 1:14.</note> Hence it was that the aforementioned Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer known for his work *Mathesis*.</note> believed the World, or rather the Sun, began its motion from the start of **Aries** <note>The sign of the Ram, marking the Spring Equinox and the traditional beginning of the astrological year.</note>, and not without reason. Consequently, it appears that the **Airy and Vernal Kingdom** is to be preferred above the other three seasons in position and dignity. And this is our reasoning in our volume titled *The Air, God's Treasury Chest* <note>original: "Aer arcâ Dei thesaurariâ."</note>, where we proved all other elements took their beginning from air, and air immediately from the winds.

Therefore, in the course of things—and especially of human life—we observe that this vernal state claims the first position. It extends from the point of infancy up to youth; this age encompasses infancy, childhood, and adolescence, like the three months of spring. For as in the springtime heat increases more and more, so too dryness gradually creeps into the human <term>economy</term> <note>the physical constitution or internal management of the body's humors</note>. Thus, the fluid limbs of the infant grow warmer—though step by step—as one moves closer to youth. Youth is the state of the "summer" of life, in which <term>cholera</term> <note>yellow bile, the hot and dry humor</note> gradually increases, just as in the preceding age of adolescence, blood and the **Vernal** disposition <note>the Sanguine temperament, which is hot and moist</note> prevail.

Nor is the reason strange why the vernal or airy time—being hot and moist—claims the first and principal place in the year, if we carefully consider the condition of the world. For the world consists of the hot effects of light and a mass of darkness, confused and full of the potential Spirit of the World. In such an action, it was necessary that the warmth of light be present along with an abundant moisture produced in the spirit of light by its power and action. For the gathering of the dark spirit in the form of a most obscure cloud is compared to a wet, cold, and shapeless **Winter**. Its coldness, corrected by the presence of light, is forced to gradually give place to heat in creation. Hence comes the life and birth (or childhood) of the year, and hence the moisture and heat of the creature from which an infant's life arises. Yet in this <term>complexion</term> <note>the combination of qualities or humors in a person</note>, the heat of divine light does not so abound that it is not tempered by the dark cold of divine power.

Furthermore, just as light excites heat by its motion, and heat in its action produces a degree of dryness, so Darkness brings forth cold through its stillness. When these are stirred by heat, they produce moisture through a middle mixing. It follows, then, that in this mixture there arises a <term>temperament</term> <note>a balanced mixture of qualities</note> of heat, moisture, cold, and dryness so equal that many authors doubt whether spring is cold or rather hot. Similarly, they hesitate over the temperament of the airy spirit. For the **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> make it hot, while the **Stoics** make it cold, as was declared before.

Considering these things, we perceive that **Spring** partakes of winter's cold; hence its beginning starts with cold. Its end, however, being not far from the fiery degree of **Summer**, is hot; thus the best balance of spring lies in the middle.

In **Autumn**, however, the air behaves like the earth between water and fire. For in the annual circle, it is situated between the fiery summer and the watery winter. For in the rotation of the Elements, we find the earth placed between fire and water. And from here, we can gather the age of the world from the course of the year: in which the Golden Age began, then the Silver, later the Leaden; and at last it will end so that, like a new year, another world may be renewed. From this, it is clear why putrefaction and corruption are so frequent in Autumn—namely, because the **Martial** heat of summer time <note>associated with Mars, hot and dry</note> and the **Lunar** cold of winter <note>associated with the Moon, cold and moist</note> are observed to concur then in the putrid temperament of **Saturn** <note>Saturn was traditionally associated with melancholy, decay, and the finality of old age</note>. But since we have discussed these at length previously, let this suffice for now.

### CHAPTER III.

->On the change of the Air's Temperament, first in each Month: then in each portion of the day.<-

In the preceding chapter, we reviewed at length the reason why the circle of the year is distinguished into quarters—corresponding to the ages of man—due to the diverse changes of the Air following the movement of the greater light <note>The Sun</note>. Here, however, we shall show how by the same reasoning the lesser light, namely the Moon (☾), is likewise accustomed to change the air fourfold in any given month. For the Moon does not seem to act upon the Air differently than the Sun itself during the time she is observed to traverse the Zodiac. Thus, the four quarters of any month relate in their condition to the four seasons of the year: from the point of the conjunction of the Lights (or the New Moon) in any month until the end of one week, the temperament of the air is referred to the Vernal <note>Spring</note> station. For the Moon in her first quarter renders the air warm and moist; for this reason, monthly humors <note>referring to cyclic bodily fluids, not solely menstruation</note> abound more in that season, just as the humors do in spring. The second week of the month (at the close of which is the Full Moon) renders the air not unlike the Solar Summer in heat and dryness. Therefore, in this quarter, the ripening of fruits is assisted. In the third week, the Moon completes her third quarter, and this claims for itself the Autumnal condition, being colder and drier; and the fourth week is occupied by the final Quarter, which is cold and moist in the manner of Winter.

It must, however, be carefully noted here that just as the Sun is the source of heat and the Moon is the Mistress of humors, so the virtue of the Sun is primarily to heat, while that of the Moon is more to moisten. Therefore, their operations in their respective circles are varied and diverse. For the manifest effect of the Sun is hot, just as that of the Moon is moist.

By a similar logic, within the space of twenty-four hours—which constitutes a whole natural day—Experience itself teaches us that the Air claims for itself the condition of the heavens in four parts. For counting from the point of Dawn (or the Horizon) to the Southern angle (or Zenith), we establish one Quarter of the day, which has the nature of Spring: namely, warm and moist. Therefore, from Dawn until Noon, the state of the whole day is healthier, as it is the time in which the bodies of both the healthy and the sick are restored. For experience teaches that in this interval—specifically in the morning time—those suffering from fevers are most relieved, the swellings of the dropsical <note>those suffering from edema or fluid retention</note> decrease, and French pains <note>original: "dolores Gallici," a historical term for syphilis</note> are mitigated, and so forth. And the reason is this: just as in the Macrocosm <note>the universe as a whole</note> at that time exhalations are dissolved by the sun, so the Microcosmic <note>the human body as a "little world"</note> vapors that are troublesome at night are dissipated and emitted from the body through subtle exhalations. Indeed, the spirits are greatly refreshed by the equilibrium of the morning Air. The second Quarter, however, which stretches from the daytime Noon to the angle of the West, is likened to Summer; for its heat is more intense than any other in the whole day. But that quarter of the day which stretches from the point of the West to the nocturnal noon (or Nadir), claims the Autumnal property for itself. Therefore, in this Quarter, some Physicians advise against giving any medicine or potion to the sick unless necessity urges it; for this time corresponds to that in which the sun declines from us toward the wintry station. Finally, that quarter which is measured from midnight corresponds to winter. Therefore, in this station, nightly pains become sharp, because the coldness of the night, by condensing the surface of the skin, prohibits the hidden evacuation or evaporation of the fumes generated in the body. And this is the reason why a "flux of the eyes" <note>watery or discharging eyes</note> happens to those whose eyes are poorly affected. At this time also, those are most troubled who [suffer] with pains...

[...those who] are weighed down by French pains <note>original: "doloribus Gallicis"; a common historical term for syphilis</note>: likewise those who suffer from a flow of the intestines <note>diarrhea</note> or from a profusion of blood. Having seen these things, it is advised for healthy people to arrange their bodies regularly, according to the dispositions of the seasons of the year, or of the months, and even of the divisions of the natural day itself.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*In which the varying temperament of different regions of the world is discussed: and afterwards, the healthy and unhealthy disposition of the air in various places, and finally how corrupted air is to be corrected.*<-

That the various parts of the world possess air of diverse quality and temperament, no one of sound mind doubts; for the various arrangement of Zones and Climates <note>In ancient geography, "climates" referred to latitudinal bands of the earth</note>, which consists of the varying temperaments of the same, clearly indicates this to us. For those parts beyond the Antarctic circle are intolerable due to cold; while those lying between the boundaries of the temperate zones are not so mercilessly cold, just as that zone called "Torrid" <note>The tropics</note> is the most immoderate of all with summer heat. These dispositions of places or regions of the earth are naturally inherent to them. Yet there are various places in the world which, by some accident and contrary to the laws of nature, have air that is variously corrupted: namely, because of the property of unhealthy waters, or of stagnant pools and muddy marshes, as in the Eastern land near Scanderone <note>modern-day İskenderun or Alexandretta</note>; or because of a corrupted breath <term>halitus</term> <note>a vapor or miasma</note> from the earth, a cave, or a lake, as in the land or promontory of Puteoli <note>Pozzuoli</note> in Italy. We see the air similarly affected by fevers and corrupt diseases in some parts of England, and in overseas regions near muddy rivers, especially those which receive the salt water of the sea.

<margin>Book 1, chapter 3, on Preserving Health.</margin>
<margin>On the Causes of Respiration, chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>On the Differences of Fevers, book 1, chapter 4.</margin>
Furthermore, we find the air of one place illuminated by Solar rays, as in flat and mountainous places; while another is shady and least adorned or purged by the Solar rays. That air which participates in the light of the Sun is warmer, and consequently, purged and thinned out. Conversely, the shady air is thicker and colder, such as that found in cities, dark valleys, and groves. The disposition of day and night air is regarded in the same respect. Therefore, bright air makes the spirit more lively and agile because of the operation of Solar heat, but shady and misty air makes it more slow and sluggish. For as the spirit is in the Macrocosm <note>the "Great World" or universe</note> surrounding the Microcosm <note>the "Small World" or human being</note>, such also will be the spirit within the Microcosm, by whose motion the body is moved in space. Galen gives the reason for this: first, because the air, as it were a surrounding body, adheres to the human as if born with him. Whence it is necessary that some part of it (though a smaller part) be carried through the nostrils to the brain, and the greater part be conveyed through the windpipe <term>aspera arteria</term> to the lungs. Similarly, it is drawn in from the arteries through the pores of the skin, as he testifies elsewhere.

We say, therefore, that in the daytime the air of the fields or open air is far healthier than shady air, such as that of cities; and also that the daytime air is healthier than the nighttime. Furthermore, open air varies according to the height or depth of the place: for mountain and high air is purer and more refined, being constantly purged by the winds and accessible to solar rays; whereas that which is deeper is the opposite.

Indeed, even coastal land possesses air that differs from that of inland regions; likewise, marshy places behave differently than dry ones.

Infinite things could be said on this subject, but we shall now descend to our primary objective: the preservation of health.

We conclude, therefore, that since the air can be corrupted in so many ways in various parts of a region, it is necessary that we sagaciously investigate the method by which it may be purged and corrected, and either restored to a healthy temperament <note>In this context, "temperament" refers to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> or at least brought close to it. It has seemed appropriate, therefore, to subjoin the following precepts conducive to this goal.

->*Rules for preserving health, highly necessary for the healthy.*<-

1. Inequality of the air is to be avoided above all else. Dry air is to be preferred over humid, and thin air over thick <note>original: "subtilis grosso"; "subtle" or thin air was thought to be easier for the spirit to process than heavy, misty air</note>. The inconstancy of the air must always be fled, for the reasons cited above. We also condemn and disapprove of any place with excessive exhalations <note>Vapors rising from the earth</note>, or where excessive heat reigns by day or intense cold by night.

2. A house situated toward the Western quarter is not in every respect suitable for health (according to some); likewise, a house near a marshy place is unsuitable, unless small sands are naturally present and the air is well known to be healthy. I approve of a southern site less, because it is most often accustomed to bring about corruption <note>Stagnation and rot caused by heat and moisture</note>. If the dwelling is in a sterile place, either upon or next to crags or stony places, it is not particularly healthy, because the solar rays strike sharply during the day and heat it excessively, and by a contrary property, the night becomes too cold; for this reason, the air is rendered too unequal in its temperament.

3. The air of such places must therefore be corrected. Above all, we should flee a place in which fresh water and seawater are mixed, as well as marshy places where exhalations are accustomed to hang suspended in the air. But if one must dwell near such a place, let the house be placed upon a hill with trees and a plain between you and the fumes; let the windows be positioned so they do not face the marsh at all, so that by this means the frequent exhalations have little or no power over that dwelling. Let there be a pond or marsh between you and the Sun, so that the malevolent influence <note>original: "virtus maleuola"</note> may be drawn away by the Sun, and that dwelling may be made freer from it.

4. Many in Italy, France, and Spain are accustomed to fortify and adorn their less-than-healthy dwellings with fragrant plants, such as Oranges, Lemons, Citrons <note>original: "Cedris"; while literal for Cedars, in this citrus context it refers to the Citron tree</note>, and so on, whose scents correct the air with their healthfulness, and whose pleasant greenery contributes much to health. Vines are very helpful for this; for their leaves provide cooling in the summer, and by their flexibility, they can be arranged across the facade <note>original: "frontispicium"</note> or all around.

5. Private air is rectified by a flaming fire (but one that smokes as little as possible). Here, dried bundles of grapevines are especially praised, as well as fragrant plants—namely Rosemary, Juniper, Laurel, and others of that kind. Fumigations <note>The practice of burning substances to "smoke out" impurities or disease</note> are also very effective, such as Olibanum, Frankincense, and Amber <note>original: "Carabas"; likely referring to Carabe, a term for yellow amber</note>. During the time of the plague, I prescribed a fumigation made of rue, liquid pitch, sulfur, and vinegar, which brought much benefit to the healthy and saved many from the rage of the plague.

### CHAPTER I.

->*On Motion, Exercise, Lust, and Wakefulness.*<-

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'C' in a square frame with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>Having completed our discourse on the Air (which is so very necessary for life and health), we shall descend to the other <term>non-natural things|In pre-modern medicine, these were six factors not innate to the body—air, food/drink, motion/rest, sleep/wake, excretion/retention, and mental passions—that humans could control to maintain health.</term> which can be harmful to Health. Indeed, the Sages agree that he who does not exceed the proper measure and norm in Motion and Rest, in Sleep and Wakefulness, in fullness and emptiness <note>Referring to the state of the stomach and bowels</note>, and in the loosening or retention of the Bowels, will be able to avoid sicknesses and diseases and preserve his health for a long time. For these things make a man live for a very long time, if the precepts are correctly observed.

First, therefore, the consideration of the **Motion** of the human body presents itself. We engage in motion in many ways, namely through labor, *Lust* <note>original: "Venere"; referring to sexual activity, which was categorized as a form of physical exertion that affected the body's balance</note>, wakefulness, and so on. To protect health, it is highly necessary that motion and exercise precede refreshment or food and drink. This is first because it excites <term>natural heat|The innate warmth believed to be the primary engine of life, residing in the heart and driving digestion.</term>, through which digestion becomes more convenient. Second, it ensures that the body's superfluities <note>Waste products or excess humors that the body cannot use</note> are dissolved; these are consumed in this way through sweat or <term>insensible exhalations|The release of vapors through the skin that are not visible as sweat.</term>. What remains of them is then prepared for expulsion, so that the food received may be more easily digested and concocted.

It must be noted that motion of this kind ought to be before Dinner, because just as it helps digestion at that time, so after dinner it is indeed inconvenient and harmful. This is because it causes the food to descend too quickly and consequently uncooked <note>original: "incoctus"; meaning undigested or not yet fully transformed by the stomach's heat</note> into the lower parts of the stomach, from which it is accustomed to produce Convulsions, or at least Hiccups, in some. For those who live sparingly, however, much exercise before food is not required, because the natural heat will be sufficient to consume the superfluities of the limbs (since they are fewer). Nay, the power of the native heat in some is so strong that it can destroy superfluities with little or no preceding labor. Hence, I advise that for those eating little, only a little exercise should precede the meal, lest they evacuate more than they receive; and those who are copiously refreshed should labor more copiously before the meal. And hence a more copious and coarser diet is attributed to Athletes, on account of their great...

That exercise may be done rightly according to the laws of Nature, the following Precepts should be observed.

### Healthy Precepts for Exercise.

1. Exercise before lunch and Dinner should not be violent, but moderate, equal, and uniform.
2. I say moderate: namely that by which the body is made more cheerful and the limbs lighter. For fatigue and pain in the limbs proves immoderate movement; wherefore if symptoms of that kind are perceived, let there be a cessation.
3. We call it uniform and equal Exercise when the upper and lower limbs are exerted proportionally and equally: whether by going on foot, or jumping, or riding, or by a game of ball, or let there be moderate wrestling, etc.
4. Finally, before the accustomed hour of eating, use moderate labor, either by riding or walking, or some such Exercise: and let it be until the skin is red but not to the point of sweating (which must always be noted); for this mode of exercise greatly benefits the body, for it drives away <term>windiness|Intestinal gas or flatulence, which Galenic medicine believed caused many ailments.</term> and fits, strengthens, and lightens the body: it excites the heat of the stomach, tightens the joints, and makes the superfluous humors that are congealing and the <term>phlegm|pituita; one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture.</term> descend upon a stomach that is too inflamed with heat and too dried out.

As for the type of movement pertaining to **Venus** <note>original: "Veneream"; referring to sexual activity, named after the goddess of love</note>: in considering it, one must look at health, age, temperament, strength, and the season of the year. For old men must use sexual intercourse very sparingly, for it weakens the <term>innate virtue|The natural power or life force of an organ or the body as a whole.</term>, renders the limbs invalid, consumes the <term>innate heat|calidum innatum; the vital heat present in the body from birth, necessary for life and digestion.</term>, and swiftly accelerates old age. Then, it does not much suit the **choleric temperament**, because on account of its more serious composition, it loses more than it can suddenly recover. For the <term>sperm|The "seed" or reproductive fluid, thought in this period to be a highly concentrated form of vital spirits and blood.</term> is very full of vital Spirits. Hence arose that well-worn saying, *Cholera in Venus* <note>original: "Cholera in Venere"</note>, wants much, but can do little. And the reason is, because the Choleric person is in a state quite dry and lacking in native humor. So too the **Melancholic temperament** should avoid [excessive] intercourse: for as sperm abounds in innate heat and radical moisture, so indeed is that temperament quite cold and dry: wherefore both its dryness and heat are the more contracted, the more copiously sperm is poured out from it. To such persons, therefore, the use of Venus should not be so frequent: for according to the old axiom, *the Melancholic can do little and does not want much.*

Finally, in Autumn and Summer, because of the dryness of those seasons, one must abstain from much intercourse, and especially in summer, because on account of the excessive dilation of the pores in that season, the internal spirits and heats easily fly out and expire, and the native virtue is weakened.

### Healthy Precepts for the use of Venus.

1. Venus is beneficial if there is such a space between intercourse that no dissolution or weakening of strength follows from it.
2. When there is intercourse, let the body be neither too full nor empty, nor let it exceed in cold, heat, moisture, or dryness.
3. It is better to have intercourse with a warm body than a cold one, and a moist one than a dry one.
<margin>Commentary 1 on book 3 of Hippocrates, *On Popular Diseases*.</margin>

<margin>Galen, Book 6, Chapter 3, *On Preserving Health*.</margin>
5. Excessive Venus is an enemy to dry temperaments: such as are the Choleric and Melancholic.

### CHAPTER II.

->On nourishment: and also on depletion and fullness.<-

**Nourishment (Refection)**
*   **External:** Consisting of food and drink.
    *   **Substance:** Liquid or solid.
    *   **Quantity:** Great variety of dishes, a single type of dish, or small amounts.
    *   **Quality:** Considered in respect to complexion, age, season, inclination, and habit.
    *   **Time:** Determined according to appetite.
    *   **Preparation:** Specifically regarding chewing.
    *   **Correction of Errors:** Remedies for errors made in the stomach regarding quantity, quality, or types of food.
*   **Internal:** Which occurs through Rest and Sleep.
*   **Evacuation of Superfluities:** The removal of waste and the reformation of the <term>complexion|The specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual</term>.

<margin>The preservation of health especially consists in two things, according to the rule of the Wise: namely, either in...</margin>

Since the preservation of health consists chiefly in two things: namely, in suitable Nourishment and the purging of unnatural <term>superfluities|Excess waste or humors that the body cannot process, which were believed to cause disease if they stagnated</term>: we shall therefore discuss these two in order. First, we speak of the two-fold Nourishment. For just as the nourishment of food and drink is the sustenance of the body, so Sleep and Rest provide relief to the soul and to exhausted limbs. I say "Rest" of the soul within the body's members and faculties; for in itself, the "radius" of the soul never rests: for it is the swiftest of all things, as Solomon testifies <note>Likely referring to the Book of Wisdom 7:24: "For wisdom is more mobile than any motion."</note>. However, the more prominent nourishment of the body consists in eating and drinking; we shall begin with that.

Just as exercise causes depletion and evacuation in the body through sweat and <term>insensible exhalations|Vapors or "spirits" believed to escape through the skin and breath without being seen, a concept central to early modern metabolic theory</term>; so, once the body is emptied, Nourishment is required to strengthen it. Furthermore, just as Labor, by emptying the body, produces an appetite for food—which is called Hunger, and which a certain author called the *Herald of Nature* <note>original: "Præconem naturæ"</note> to declare the necessity of nourishment—so indeed nature requires a due measure or "fodder" to satisfy the body's desire. I will briefly explain what must be considered before nourishment.

In nourishment, therefore, before it is either rationally prescribed by a Physician or accepted by a healthy person, these things must especially be observed: namely, *Its Substance, Quality, Quantity, Time, and Preparation.* Also, the variety within the stomach and the correction of effects that are sometimes unhealthy. Before we explain these, it must be known that according to the opinion of all the Sages, any being composed of the four Elements and contrary humors always requires food and drink; if it lacks these, its substance is corrupted. For that which is "simple" <note>An entity not made of mixed, conflicting elements</note>, or forged of the thinnest fire, and in which there are no contrary Elements—such as the Angels—neither eat nor drink, but exist of themselves, as all Philosophers testify. Therefore, a substance of that kind is never changed by generative or corruptive alteration. But before we descend to the specific parts of nourishment, we will briefly explain the mystery of replenishment and depletion.

<margin>What Hunger is.</margin>

Just as human bodies are receptacles for foods and drinks, so indeed the substance of this kind of nourishment passes into the substance of the recipient. For heat... always strives toward building up the moisture of bodies, by which it is afterward built up and fed. Thus also bodies, which are the receptacles of the contained Elements, are accustomed to be dissolved into the receiving air by the heat of the Sun and the Wind; these build up the moisture of all bodies, and the heat of the Sun and Wind is fed and nourished by the moisture of both the bodies so dissolved and of rivers. And this is the cycle of things, a kind of <term>Rotation of the Elements|The natural cycle where elements transform into one another, such as water turning to air through evaporation</term>; namely, of one into another. For if bodies were not diminished every hour by insensible breathing out, in the manner of nourishment in the body, hunger would in no way consume the body, nor would abstinence from food and drink render it thin and lean; nor would nourishment be required with such necessity. But to come to the nourishment of the body and its substance—

# On the Elementary Method of Maintaining Health.

Let us examine the nature of substance: we perceive that it is either solid or liquid. Where a body is hot and vaporous <note>characterized by high metabolic heat and "internal steam"</note>, coarse foods are beneficial; this is because the substance that is dissolved and emitted from such a body is of great quantity and thick consistency due to the excessive heat and vapor of the body. Conversely, where a body is dense and dry, thin and moist foods are beneficial, such as broths, drinks, milk, and so on. As a general rule, there should be an equal mixture in one's feeding, yet with this law: drier bodies should be allowed more generous moistening, while more humid bodies should receive less.

The quantity of both food and drink must also be observed: it is either small or large. A small quantity is praised by almost all wise men. For all confess that he who guards against excessive filling with food, and observes equality and moderation in refreshment, will partake of health and longevity.

Hence, a disciple of Hippocrates, seeing his abstinence, is said to have addressed him thus: "Exalted Teacher, if you wished to eat well, you would not endure such weakness of body." To which Hippocrates replied, *"Son, I eat that I may live, I do not live that I may eat"* <note>original: "Fili, ego comedam vt viuam, non viuam vt comedam." This famous aphorism emphasizes food as a functional necessity rather than a pursuit of pleasure.</note>. From this, he argued that nourishment is to be sought for the sake of endurance, and not endurance for the sake of nourishment.

Indeed, experience proves that this frugality has granted many people long and happy days: to such an extent that, because of this habit, they have remained of most pleasant appearance, with very light and agile movements, longer life, and a good appetite.

However, this Rule sometimes admits an Exception: where there is constant and vehement Exercise, a copious Diet is indeed required. For excessive labor, such as that of an Athlete, consumes the flesh too much: because, either through sweat or insensible evaporations, there is an excessive flow out of the body's substance. So that it may be restored by the addition of new substance, an ample refreshment is required. We, however, are directing our discourse in this place toward men leading an equal and non-violent way of life.

The quality of food and drink must also be considered in many ways: for first and foremost, people should look to the health of their <term>complexion|The unique balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's physical and mental temperament</term>. Therefore, to begin with drinks: for those with tempered and <term>sanguine|A temperament dominated by blood, usually considered warm and moist</term> bodies, as well as those who are <term>choleric|A temperament dominated by yellow bile, considered hot and dry</term>, naturally weak wines are suitable when mixed with a little water; or at least stronger wines with much water. For by this method, the fiery condition in bilious people will be blunted, and the Sanguine will be preserved from easily passing over into a bilious nature. Furthermore, in the summer season, care must be taken that wine is not excessively sharp and fiery, or thick and sweet, but is instead a claret or white wine of moderate strength. In winter, it should be reddish in color, and in substance clear and thin, with a scent and flavor that is good and pleasant.

Regarding other drinks—namely, Beer and Ale—let them be thin and weak in the Summer, but mature and not recently made; in winter, however, they should be stronger and more lively. Moreover, in old age, a stronger and warmer drink is required, since in that stage of life the <term>native heat|The vital, innate warmth believed to drive all biological processes, which was thought to diminish as one aged</term> is weak and coldness more greatly abounds. Conversely, youth requires weaker drinks that are not sharp, hot, or fiery, lest they be set too much aflame by their excessive use.

Since, however, others drink cold water, I advise them not to drink excessive water during a meal suddenly and against their habit. For drinking cold liquid on top of food chills the stomach, extinguishes the heat of digestion, and renders the food undigested. The liver is also weakened, than which nothing is worse: for since the nature of the liver is hot—without which it does not know how to produce blood—and without <term>sanguification|The process of turning digested food into blood</term> (which is the primary power of the natural faculty), the secondary powers that consist in the making of flesh cannot perform their roles. To extinguish the natural heat of that faculty would be most harmful.
