### Volume I. Tractate I. Section II. Part III. Book II.

Finally, the **Quality** of nourishment must be considered, especially where the condition of the body is susceptible to disease. For example: a healthy person who is naturally predisposed to flowing hemorrhoids <note>original: "hæmorrhoidas"</note> and similar conditions should avoid sharp, sweet, and salty drinks. For these types of drinks or foods thin and heat the blood, making it more prone to flow.

Regarding the qualities of foods, almost the same must be said as was said for **Drinks** <note>original: "Poculentis"</note>. That is, those foods should be chosen for a healthy person's nutrition which are contrary in quality to their temperament <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four "humors" or bodily fluids in an individual</term>, the season of the year (as discussed previously), their age, and any diseases threatening their health. First, it should be known that for a "porous" or "vaporously hot" body <note>a body with high metabolic heat that releases much "internal steam"</note>, foods of a coarse quality, cooler and tending toward dryness, should be used. However, for dense and dry bodies, subtle and moist foods are effective, for *opposites are usually cured by opposites* <note>original: "contraria contrariis curari solent"</note>.

It also contributes to the preservation of health that a healthy person uses foods agreeable to their own temperament: for instance, if someone is of a bilious and hot nature, temperate cold things are suitable for them; and so it is with the other temperaments.

*The Time and Hour should also be observed in eating and drinking.* Regarding Time, there are various opinions among the Authors. Some advise that food and drink should not be taken except at the accustomed hour. Regarding the habit of eating, they do not advise that a meal be provided unless the desire to eat is present at the accustomed hour. Nor should one eat again until the stomach is emptied of the previous meal. This "mystery" is revealed to us in two ways: namely, if there is a genuine appetite for eating, and if the saliva in the mouth is observed to be thin <note>original: "subtilis"</note> and not sticking to the throat at all.

For those who take food involuntarily <note>without hunger or against their will</note>, these disadvantages follow: they will feel their natural heat as if it were cold and powerless; and food taken without desire will be carried by the stomach and other organs like a heavy burden of nature, in which it will rot <note>original: "corrumpetur"</note> rather than be converted into health.

In the matter of habit, they should observe this: He who usually eats twice a day, if he suddenly restricts himself to a single meal, will perceive some disadvantage approaching him. Similarly, if someone is accustomed to taking only one meal a day and then takes two, he will undoubtedly find an equal disadvantage. The reason is that nature, not knowing how to digest more nourishment than is customary, or perhaps being insufficient, allows the food to remain undigested in the stomach.

Furthermore, he who is accustomed to receiving nourishment at a certain hour of the day and later transfers it to another, will perceive that this change of habit will harm him more than it helps: because *custom is a second nature* <note>original: "consuetudo est altera Natura"</note>.

But if necessity (which admits no law) <note>original: "necessitas (quæ Legem non admittit)"</note> requires an irregularity in eating, let that change of habit be done wisely—that is, step by step, and one instance after another.

There are some, however, who, having no regard for habit, claim that for healthy bodies in any season of the year, there is no more suitable way of eating than whenever the natural appetite urges. From this they conclude that the common observation of lunch and dinner times is useless, and consequently, that food should be taken according to the natural craving (whenever it happens) and not according to the laws of custom.

# On the Elementary Method of Preserving Health.

In my opinion, it is most advisable for a healthy person to observe custom rather than a passing appetite. For there is no certain rule or consistency in appetite: even though the stomach <note>original: "ventriculus"</note> is satisfied with food, as soon as a piece of fruit or some other dish is seen, it begins to hunger again. And thus it sometimes happens that by following this repeated appetite, we fall into gluttony and so on. It is better, therefore, to take food according to the custom of the time, and with such moderation that the feasting ceases while there is still a desire to eat; lest the stomach be burdened by a superfluity of foods.

Furthermore, a set time will ensure that the hungry person desires their meal all the more: and eager expectation will make the food and drink more pleasing and the taste sweeter at the appointed hour.

Regarding the variety of foods and dishes, authors differ somewhat. Some advise that many foods be placed on the table so that one may choose one or another according to their appetite, along with well-raised bread that is perfectly fermented. Another says that such a variety of dishes creates a disgust in the stomach; further, he says that since the differences between foods are so great—one dish being easy to digest, another difficult—the proper nourishment of the limbs will be hindered. Because when one is digested before the other and they are mixed together, either the undigested food slips away with the digested, or if it remains until the other is perfectly digested, it will spoil: for instance, if the meat of a kid or chicken is mixed with beef. For this reason, one or two dishes of a similar nature are more highly praised.

Indeed, it is necessary that the food itself be excellently prepared by chewing and the grinding of the teeth. For imperfect chewing <note>original: "masticatio"</note> does a great injury to Nature, as the food is not properly prepared according to Nature's intention; she assigned teeth to animals for this very reason: to grind and crush solid and hard food. For any solid thing is dissolved more easily in any solvent <note>original: "Menstruo": in early medicine, a liquid used to dissolve or extract nutrients</note> the more it is reduced to powder: for in this way, the entry for dissolution becomes better. Thus also Nature, by means of drinks, will better dissolve the matter prepared for nourishment than if it were minimally prepared and not enclosed in the stomach as if in a <term>Bain-marie: or "Mary's Bath," a culinary and chemical method where a vessel is placed in hot water to provide gentle, even heat</term> with its liquid solvent. Hence, for those who eat greedily, the digestion of foods becomes more difficult, specifically because of the imperfect chewing of the food.

Finally, if after taking food—either because of the quantity, the poor quality, or the difficulty of cooking—pain and heaviness are felt in the stomach or belly, whether before sleep or after it: then place a doubled linen cloth, quite warmed, over the stomach and belly, and sometimes lie on your belly so that the internal heat may be assisted in digesting.

But if a large meal is followed by a sour burping: it denotes indigestion because of the excessive coldness of the stomach. In this case, a gentle vomiting is to be induced at the proper time, so that the slow phlegms <note>original: "pituitæ": one of the four bodily humors, associated here with coldness and congestion</note> cooling the bottom of the stomach may be reduced.

With these things established, we shall propose the rules of diet that are healthy in principle.

->*Rules to be observed in eating and drinking.*<-

->ON FOOD.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
He who guards against excess and deficiency by maintaining equality and temperance will enjoy health and longevity.

<margin>2.</margin>
Moderate refreshment is most pleasing to the wise, as it is their way to eat to live, not live to eat. Therefore, those who feed on little food usually reach a mature old age. But he who is devoted to the engorging of food is either extinguished before old age, or his old age will be very premature.

Volume I, Treatise I, Section II, Part III, Book II.

<margin>3.</margin> He who cares for his health should use foods that are suitable for his age, temperament <note>original: "complexioni"</note>, habits, and his specific nature, as well as for the season of the year.

<margin>4.</margin> When the stomach is strong, healthy, and powerful in its heat, coarser and heavier foods are most suitable for it; for where the fire is strong, it is capable of burning thick logs. *The signs of a good stomach are agility of the body, lightness in movement, a good appetite, and so on.* But for a weak and cold stomach, subtle and light foods are beneficial; for a small fire can only burn small sticks. *The signs of a weak stomach are difficult digestion, heaviness of the body, sluggishness, a discharge or heaviness of the eyes <note>original: "oculorum grando," likely referring to a stye or heaviness in the eyelids</note>, a bloated face, bad burping—whether foul, sour, or bitter—gas, bloating of the belly, and a loss of appetite.*

<margin>5.</margin> Before lunch, or at your usual hour of eating, engage in moderate labor, either by riding a horse or by walking. For exercise prepares the body, drives away wind <note>gas</note>, and kindles and strengthens the heat of the stomach; it tightens the joints and melts away superfluous humors that remain after the final digestion <note>original: "concoctionem," the process where the body 'cooks' food into nutrients</note>.

<margin>6.</margin> At lunch and dinner, stop eating while you still have some desire to eat.

<margin>7.</margin> If anyone at lunch or dinner takes a pottage that softens the belly and another that binds it, he should know that if the soft one—such as that made from barley, violets, etc.—comes first, it makes digestion easier and smoother. But if the binding one is swallowed first—namely, made from rice and herbs or dry spices—it retains the food too long in the bottom of the stomach, where digestion usually takes place because of its cavity and its proximity to the Liver.

<margin>8.</margin> If someone is accustomed to eating twice a day, let him not break his own habit; likewise, let him who used to refresh himself once a day keep his habit, under penalty of future illness, unless necessity urges it; and this should be done with the caution expressed before, because habit is a second nature.

<margin>9.</margin> Care must be taken that a large amount of food is not taken (even if the usual hour prompts a healthy person), unless the healthy person knows his stomach to be empty; that is, when his appetite urges him to eat.

<margin>10.</margin> In eating, the stomach should be measured: it should not be burdened by tension, for that is a sign that food has been taken immoderately.

### ON DRINKING.

<margin>1.</margin> Frequent drinking during lunch or dinner hinders digestion, just as if water were frequently poured into a boiling pot, it hinders its heat. Therefore, drink should be taken soberly, in a way that suits the body and the season.

<margin>2.</margin> In summer, one must beware of sharp and very hot wine, and also of sweet wine; instead, let it be a Claret <note>a light-colored wine</note> that is not too strong, or a white wine, clear in its substance. In winter, however, let it be stronger and hotter. The same logic applies to beer; for winter requires stronger drinks, while the heat of summer requires weaker ones.

<margin>3.</margin> For those with a temperate, sanguine, or choleric temperament, weak drinks are suitable, for the reasons previously mentioned.

<margin>4.</margin> But if someone is accustomed to drinking cold water, let him not swallow too much of it over his food, unless led to do so by habit. For it cools the stomach and extinguishes the heat of digestion, especially if a great deal is taken.

## On Sleep and Rest: and how they are to be used healthfully.

<margin>Galen in book 6 of Hippocrates's *Of Popular Diseases*, 16.</margin>
We have therefore identified sleep as a kind of refreshment, inasmuch as by it not only are fatigued limbs restored, and the animal spirits <note>In early medicine, "animal spirits" were subtle fluids responsible for sensation and movement, not "ghosts."</note> seen to rest, but the body is also moistened and made plumper; whereas, on the other hand, *Wakefulness* is known to dry out bodies. Nor is this surprising, since these two states usually differ not only in quality, but entirely in their nature and essence. For just as *Wakefulness* is the extension of the Soul from its beginning to its ends—that is, to all parts and particles of the body, which is the emission or emanation of the vital light from the internal Center of the body (into which it had been contracted during sleep) to its circumference—so indeed *Sleep* is the withdrawal or contraction of the vital ray, driven from the ends or circumference back to its center and origin. In these two states, we can behold the wondrous properties of light and darkness within a single body. For *Darkness*, which is the seat of Rest, cold, and moisture alike, is created by the contraction of the divine light into itself, as if into a Center or Point; just as *Light*, which is the origin of motion, heat, and likewise dryness, is the Emission or Expansion of lucid rays from the Center to the circumference. But regarding this mystery, we shall (with God's blessing) treat more extensively elsewhere.

It is declared that sleep is a kind of restoration for both the Spirits of the body and the solid parts; for in sleep, the concoction <note>original: "concoctio," the metaphorical "cooking" or digestion of food into nutrients by the body's internal heat.</note> of matter is better performed, insofar as it strengthens and aids the digestive power by drawing the rays of native heat more toward the inside. This it possesses from its very nature, which is to pull back the rays of life from the Circumference to the Center <margin>Aphorism 4. 65.</margin> or, to use the words of *Galen*, to relax the soul according to nature from the ends to the beginning. But insofar as it cools and moistens, it does so not only through bodily nourishment, but also by condensing the air introduced through respiration; it converts that thickened air into fat. For it is necessary that if it contracts the rays of heat toward the Center, it must also introduce Air abundantly with them through all the pores <note>original: "spiracula," breathing-holes or pores</note> of the body. This air is observed to be converted into nourishment by thickening, as can be seen in Northern bears; they live through the whole of Winter in caves covered by snow, always sleeping and eating nothing—except that they are said sometimes to lick and suck their own claws—yet they are observed to emerge from the snow quite fat. Therefore, we have not unjustly called it a "Refreshment" in the preceding sections. But let us return to our purpose regarding Health.

### Things we observe regarding Sleep:

*   **During sleep:**
    *   Its **Time**:
        *   Nighttime.
        *   Daytime (divided into **Before lunch** and **After lunch**).
    *   Its **Quantity**.
    *   Its **Quality**.
    *   The **Position of the body**:
        *   On the **Side** (either **Right** or **Left**).
        *   **Upon** the **Belly** or the **Back**.
*   **After sleep:** The **Disposition of the body**.

The nighttime is most suitable for healthy sleep; primarily because the night enjoys a cold and moist temperament. External cold strengthens and increases natural internal heat, because through *antiperistasis* <note>A philosophical concept where one quality is strengthened by being surrounded by its opposite, like heat being concentrated inside the body by external cold.</note> and the closing of the pores, it does not allow the heat to exhale from the body. Furthermore, the nocturnal cold repels the heat from the Circumference, which results in perfect digestion at that time. Secondly, the state of night is more expedient for the tranquility of the soul, the body, and the exhausted Spirits. For then, the Meditations and Actions of the day cease. Finally, because sleep is interrupted neither by noise nor shouting, nor is it shortened by light striking the eyes. And since sleep is the *Contraction of the rays of light and life from the Circumference to the Center*—which is the very property of darkness—sleep in the dark is therefore more natural to it; just as, conversely, *Wakefulness* more gladly embraces the light of day by its very nature.

# Volume I. Treatise I. Section II. Part I. Book II.

As for daytime sleep, it should be known that sleeping in the morning—whether before noon or before the midday meal—makes the body lean and dries out the moisture of the healthy; therefore, it is to be avoided above all else. In its place, the <term>natural heat<note>In early medicine, "natural heat" was the innate warmth believed to drive all life processes, especially digestion and vitality.</note></term> should be stirred up by moderate exercise. However, afternoon sleep—that is, after the midday meal—is praised for various reasons; for it fills and strengthens both the digestive power and the stomach itself, as well as the attractive faculty. For during the space of such sleep, the natural heat (as has been said) is drawn toward the center and the interior of the stomach, whereas before it had been diffused throughout the entire body. And in this the Philosophers agree: that the evening meal should be larger in quantity than the midday one. This is because the midday period receives the heat of the day, along with dryness and the vertical rays of the Sun; therefore, wakefulness is more suited to this time than sleep, which is concerned with cold and moisture. For this reason, they maintain that nocturnal sleep is more fit for <term>concoction<note>original: "concoctio"; the process of "cooking" or ripening food in the stomach to turn it into nutrients.</note></term>, and is to be preferred over daytime sleep; consequently, a more bountiful supper should be taken than dinner. And yet, afternoon sleep after a meal is praised where digestion is weak; but let such sleep be brought on in a place suited to the temperament of the night—namely, somewhere cool, dark, and quiet—following the precautions explained below. Finally, we say that afternoon sleep is suitable for many <term>bilious<note>Those with a "choleric" temperament, traditionally characterized as hot and dry.</note></term> bodies, because its moist disposition resists dryness and benefits the <term>radical moisture<note>The fundamental life-fluid or "fuel" believed to sustain the body’s vital flame.</note></term>. For this reason, it often tends to fatten thin bodies. But indeed, it is found to be harmful to the <term>phlegmatic<note>A temperament characterized by cold and wet qualities.</note></term> complexion, as it is said to multiply phlegmatic superfluities. Hence, according to the School of Salerno <note>A famous medieval medical school that produced a widely read poem on health, the *Regimen Sanitatis Salernitanum*.</note>, it appears that afternoon sleep should be avoided only by Phlegmatic individuals.

<margin>
Galen, *On the Causes of Symptoms*, Book 1, Chapter 8.
</margin>
The quantitative proportion of sleep ought to be moderate—neither excessive nor too short—unless a suitable reason precedes it. For if someone has exerted himself quite freely, it is no wonder if a deeper sleep weighs upon him (as Galen testifies), both because of the exhaustion of the power he put forth and because of fatigue. Nevertheless, we do not deny that a longer sleep is appropriate for those who, due to a weakness of the stomach, find the concoction of food difficult; for (as has been said) a fuller concoction is achieved through sleeping.
<margin>
Hippocrates, *Book on a Salubrious Diet*, 29.
</margin>

We have explained the quality of sleep in the preceding sections: namely, that it is cold and moist, whereas, conversely, wakefulness is hot and dry. It is for this reason that in phlegmatic people, sleep is deeper. Therefore, Galen testifies that deep sleeps are signs of phlegm. From this it also follows that neither **Melancholic** nor **Choleric** types sleep excessively, due to their own dryness. Likewise, in Summer and Autumn, sleep is usually shorter, as well as more troubled and restless, because of the dryness of the season. Nature even provided for this by making the nights shorter in summer and the days longer; arguing from this that due to the dryness and heat of the summer season, wakefulness ought to reign more than sleep. But as the nights grow longer, so sleep tends to hold greater dominion.

Furthermore, the position and placement of the sleeper in the bed should not be overlooked. Once the body is arranged upon a soft bed, rest for one hour or longer, according to your convenience, upon your **right side**; then turn yourself to the **left side**, and finish your sleep upon it. The reason for this is readily apparent: since the excellent heat for concocting food flows from the **liver**, the more powerful force and virtue in digestion resides in the right side. Therefore, the entire difficulty in concoction is to be attributed to the power of the liver; consequently, a healthy person ought to lie upon that side so that the greater portion of concoction may be completed. When that is finished, one should turn to the left side; for because the **spleen** is much colder than the liver, less labor is to be assigned to it. However, it is not suitable for healthy people to sleep upon their bellies, on account of the twisting of the neck and the compression of the stomach.

# On the Elementary Method of Preserving Health.

But when, during sleep around the time of <term>digestion<note>original: "concoctio"; the process of "cooking" or ripening food in the stomach to turn it into nutrients.</note></term>, pain or other signs of indigestion are felt, it is by no means unsuitable to lie *upon the belly*; in such a case, it is permissible to apply a pillow or something warm to the stomach, or to place it underneath. In this way, the <term>natural power<note>The internal biological force believed to govern bodily functions like growth and digestion.</note></term> will be aided in digestion, and by such compression, the dormant and, as it were, chilled heat is partly stirred up and partly strengthened in its digestive business by the external warmth. To sleep *on the back* is not so suitable; for in this way, the <term>superfluities<note>Waste products or excess fluids that the body has not processed.</note></term> which usually flow to the palate and nostrils are poured back toward the brain, which they believe can "drown" the memory. However, once awakened from sleep, it is appropriate for a person to rest on their back for a short time for the purpose of straightening the limbs and refreshing the sides. These and similar matters regarding sleep (for the sake of a better method) we have organized into the following series.

**Sleep**
* **Is Discouraged:**
    * *On an empty stomach:* because it chills the body, brings on weariness, and makes the natural faculty heavy and sluggish.
    * *On a full stomach:* because it moistens too much, dims the eyesight, and generates restlessness.
    * *Preceded by exercise, bathing, or <term>evacuation<note>The removal of humors, such as through bloodletting or purging.</note></term>:* because it makes the natural color (weakened by the aforementioned actions) faint; indeed, it affects the body with wasting and diminishes the strength.
    * *Immediately after food, or a short time later:* because it harms the eyes, fills the head with superfluities, weakens the body, and renders the limbs less agile and sometimes weary.
    * *At midday, on a fasting stomach:* because the <term>natural heat<note>The innate warmth of the body required for life and health.</note></term>, on an empty stomach, takes up raw and unnatural humors and, instead of good juice, draws them to the liver, infecting it; it affects the blood and the color of the body, makes the nerves weak due to vapors rising to the brain, produces laziness due to the weakness of the spirits, causes fevers and abscesses, and numbs the memory.
    * *Restless or disturbed:* since it generates hindered digestion, which is followed by gas and belching.
* **Is Judged according to the position of the body in bed:**
    * **On the Side**
        * *The Right Side:* provides relief of the bowels for those having a constricted stomach; it distributes nourishment through the body more quickly; it is always suitable at the beginning of sleep.
        * *The Left Side:* is suitable for those with loose bowels, those with a cold stomach, those affected by heat in the liver, and those who feel their digestive power is weak.
    * **Lying Upon**
        * *The Belly:* wonderfully aids a healthy person and preserves the innate heat.
        * *The Back:* is worst for those affected by <term>catarrh<note>original: "fluxione"; a downward flow of humors/fluids.</note></term>; it gives rise to <term>Phrenitis<note>Inflammation of the brain or delirium.</note></term>, <term>Epilepsy</term>, <term>Apoplexy</term>, and <term>Paralysis</term>.

Now indeed we shall subjoin certain Rules by which a healthy person may be governed after rising from sleep in the morning time: for when sleep is finished, a proper preparation and cleansing of the body is required. For man is, by nature, a <term>clean animal<note>original: "Animal mundum"; the author suggests that human nature inherently seeks cleanliness and order.</note></term>.

### ->Healthy precepts to be observed after sleep.<-

<margin>1.</margin>

Next, and especially if it is *Summer*, he should wash his face and hands with cold water:

3. Afterward, **Clean and ornate garments** should be put on; let the linen cloths required for your adornment be clean and not soiled. For the human soul, which is in itself pure and unstained, rejoices and delights in things that are pure, clean, and purged.

He who fears disease should employ suitable smokes; for example, if someone is prone to <term>catarrh<note>original: "catharrus"; an excessive buildup of mucus in the nose or throat.</note></term>, he should use fumigations of amber, laudanum, storax calamita, etc. If the memory is weak, he should use fumigations that help the memory: similarly, in a time of plague, he should use those things opposed to the plague: and so with the rest.

6. **Fragrant pomanders and ointments** greatly refresh the spirits. For the soul is restored by scent. A sweet odor is food for the soul: and when the soul is restored and comforted, it expands more easily; in this expansion, the body receives solace, and the heart rejoices. Indeed, even the blood filling the veins and arteries seems to exult from the joy of the soul and the refreshment of the spirits. It will also be permissible to use <term>electuaries<note>original: "electuaria"; medicinal pastes usually made with honey or syrup.</note></term>, whether they are comforting, or for dispersing gas, or for strengthening the stomach, or for awakening the dormant animal spirits, if it pleases you. And if the bowels are too constricted, a certain gentle soothing thing will do no harm.

7. Finally, after these things, use **Exercise** before the hour of refreshment, in the manner and form prescribed: in which it is necessary that you stretch your joints and limbs equally: for this strengthens the body.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### Concerning those passions, or accidents, which follow the soul.

<margin>
Galen, *On the Differences of Symptoms*, chapter 3.
Galen, *On Pulses*, book 1, *On the Differences of Pulses*.
Avicenna, book 2, doctrine 1, chapter 3.
Avicenna, *On Cordial Medicines*, chapter 7.
</margin>
Since the entire health and happiness of the body consists in the Rest and Tranquility of the Soul (for who is ignorant that disturbances of the body for the most part follow the passions of the mind?), we shall therefore say a few things about its **Accidents**, insofar as the body is effectively altered by them. These <term>suffering states<note>original: "pathemata"; emotional or mental disturbances that affect the physical body.</note></term> or accidents are distinguished from those things which are according to the laws of nature; wherefore they are called **Accidents of the Mind**. For just as certain vital actions are observed to consist either in the <term>dilation<note>original: "diastole"; the expansion of the heart or arteries.</note></term> of the heart alone or in its <term>contraction<note>original: "systole"; the shortening or tightening of the heart or arteries.</note></term> alone, as if at extremes, so too there is a middle action consisting of both contraction and dilation together. Indeed, we shall find the first extreme on the side of Light, and the property and condition of life and health: indeed, it excels that state of life which consists only in the standard way of living—that is, in the middle action of both contraction and dilation together, by which mixed action the pulse is perceived to move in systole and diastole. For in this middle state of life, a person can be either sick or healthy: but in that state where the dilation of the heart especially exercises itself, the Soul can never be sick, but is delighted by pious, healthful, and placid passions: these passions are therefore above the common laws of Nature. For in this state the Soul rejoices and exults: the anchor of hope is fixed in the supreme Goodness, it rests in secure confidence, it is kindled with love and charity, and through it, it ascends and penetrates into the sight of Truth itself.

[It] penetrates, performs works of mercy, and renders the heart soft and flexible to observe the laws of God: through humanity, it makes one humble and considers anyone to be his brother, as one who has a common Father, and lives and breathes from and through one eternal Light.

From these things, one may see that these holy Passions—namely, the actions of a healthy Mind—conduce to both divine and worldly health. But those accidental passions which are said to change the body, consisting only in the contraction or constriction of the heart, belong to the side of Darkness. For in Sadness, a kind of barrier is constructed between the sight of the Light and the Soul: the Spirit is enveloped in darkness; through cares and anxieties, joy and pleasure are dispelled; the intellect is thickened; Judgment is obscured; Memory is dulled; and finally, the Body (in the manner of terrestrial darkness) is chilled and dried out. The Soul is also plunged into the abyss of darkness by despair; all hope within it is killed; it is driven hither and thither at every moment by fear, and with confidence driven into exile, it is put at risk. Likewise, the brightest rays of Charity are extinguished by Hatred: *Envy* fiercely persecutes mercy. The Soul is torn apart by *Anger and fury*; hence Solomon says: <note>Proverbs 11:17 or similar themes in Wisdom literature.</note> *The fool tears his own soul with fury:* indeed, the Body suffers no small amount even from shame.

These, therefore, are the Accidents, or Passions, which affect the Spirit and Soul contrary to the Laws of Nature: to avoid them, the following Precepts should be observed.

### *Healthy precepts against the accidents and passions of the soul.*

The general precept is that those Objects should be avoided which usually nourish the heavy Passions of the Soul: for example, where there is an inclination toward Sadness, there it is proper to introduce oneself into jovial company and, contrary to one's own propensity, to pursue those things which usually produce laughter and pleasure: provided, however, that this is done modestly and with the avoidance of notable vice.

In sad and Melancholic passions, all things that distract with cares and anxieties must be excluded, and if possible, the mind should flourish again with joy and honest pleasures and delights or comforts; and the spirits should be refreshed in a temperate manner with food, drink, <term>fumigations<note>original: "suffumigiis"; the medicinal use of aromatic smoke or incense.</note></term>, suitable odors, and musical harmony.

But where Fury or anger is ready to disturb the soul, there the <term>choler<note>original: "Cholera"; the humor of yellow bile, which was believed to cause irritability and heat when in excess.</note></term> must be evacuated (for the sake of precaution), and the bilious attacks must be blunted: and drinks and foods should be taken which have the power both to alter and to nourish. Furthermore, all objects exciting Choler or anger are to be avoided above all else. And so it is with the rest.

## CHAPTER V.

### *Concerning external non-natural things that do not necessarily alter the body, and those things which usually change the body internally.*

<margin>The Art of Medicine, 43.</margin>
In the preceding sections, we have spoken abundantly about the external <term>non-natural things<note>original: "rebus non naturalibus"; a standard medical category including air, exercise, sleep, diet, etc., which affect health but are not innate to the body.</note></term> which necessarily alter the body. Now we shall discuss a few things concerning external things that do not necessarily alter the body, and afterward, concerning internal things. Just as we understood those things that necessarily alter us (following Galen) in the preceding Discourse as those which are born with us and can in no way be avoided: so indeed we say that other things do not necessarily happen: and they can be avoided as they do not originate from us at all. Such things include everything that wounds, bruises, or strikes.

<margin>On the Preservation of Health, book 1, chapter 2.</margin>
Regarding the internal non-natural things that change our bodies, three are numbered by Galen: namely, *Dryness, the wasting of substance, and the production of Excrement.* Thus, when all parts become drier than is right, not only is each one’s duty performed less properly, but the body is rendered leaner and more slender than before: and consequently more wrinkled, insofar as it has been dried out of its own accord.

<meta>This page continues the medical discussion from the previous section, moving from the psychological "passions of the soul" to the physical maintenance of the body's substance and the management of "superfluities" or waste through Galenic medicine. The catchword "enim" (for/indeed) links the transition between the discussion of the body's flow and its restoration.</meta>

Volume I. Treatise I. Section II. Part III. Book II.

The flow of substance in animals is caused by the **internal heat** <term>Latin: *calor insitus*; the innate vital heat believed by early physicians to drive metabolism and life</term>; for by means of this heat, a certain portion of substance flows away from all animals. Indeed, the entire mass of animals is in a perpetual state of flow (to use the words of Galen), which is most easily seen in those who are starving. It is necessary, therefore, that what has flowed out of the body be restored by food and drink: namely, food, so that whatever drier substance of the body is lost may be restored; and drink, so that the moister portion of the body which has flowed out—whether in the form of sweat or **insensible perspiration** <note>original: *insensibilis exhalationis*; the concept that moisture leaves the body through the skin even when not visibly sweating</note>—may be replaced. By this reasoning, both of those losses are reduced back to their original balance.

<margin>Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, Book I, ch. 2.</margin>
Finally, regarding **Excrements**, we say with Galen that since eating and drinking are necessary for animals, it follows that the generation of waste products must occur. This being the case, it must be believed that provident Nature ordained suitable Organs in the animal for the purpose of secreting such waste. She did not forget to adorn these organs with gifts destined for such a duty: namely, **Faculties** by which the waste products are driven along. For some of these faculties draw the waste to themselves through straight fibers; some transmit and retain it by means of oblique fibers; and some expel the waste by the force of transverse fibers. There is also an expulsion of waste through the pores of the skin and through the urine.

By these faculties, therefore, the body is continually cleansed of waste, and in this manner, it is preserved for a long time in its accustomed health.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Concerning certain Medications that preserve Health: and first, concerning purgatives.*

According to the consensus of all the Sages, the protection of Health consists not only in the proper observation of fullness and emptiness, sleep and waking, motion and Rest, but also in the matters of dissolution or retention. For Health consists not only in the consumption of food and drink, but also in the moderate evacuation and excretion of **superfluities** <note>Waste products or excess humors that the body cannot use.</note>. We shall, therefore, deal briefly here with this last method of protecting Health.

There are many circumstances occurring in the human body by which we may be moved toward the evacuation of the Belly, or the retention of waste that is flowing too freely. For if we observe old age, we will perceive that in it the **natural heat** is weak, and the passages of the body are narrower than in Youth due to the dominance of cold. Hence it is that raw and **phlegmatic** superfluities increase and congeal more and more within it every day. By the multitude of these, the native heat is gradually extinguished, digestion is dulled, and the stomach is weakened by the cold disposition of the excess material. In this case, the frequent evacuation of these superfluities is very appropriate; for in this way nature is helped and harmed as little as possible. But it should be noted in passing that the purging of such superfluities should be done with gentle or **diminishing** medications, and not robust or **eradicating** ones; for eradicating and robust medicines, insofar as they pluck the humors from the Center of the body, lead out the good along with the bad, and consequently tend to weaken the strengths of the body too much.

In **bilious** and **Melancholic** bodies, the Belly tends to be constricted because of the dryness of those humors; and indeed, people of this sort, having a bound-up bowel, tend to fall into many infirmities. Specifically, the Bilious fall into fevers and hot imbalances; the Melancholic very often fall into **hypochondriac winds** <note>Vapors or gas originating in the upper abdomen, thought to affect the mind.</note> that violently strike the diaphragm, and into fantastic imaginations of the Brain. Similarly, **Phlegmatic** persons, being swollen with excess phlegm, require a light purging to evacuate useless humors. And so it is with the rest.

In these cases, therefore, sweetly soothing remedies are to be embraced and chosen. And since a question is very often raised regarding the formula of a purgative Medicine (for others...

# On the Elementary Method of Maintaining Health

(for some people favor these, while others favor those) we therefore advise that medicine be stored and compounded in various forms: namely, in the form of pills, or an **Electuary** <term>a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term>, or a Syrup, or a Tablet, or a broth or soup, or an ale or beer, or a potion.

Where, therefore, the belly is packed with excessive dryness, there pills—on account of the aridity of their composition—are not so suitable; rather, they are better for those who swell with superfluous moisture. And yet, for those of a Melancholic temperament, the **Mastic Pills of Fernel** <note>original: *Pillulæ Mastichinæ Ferneli*; Jean Fernel was a famous 16th-century French physician. Mastic is a resin used to aid digestion</note> are praised: they should be taken for a full or half hour before Dinner. Thus, the pill is cast into the bottom of the stomach at one time and then covered by food afterward, so that immediately before it acts during the time of digestion, it may soften and dissolve the waste in the bowels. It should, however, work slowly, so that a healthy person is not disturbed during the night or while sleeping. I have a thousand times prescribed such a pill, imbued with oil of thyme, to be administered at the aforementioned time in the cases cited, and with quite a happy success. But above all others (to speak truly and freely), I praise the **Blessed Pill** (*Pillula Benedicta*) invented by us, the composition of which we shall set forth (God willing) in the chapter **On Antimony** in the *following Volume*. For its nature is such that it is taken in a small quantity—namely, seven grains—and once taken, it purges gently, without offense, and in a natural manner; it strengthens the stomach, opens the obstructed passages to the liver, tempers a liver that is too hot, and if it inclines toward coldness, it rouses it to its duty by strengthening its action. In all my practice, certainly, I have not found an equal to this pill.

### *Among the gently purging Electuaries, we praise this one:*

*Take: **Bayer’s Electuary of Prunes with Costus** <note>original: *Diapruni Cariicostini Bayeri*; a standard laxative recipe of the period</note>, Preserve of Damascus roses, 1 ounce of each. Let them be mixed faithfully.*

*The dose of this for loosening the Belly will be from 1 **drachm** <term>approx. 3.9 grams</term> to 2 drachms in the morning. And if on the first day it does not make the bowels slippery, let it be used again the next day, in either the same or a larger quantity. This is said to comfort the stomach, help the liver, and benefit the heart.*

In the form of a **Tablet** <note>original: *Tabula*; a lozenge or medicinal candy</note> also, made from sugar with suitable cordials, I have administered 9 or 10 grains of **our Mineral Manna** (which we shall reveal in the chapter **on Mercury** in the *following Volume*) without any loathing during the taking of it, or any disturbance in its operation, and that in the morning time, with happy success. For it relaxes the belly, kills worms, stops itching, and is of benefit to those suffering from **Gonorrhea** <note>in this period, this often referred to any genital discharge</note> and **white menses** <note>original: *menstruis albis*; likely leukorrhea</note>, etc.

There are also other medicines that alter the body and strengthen the stomach, and dispel gas: among which I shall describe one in this place, which I have advised to be given after food in the form of a powder to those who have weak digestion and feel vapors ascending to the head after eating.

->*Its preparation is as follows:*<-

*Take: **Biscotto** <note>twice-baked bread or sea biscuit</note> 2 ounces. Prepared Coriander half an ounce. Gizzard of a rooster dried in an oven 1 drachm. Cloves, Cinnamon, Red rose leaves, White sandalwood, 2 drachms of each. Sugar, triple the amount of all other ingredients.*

*Let them be mixed and diligently powdered, and passed through a fine sieve, and kept in a suitable box for use. One spoonful of this powder is to be taken immediately after any meal and held in the mouth for a little while, so that it may gradually liquefy and dissolve. And so (with the assistance of the Divine Will) you have the Universal Mystery of Health, or the **Quadrangular Bulwark of Health**, described according to the meager powers of our intellect. Concerning the encampment of the **Cardinal diseases** <note>the major, "hinge" diseases that govern health</note> and their violent eruption from the four corners of the world into our Bulwark, or their invasion of human health, we have proposed to speak at length in the following Treatise.*

<meta>This page serves as the title page for a polemical work by Robert Fludd. The tone shifts from pedagogical to confrontational.</meta>

### THE CONTEST OF WISDOM AGAINST FOLLY,
<note>original: "Sophiae cum Moria Certamen"; Sophia is the Greek personification of Wisdom, while Moria is Folly.</note>
#### In which,
# THE TOUCHSTONE REJECTED 
<note>original: "Lapis Lydius"; a Lydian stone used to test the purity of gold, here used metaphorically for a test of truth.</note>
# BY THE FALSE BUILDER, 
# BROTHER MARIN MERSENNE, A MONK,
## accurately examines the fictions of his most celebrated Babylonian Volume (on Genesis).
<note>Mersenne’s "Quaestiones Celeberrimae in Genesim" (1623) was a massive commentary on the Book of Genesis that included a famous and stinging attack on Fludd and other "Hermetic" philosophers, accusing them of magic and heresy.</note>

---

<margin>
Namely, he who in that work—blinded by Self-love—believed he could acquire for himself the title of the greatest and only Wise Man in the whole world,
</margin>

<margin>
by falsely branding Men of the greatest Fame and those to be preferred for their long-standing learning with the mark of either Atheism, Blasphemy, Heresy, Black Magic, Ignorance, or Stultitude.
</margin>

## By the Author Robert Fludd, also known as "of the Floods," Esquire and Doctor of Medicine of Oxford: Who, by the slanders and insults cast upon him by the Sycophant Mersenne, is stirred up to this work, contrary to the peaceful disposition of his own nature.

#### Isaiah 5:20-21.

> Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter! Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
